1.pericope_label: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect sojourners of the dispersion

schools.summary: Gill says the writer describes himself first by his name, Peter, the same with Cephas, which signifies a rock or stone, a name given him by Christ at his first conversion and which respected his after firmness, solidity, resolution and constancy, for his former name was Simeon or Simon. He further describes himself by his office, an apostle of Jesus Christ, Gill says, being one of the twelve and the first of that number, who saw Christ in the flesh, was conversant with him, had his call and commission immediately from him, and was qualified by him to preach the Gospel, being sent out first into Judea and then into all the world, with a power of working miracles to confirm it; and this character he mentions in order to give the greater weight and authority to his epistle. It is to be observed, Gill adds, that he does not style himself, as his pretended successor does, the head of the church and Christ's vicar on earth, nor does he call himself the prince of the apostles, but only an apostle. Calvin says that what in this salutation is the same with those of Paul requires no new explanation, and that though Peter adds a word Paul leaves out, the meaning is the same, for Paul did not wish the faithful the beginning of grace and peace but the increase of them, that God would complete what he had begun. It may be asked, Calvin says, how the election of these could be found out, for the election of God is hid and cannot be known without the special revelation of the Spirit, and as every one is made sure of his own election by the testimony of the Spirit, so he can know nothing certain of others. To this he answers that we are not curiously to inquire about the election of our brethren, but ought on the contrary to regard their calling, so that all who are admitted by faith into the church are to be counted as the elect, for God thus separates them from the world, which is a sign of election. It is no objection to say that many fall away, having nothing but the semblance, Calvin says, for it is the judgment of charity and not of faith when we deem all those elect in whom appears the mark of God's adoption; and that Peter does not fetch their election from the hidden counsel of God but gathers it from the effect is evident from the context, since as far as they proved that they were regenerated by the Spirit of God, so far did he deem them the elect of God, for God does not sanctify any but those whom he has previously elected. At the same time Peter reminds us whence that election flows, Calvin says, for God knew before the world was created whom he had elected for salvation; but we ought wisely to consider what this foreknowledge is, for the sophists, in order to obscure the grace of God, imagine that the merits of each are foreseen by God, and that thus the reprobate are distinguished from the elect, as every one proves himself worthy of this or that lot. But Scripture everywhere sets the counsel of God, on which is founded our salvation, in opposition to our merits, Calvin says; hence, when Peter calls them elect according to the foreknowledge of God, he intimates that the cause of it depends on nothing else but on God alone, who of his own free will has chosen us, so that the foreknowledge of God excludes every worthiness on the part of man.

Matthew Henry says that in this inscription we have three parts, and first the author of it described by his name, Peter, his first name having been Simon, and Jesus Christ having given him the surname of Peter, which signifies a rock, as a commendation of his faith and to denote that he should be an eminent pillar in the church of God. Secondly he is described by his office, an apostle of Jesus Christ, Henry says: the word signifies one sent, a legate, a messenger, any one sent in Christ's name and about his work, but more strictly it signifies the highest office in the Christian church, since God hath set some in the church, first apostles. Their dignity and pre-eminence lay in these things, Henry says: they were immediately chosen by Christ himself; they were first witnesses and then preachers of the resurrection of Christ, and so of the entire gospel dispensation; their gifts were excellent and extraordinary; and they had a power of working miracles.

Albert Barnes says the first epistle of Peter has never been doubted to be the production of the apostle of that name, the unvarying testimony of history and the uniform belief of the church ascribing it to him, and indeed there is no ancient writing whatever of which there is more certainty in regard to the authorship. The history of Peter is so fully detailed in the New Testament, Barnes says, that it is not necessary to go into any extended statement of his biography in order to an exposition of his epistles, and he refers those who wish fuller information to Lardner, Koppe and Bacon's Lives of the Apostles. There are questions, however, which it is important to consider, and the first is who the persons were to whom the epistle was addressed. It purports to have been addressed to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, all provinces of Asia Minor, so that there is no difficulty about the places where they resided; the only question is who they were who are thus designated as strangers scattered abroad, or strangers of the dispersion, and in regard to this various opinions have been held. The first is that they were native-born Jews who had been converted to the Christian faith, Barnes says, and of this opinion were Eusebius, Jerome, Grotius, Beza, Mill and Cave, the principal argument being the appellation given to them and what is said later in the epistle, which it is supposed is language that would be applied only to those of Hebrew extraction. A second opinion has been that the persons to whom it was sent were all of Gentile origin, Barnes continues, and of this opinion were Procopius, Cassiodorus and, more recently, Wetstein, this belief being founded chiefly on other passages in the letter. Charles Ellicott says the authoritative tone of this Epistle is shown at the outset, for the writer assumes his full titles: not, as in the Second Epistle, his merely human name of Simeon, nor his humble capacity of servant, but the Rock-name which Christ had given him, and the official dignity of an Apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, one charged with full legatine authority from Christ, a vicar of Christ to the Church and not only a representative of the Church to Godwards. Observe also, Ellicott says, that while St Paul constantly adds by the will of God, or some similar phrase, by way of justifying his assumption of the title, St Peter has no need to do more than mention it, his claim never having been questioned; and again, though St Silas and St Mark are with him they are not associated in the initial greeting as they would probably have been by St Paul, for Silas's support would have added but little weight to the utterances of the Rock-Apostle. And yet, with all this quiet assumption of dignity, Ellicott says, St Peter knows no higher title to bestow on himself than that which he held in common with the other eleven, an Apostle, not the Apostle, nor bishop of bishops, nor, which means the same thing, servant of servants. The address is literally, to the elect, sojourners of the dispersion of Pontus, Ellicott says, and the persons for whom the letter is destined are very clearly specified: in John we have the dispersion of the Greeks, where it clearly means those of the dispersed Jews who live among the Greeks, so here the dispersion of Pontus will mean those of the dispersed Jews who live in Pontus; in James the same word is used, and in fact it seems to have been the recognised name for all Jews who did not live in Palestine. The word rendered by sojourners means people who are resident for a time among strangers, Ellicott says: it might, for instance, describe English people who have taken houses in Paris without becoming naturalised, and as it is here in so close a connection with geographical words it seems forced to interpret it metaphorically, since Palestine, not Heaven, is the home tacitly contrasted, and Pontus, not earth, is the place of sojourn. A.T. Robertson says Peter is the Greek form for the Aramaic Cephas, the nickname given Simon by Jesus when he first saw him and reaffirmed in the Greek form on his great confession, with an allusion to another form of the word for a rock, ledge or cliff; in the second epistle we have both Simon and Peter. Paul in his epistles always terms himself Paul and not Saul, Robertson says, and so Peter uses this name, not Cephas or Simon, because he is writing to Christians scattered over Asia Minor; the nominative absolute occurs here as in James, but without the usual greeting word so common in the papyri. An apostle of Jesus Christ is his official title, Robertson says, but in the second epistle slave is added, which occurs alone in James; in the second and third letters of John we have only the elder, as Peter terms himself fellow-elder in the fifth chapter here. Paul's usage varies greatly, Robertson observes: only the names in the two Thessalonian letters; the title apostle added and defended in Galatians and Romans, as also in the Corinthian letters and Colossians and Ephesians and second Timothy with by the will of God added, and in first Timothy with the addition of according to the command of God; in Philippians only slave of Christ Jesus, like James and Jude; in Romans and Titus both slave and apostle, like second Peter; while in Philemon he uses only prisoner of Jesus Christ. To the elect stands without the article and in the dative case, Robertson says, that is, to elect persons viewed as a group, though Bigg takes the word as an adjective describing the next, to elect sojourners, which is possible; and he recalls the distinction between the called and the chosen. Who are sojourners is a late double compound adjective meaning strangers sojourning for a while in a particular place, found in Polybius and the papyri, twice in the Septuagint and in the New Testament only here, in the second chapter and in Hebrews; the picture in the metaphor, Robertson says, is that heaven is our native country and we are only temporary sojourners here on earth.

Adam Clarke prefixes to the epistle a long account of the apostle and his readers, extracting what makes for his purpose from Dr Lardner and Professor Michaelis, and quoting Cave that the land of Palestine at and before the coming of our blessed Saviour was distinguished into three provinces, Judea, Samaria and Galilee. In the upper, called also Galilee of the Gentiles, within the division belonging to the tribe of Naphtali, stood Bethsaida, Clarke reports, formerly an obscure and inconsiderable village till lately re-edified and enlarged by Philip the Tetrarch, and in honour of Julia, daughter of Augustus, called by him Julias; it was situated upon the banks of the sea of Galilee, called also the lake of Tiberias and the lake of Gennesareth, and had a wilderness on the other side called the desert of Bethsaida, whither our Saviour used often to retire. At this place was born Simon, surnamed Cephas or Peter, signifying a stone or fragment of a rock, Clarke says, and he was a fisherman upon that lake. John Wesley says the sojourners are such upon earth, the Christians, chiefly those of Jewish extraction, and that scattered means long ago driven out of their own land, those scattered by the persecution mentioned in the Acts having been scattered only through Judea and Samaria, though afterwards some of them travelled to Phenice, Cyprus and Antioch. He names these five provinces in the order wherein they occurred to him, writing from the east, Wesley says, all these countries lying in the Lesser Asia; and the Asia here distinguished from the other provinces is that which was usually called the Proconsular Asia, being a Roman province.

debates: Who the readers were: Barnes catalogues the parties, native-born Jews converted on the authority of Eusebius, Jerome, Grotius, Beza, Mill and Cave, and Gentiles throughout on that of Procopius, Cassiodorus and Wetstein; Ellicott decides for dispersed Jews and holds that Palestine, not heaven, is the home tacitly contrasted, and Pontus, not earth, the place of sojourn; Wesley agrees they were chiefly of Jewish extraction; Robertson takes the metaphor the other way, that heaven is our native country and we are only temporary sojourners here

What the title an apostle implies and refuses: Gill notes that Peter does not style himself head of the church or Christ's vicar on earth, as his pretended successor does, nor prince of the apostles; Ellicott says the same of the article, that he claims to be an Apostle and not the Apostle, neither bishop of bishops nor servant of servants, though he has himself just described the office as a vicarship of Christ to the Church

How the elect could be known: Calvin holds that election is hidden and that we are not curiously to inquire into our brethren's, but to regard their calling and count as elect all admitted by faith into the church, this being the judgment of charity and not of faith; Robertson keeps to the grammar, that the word stands without the article, and reports Bigg's proposal to read it adjectivally as elect sojourners

What the foreknowledge of God means: Calvin denies that it can look to foreseen merits, since the sophists imagine so only to obscure the grace of God, and Scripture everywhere sets the divine counsel against our merits, so that foreknowledge excludes every worthiness on the part of man
outliers: Barnes's judgement that there is no ancient writing whatever of which there is more certainty in regard to the authorship
Clarke's account of Bethsaida, an inconsiderable village until Philip the Tetrarch rebuilt it and named it Julias for the daughter of Augustus
Ellicott's illustration of the word for sojourners as describing English people who have taken houses in Paris without becoming naturalised
Ellicott's remark that Silas's support would have added but little weight to the utterances of the Rock-Apostle
Robertson's survey of how Paul varies his self-designation from letter to letter, from bare names to slave, apostle, or prisoner
Wesley's note that the five provinces are named in the order in which they occurred to a writer working from the east

2.pericope_label: Elect according to the foreknowledge of God, through sanctification of the Spirit

schools.summary: Gill says that elect here is not to any office, as to that of bishops or presbyters, for though the apostle writes to some of them under this character, yet not all; nor were they so called as a nation, for they were persons scattered about in several countries; nor as a church, for they are not written to as such; nor does this character merely design their effectual calling, though as that is a fruit and evidence of election it is sometimes so styled, and the saints called by grace are said to be chosen. It intends, Gill says, the eternal election of those persons both to grace and glory, which the apostle knew of not by divine revelation or any particular discovery made to him, but which he concluded in a judgment of charity, they being all under a profession of faith in Christ, and he having reason to believe that the greater part of them were truly partakers of that faith which demonstrated them to be the elect of God. The cause, spring and source of their election was the foreknowledge of God the Father, Gill adds, to whom election is commonly ascribed.

Albert Barnes says we become in fact the chosen or elect of God by a work of the Spirit on our hearts making us holy, that is, renewing us in the Divine image: we are chosen by the Father, but it is necessary that the heart should be renewed and made holy by a work of grace in order that we may actually become his chosen people. Though we are sinners he proposes to save us, Barnes says, but we are not saved in our sins, nor can we regard ourselves as the children of God until we have evidence that we are born again; the purpose of God to save us found us unholy, and we become in fact his friends by being renewed in the temper of our mind. A man has reason to think that he is one of the elect of God, Barnes says, just so far as he has evidence that he has been renewed by the Holy Spirit, and so far as he has holiness of heart and life, and no farther. Unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ expresses the design for which they had been chosen by the Father and renewed by the Spirit, that they might obey God and lead holy lives; and the sprinkling means cleansing from sin, or holiness, since it was by the sprinkling of that blood that they were to be made holy. From this verse we may learn that they who are chosen should be holy, Barnes says: just in proportion as they have evidence that God has chosen them at all, they have evidence that he has chosen them to be holy, and in fact all the evidence which any man can have that he is among the elect is that he is practically a holy man and desires to become more so. No man can penetrate the secret counsels of the Almighty, Barnes says; no one can go up to heaven and inspect the book of life to see if his name be there; no one should presume that his name is there without evidence, nor depend on dreams or raptures or visions as proof, nor expect a new revelation declaring him among the elect; all the proof any man can have is to be found in the evidences of personal piety, and any man who is willing to be a true Christian may have all that evidence in his own case. If any one wishes to settle the question whether he is among the elect or not, Barnes says, the way is plain: let him become a true Christian, and the whole matter is determined, for that is all the proof anyone has that he is chosen to salvation; and till a man is willing to do that he should not complain of the doctrine of election, for if he is not willing to become a Christian and to be saved, assuredly he should not complain that those who are think they have evidence that they are the chosen of God. Charles Ellicott says elect means a true chosen people, and that this word marks them off from the rest of the Jewish settlers in those parts; it is an evasion of the difficulty to say that they were elect only in the mass, as a body, for the election was individual and personal, God selecting these particular Hebrews out of the whole number and making them Christians. But what he elected them to is abundantly shown in the next words, Ellicott says: for all their election they are not certain of salvation, and their title of elect implies no more than the fact that God has put them into the visible Church. The origin of this election, the aim, and the means employed are now touched upon and connected with the three Divine Persons respectively, Ellicott says. As to the origin, their election is not accidental, nor something done on the spur of the moment, an afterthought of God, but according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, that is, in execution of his fore-arranged scheme, the word implying not simply a perception of the future but the forming of a decision; and though the thought is common also to St Paul, St Peter was familiar with it before St Paul's conversion. As to the means, Ellicott continues, the preconcerted scheme of God embraced not only the choice of these particular persons for a blessing but the lines on which the choice was to work itself out, in a course of sanctification by the Spirit, the words and the thought being identical with those of the second letter to the Thessalonians, though probably differing so far in exact meaning that there the Spirit is the spirit sanctified and here the Spirit which sanctifies; we see that even the blessing of obedience and sprinkling, much more that of glory hereafter, is unattainable except in the path of sanctification. As to the end, Ellicott says, that to which God had elected them was not in the first instance the participation of the joys of the post-resurrection life, but the benefits of redemption on this side of the grave. A.T. Robertson says the preposition is probably to be connected with the word for elect rather than with apostle, in spite of a rather loose arrangement of words and the absence of articles in these two verses. Foreknowledge is a late substantive found in Plutarch and Lucian and the papyri, from a verb meaning to know beforehand, and occurring only twice in the New Testament, here and in Peter's sermon in the Acts; in this epistle Peter often uses substantives rather than verbs. Peter here presents the Trinity, Robertson says, God the Father, the Spirit and Jesus Christ; and in sanctification of the Spirit clearly means the Holy Spirit, though the phrase is without the article, the genitive being subjective, sanctification wrought by the Spirit. Unto obedience means obedience to the Lord Jesus, the result of the sanctification, Robertson says; and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ is a late substantive from a verb meaning to sprinkle, a word used in the Greek Old Testament of the sacrifices but not in any non-biblical source so far as known, occurring in the New Testament only here and in Hebrews. The reference is to the death of Christ on the Cross and to the ratification of the New Covenant by his blood, Robertson says, with allusion to Exodus; Paul does not mention this ritual use of the blood of Christ, but Jesus does, so it is not surprising to find the use of it by Peter and the author of Hebrews. Hort suggests that Peter may also have an ulterior reference to the blood of the martyrs, Robertson notes, but only as illustration of what Jesus did for us, not as having any value; and Bigg says the whole epistle is a commentary upon the three phrases of this verse. Peter is not ashamed of the blood of Christ, Robertson concludes.

Adam Clarke says that if the apostle had directed his letter to persons elected to eternal life, no one, as Doctors Lardner and Macknight properly argue, could have received such a letter, because no one could have been sure of his election in this way till he had arrived in heaven. But the persons to whom the apostle wrote were all, with propriety, said to be elect according to the foreknowledge of God, Clarke says, because, agreeably to the original purpose of God discovered in the prophetical writings, Jews and Gentiles indiscriminately were called to be the visible Church and entitled to all the privileges of the people of God on their believing the Gospel; and in this sense the word elected is used in other places of Scripture. Clarke then says that the Rev. J. Wesley has an excellent note on this passage, which he will transcribe for the benefit of those of his readers who may not have his works at hand, and copies it out entire. John Wesley says that, speaking after the manner of men, strictly there is no foreknowledge, no more than afterknowledge, with God, but all things are known to him as present from eternity to eternity, so that this is no other than an instance of the divine condescension to our low capacities. Elect means, by the free love and almighty power of God, taken out of and separated from the world, Wesley says; election in the scripture sense is God's doing anything that our merit or power have no part in. The true predestination or fore-appointment of God is this, Wesley says: that he who believeth shall be saved from the guilt and power of sin; that he who endureth to the end shall be saved eternally; and that they who receive the precious gift of faith thereby become the sons of God, and, being sons, shall receive the Spirit of holiness to walk as Christ also walked. Throughout every part of this appointment of God promise and duty go hand in hand, Wesley says: all is free gift, and yet such is the gift that the final issue depends on our future obedience to the heavenly call; but other predestination than this, either to life or death eternal, the scripture knows not of. Moreover, Wesley continues, it is cruel respect of persons, an unjust regard of one and an unjust disregard of another, mere creature partiality and not infinite justice; it is not plain scripture doctrine, if true, but rather inconsistent with the express written word, which speaks of God's universal offers of grace, his invitations, promises and threatenings being all general; we are bid to choose life, and reprehended for not doing it; it is inconsistent with a state of probation in those that must be saved or must be lost; and it is of fatal consequence, all men being ready on very slight grounds to fancy themselves of the elect number. But the doctrine of predestination is entirely changed from what it formerly was, Wesley adds: now it implies neither faith, peace nor purity, being something that will do without them all; faith is no longer a divine evidence of things not seen wrought in the soul by the immediate power of the Holy Ghost, but a mere notion; neither is faith made any longer a means of holiness, but something that will do without it.

debates: How far the word elect reaches: Gill takes it of eternal election both to grace and glory, known to the apostle only by a judgment of charity; Barnes grants the election but confines the evidence to holiness of heart and life, and no farther, since no one can go up to heaven and inspect the book of life; Ellicott calls it individual and personal, refusing the evasion that they were elect only in the mass, yet holds that it implies no more than admission to the visible Church and leaves them uncertain of salvation; Clarke restricts it to the visible Church outright

Whether a letter could be addressed to the eternally elect at all: Clarke argues with Lardner and Macknight that no one could have received such a letter, since no one could be sure of his election in that way till he had arrived in heaven; Gill answers the same difficulty by making the apostle's confidence a judgment of charity, and Barnes by making the evidence wholly practical

What foreknowledge means: Wesley denies it in the strict sense, since with God there is no more foreknowledge than afterknowledge, all things being known as present from eternity to eternity, and calls the word a condescension to our low capacities; Ellicott says it implies not simply a perception of the future but the forming of a decision; Robertson notes it is a late substantive found in the New Testament only here and in Peter's own sermon

What predestination properly is: Wesley reduces it to three propositions about believing, enduring and receiving the Spirit, in which promise and duty go hand in hand, and charges any other with being cruel respect of persons, contrary to the universal offers of grace, destructive of probation, and of fatal consequence; Gill and Barnes both retain an eternal decree, differing only over how its presence may be known
outliers: Clarke's transcription in full of a fellow commentator's note, whose own block stands further down the same catena, for readers who may not have his works at hand
Barnes's warning that no one should depend on dreams, raptures or visions as proof of election, nor expect a new revelation declaring him among the elect
Barnes's retort that a man unwilling to become a Christian should not complain that those who are think they have evidence of being chosen
Wesley's charge that the doctrine of predestination is entirely changed from what it formerly was, now implying neither faith, peace nor purity
Bigg's judgement, reported by Robertson, that the whole epistle is a commentary upon the three phrases of this verse
Hort's suggestion, reported by Robertson, of an ulterior reference to the blood of the martyrs, though only as illustration

3.pericope_label: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who begat us again unto a living hope

schools.summary: John Gill says the epistle begins with thanksgiving to God, or an ascription of blessing, praise and glory to him, for this does not mean an invoking or conferring a blessing on him, neither of which can be, since there is not a greater than he to be invoked, nor can anything be added to his blessedness; but God may be blessed by his creatures when they speak well of him and his wonderful works of creation, providence and grace, when they ascribe all their mercies, spiritual and temporal, to him, give him the glory of them, and express their thanks in heart, lip and life; and such a blessing of God for a special and spiritual favour, the grace of regeneration, is intended here. By God is meant, Gill says, not God essentially but personally considered, even God the Father, as is clearly expressed, the words being rendered in the Arabic and Ethiopic versions without the copulative and, thus, blessed be God the Father; and if that is retained they may be rendered blessed be God, even the Father. John Calvin says the main object of the epistle is to raise us above the world in order that we may be prepared and encouraged to sustain the spiritual contests of our warfare, and that for this end the knowledge of God's benefits avails much, for when their value appears to us all other things will be deemed worthless, especially when we consider what Christ and his blessings are, since everything without him is but dross. For this reason he highly extols the wonderful grace of God in Christ, Calvin says, that we may not deem it much to give up the world in order to enjoy the invaluable treasure of a future life, and that we may not be broken down by present troubles but patiently endure them, being satisfied with eternal happiness; and when he gives thanks to God he invites the faithful to spiritual joy, which can swallow up all the opposite feelings of the flesh. As formerly, by calling himself the God of Abraham, God designed to mark the difference between himself and all fictitious gods, so after he has manifested himself in his own Son his will is not to be known otherwise than in him, Calvin says; hence they who form their ideas of God in his naked majesty apart from Christ have an idol instead of the true God, as the case is with the Jews and the Turks, and whosoever seeks really to know the only true God must regard him as the Father of Christ, for whenever our mind seeks God, except Christ be thought of, it will wander and be confused until it be wholly lost. Peter meant at the same time to intimate how God is so bountiful and kind towards us, Calvin says, for except Christ stood as the middle person his goodness could never be really known by us. He shows that supernatural life is a gift, because we are born the children of wrath, for had we been born to the hope of life according to the flesh there would have been no necessity of being begotten again by God; therefore Peter teaches us that we who are by nature destined to eternal death are restored to life by God's mercy, and this is, as it were, our second creation. He first mentions the efficient cause and then points out the mediating cause, Calvin says: he shows that God was induced by no merits of ours to regenerate us unto a living hope, because he assigns this wholly to his mercy; and that he might more completely reduce the merits of works to nothing, he commends mercy alone, for all indeed confess that God is the only author of our salvation but they afterwards invent extraneous causes which take away so much from his mercy. That Christ's death is not mentioned but his resurrection involves no inconsistency, Calvin says, for it is included, because a thing cannot be completed without having a beginning, and he especially brought forward the resurrection because he was speaking of a new life. The editorial matter printed within Calvin's block dissents, saying that the begetting again seems not to refer to inward renovation but to what God did by raising Christ from the dead, since to beget sometimes means to put one in a new state or condition, as the expression this day have I begotten thee means that God had then constituted his Son a king and publicly invested him with that office; similar is the meaning here, that God through the resurrection of Christ restored to the hope of life his desponding followers, which it says is the import of the word again, though another authority is cited as referring it to the covenant of grace made with our first parents after the fall.

Matthew Henry says we come now to the body of the epistle, which begins with a congratulation of the dignity and happiness of the state of these believers, brought in under the form of a thanksgiving to God, as other epistles begin in like manner. Here we have the duty performed, which is blessing God, Henry says, and a man blesses God by a just acknowledgment of his excellency and blessedness; and the object of this blessing described by his relation to Jesus Christ, where three names of one person denote his threefold office, Lord as a universal king or sovereign, Jesus as a priest or Saviour, and Christ as a prophet anointed with the Spirit and furnished with all gifts necessary for the instruction, guidance and salvation of his church. This God, so blessed, is the God of Christ according to his human nature and his Father according to his divine nature, Henry says. The reasons that oblige us to this duty are comprised in his abundant mercy, since all our blessings are owing to God's mercy and not to man's merit, particularly regeneration; and this deserves our thanksgiving especially if we consider the fruit it produces in us, which is that excellent grace of hope, and not such a vain, dead, perishing hope as that of worldlings and hypocrites, but a lively hope, a living, strong, quickening and durable hope, as that hope must needs be that has such a solid foundation as the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Henry draws the lessons: a good Christian's condition is never so bad but he has great reason still to bless God, for as a sinner has always reason to mourn notwithstanding his present prosperity, so good people in the midst of their manifold difficulties have reason still to rejoice; in our prayers and praises we should address God as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, since it is only through him that we and our services are accepted; the best of men owe their best blessings to the abundant mercy of God, for all the evil in the world is from man's sin but all the good in it is from God's mercy; regeneration produces a lively hope of eternal life, every unconverted person being a hopeless creature whose pretences of that kind are all confidence and presumption; the hope of a Christian is a living hope that keeps him alive, quickens him, supports him and conducts him to heaven, invigorating the soul to action, patience, fortitude and perseverance to the end, whereas the hypocrite and his hope expire and die both together; and the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead is the ground or foundation of a Christian's hope, being the act of the Father as a Judge and of the Son as a conqueror, demonstrating that the Father accepts his death in full discharge for our ransom and that he is victorious over death, the grave and all our spiritual enemies, and being also an assurance of our own resurrection, since there is an inseparable union between Christ and his flock and they rise by virtue of his resurrection as a head rather than by virtue of his power as a Judge.

Albert Barnes says the idea is that there was great mercy shown them in the fact that they were renewed, since they had no claim to the favour and the favour was great, men not being begotten to the hope of heaven because they have any claim on God or because it would not be right for him to withhold the favour. The meaning of the phrase is that as God is the Author of our life in a natural sense, so he is the Author of our second life by regeneration, Barnes says: the Saviour said that except a man be born again, or begotten again, he cannot see the kingdom of God, and Peter here affirms that that change had occurred in regard to himself and those he was addressing. The word used here as a compound does not elsewhere occur in the New Testament, Barnes notes, though it corresponds entirely with the words used by the Saviour, and perhaps the phrase begotten again would be better in each instance where the word occurs, the sense being rather that of being begotten again than of being born again. The word lively we now use commonly in the sense of active, animated, quick, Barnes says, but the word here used means living in contradistinction from that which is dead: the hope they had had living power, it was not cold, inoperative, dead, not a mere form or a mere speculation or a mere sentiment, but that which was vital to their welfare and which was active and powerful. The resurrection of the Lord Jesus is the foundation of our hope, Barnes says, being a confirmation of what he declared as truth when he lived, a proof of the doctrine of the immortality of the soul, and a pledge that all who are united to him will be raised up. Charles Ellicott says blessed is a form consecrated to God alone, a completely different word from the blessed or happy of the Beatitudes, and differing from the blessed of the Virgin Mary in that this form implies that blessing is always due on account of something inherent in the person while that only implies that a blessing has been received; and the idea of blessing God, literally speaking him well, is of course wholly Hebrew. He is no longer only the Lord God of Israel, Ellicott says, but is now in a nearer, tenderer relation to these members of the new covenant, the Father of the Messiah and yet the God whom Jesus adores. The word according never means exactly the same as in or by, Ellicott says, and here rather shows that the particular instance was in keeping with what might have been expected, had we but known, from the much pity which God must have felt for creatures so forlorn, our regeneration being no sudden capricious favour. The rendering should be begat us again, Ellicott says, the historical moment being here given as that of the resurrection of Christ; and this great word, which is Peter's own and found again only later in the chapter, evidently contains the whole meaning of the being born from above or begotten all over again, of the fresh creation, of the regeneration of Titus, of the begotten of God in John's epistle, and to a certain extent of the brought he us forth of James. It seems to indicate that, if it takes effect, it makes a complete change not only in the condition and prospects of the man but in the man himself, Ellicott says, such a change as would pass over an animal if it were suddenly to receive the powers of a human being; and it is no metaphor when the change from the natural man to a man united with the Incarnate God is described as an act of creation parallel only to those of the creation of matter and force, the creation of life and the creation of humanity, for according to Peter's teaching we are thus actually made partakers of the divine nature. Before this regeneration there was nothing to look forward to, Ellicott says, at best a kind of dead-alive surmise that there might be something beyond the weary world, but as the animal we have imagined would find himself suddenly new-begotten into a state in which he was conscious of himself and of God, so we found ourselves new-begotten into a state of definite and most energetic expectation. Mystically speaking, the moment of our emergence into this new glow of expectation was that when the Messiah Jesus, who had been cut off, emerged from among the dead, Ellicott says; Peter indeed is speaking, so far as himself was concerned, not mystically but literally, as his history before and after the resurrection shows, for to him and to the other Apostles the resurrection was a regeneration and they became new beings, and to subsequent Christians precisely the same effect takes place when the fact of the resurrection is acknowledged and its significance realised. Yet we must not confine the meaning of the words to the effects of this conscious realisation, Ellicott insists, for Peter is viewing the transaction theologically, that is from God's point of view and not phenomenally from man's: he speaks of the begetting and not of the being born, of the resurrection itself and not of the preaching of the resurrection, and to God, with whom time does not exist, there is no interval between his begetting of Christ again from the dead and his begetting of us again thereby; in the mystery of our union with the Incarnate Word his historical resurrection did, through baptism, in some ineffable manner infuse into us the grace which makes new creatures of us. He quotes Archbishop Leighton as saying well that the resurrection is not only the exemplar but the efficient cause of our new birth. A.T. Robertson notes that there is no copula in the Greek and that the verbal adjective occurs in the New Testament only of God, as in the Greek Old Testament, the precise language of the whole phrase appearing also in the Corinthian and Ephesian letters and part of it elsewhere in Paul, with similar language used by Jesus himself. Begat us again is a first aorist active articular participle of a late and rare word, Robertson says, found in a manuscript reading, in Philo, in the Hermetic writings, and in the New Testament only here and later in the chapter; he quotes Bigg that it was probably borrowed by the New Paganism from Christianity, and notes that the Stoics used the cognate noun for the word rendered regeneration in Titus. Peter is fond of the word living, Robertson observes, using it repeatedly through this epistle: the Pharisees cherished the hope of the resurrection, but the resurrection of Jesus gave it proof and permanence, so that it is no longer a dead hope like the dead faith of James; this revival of hope was wrought by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and hope rose up with Christ from the dead, though the disciples, Peter included, were slow at first to believe it.

Adam Clarke says the connecting word is omitted by the Syriac, Erpen's Arabic and the Ethiopic, but that if we translate it even, a meaning which it frequently has in the New Testament, we have a very good sense: let that God have praise who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and who deserves the praise of every human being for his infinite mercy to the world in its redemption by Christ Jesus. Clarke thinks the apostle has a reference here to his own case and that of his fellow apostles at the time that Christ was taken by the Jews and put to death: previously they had strong confidence that he was the Messiah and that it was he who should redeem Israel, but when they found that he actually expired upon the cross and was buried they appear to have lost all hope of the great things which before they had in prospect, as is feelingly expressed by the two disciples whom our Lord after his resurrection overtook on the road going to Emmaus. The hope that with them died with their Master, and seemed to be buried in his grave, was restored by the certainty of his resurrection, Clarke says: from Christ's preaching and miracles they had a hope of eternal life and all other blessings promised by him; by his death and burial this hope became nearly if not altogether extinct; but by his resurrection the hope was revived, and this is very properly expressed here by being begotten again to a living hope. He notes that some manuscripts and versions read to the hope of life, which one copy of the Itala, with Augustine, Gildas, Vigilius of Tapsum and Cassiodorus, has considered as meaning eternal life agreeably to the context, and therefore they read of life eternal. The expressions, however, may include more particulars, Clarke says, since none can inherit eternal life except those who are children in the heavenly family, and none are children but those who are born again; then Peter may be considered as laying here the foundation of the hope of eternal life in the regeneration of the soul, for none can legally inherit but the children, and none are children of God till they are spiritually begotten and born again. It is the Gospel alone that gives the well grounded hope of eternal life, and the ground on which this hope rests is the resurrection of Christ himself, Clarke says: the certainty of our Lord's resurrection is the great seal of the Gospel, for without this what is vision, what is prophecy, what is promise, what are even miracles, to that unbelief which is natural to man on such a subject; but the resurrection of the human nature of Christ, the incontestable proofs of it, and the ascension of our nature to heaven in his person, are such evidences of the possibility and certainty of the thing as for ever to preclude all doubt from the hearts of those who believe in him. John Wesley says God is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect to his divine nature and his God with respect to his human. Who hath regenerated us to a living hope means a hope which implies true spiritual life, which revives the heart and makes the soul lively and vigorous, Wesley says; and the resurrection of Christ is not only a pledge of ours but a part of the purchase-price, having also a close connexion with our rising from spiritual death, that as he liveth so shall we live with him. He adds that Christ was acknowledged to be the Christ but usually called Jesus till his resurrection, and that then he was also called Christ.

debates: What the begetting again refers to: Clarke takes it of the apostles' own case, their hope dying with their Master and reviving with the certainty of the resurrection; Calvin takes it as a second creation of those born children of wrath and destined by nature to eternal death; the editorial matter inside Calvin's own block sides with Clarke, holding that it refers not to inward renovation but to God's act in raising Christ, since to beget can mean to put one in a new state; Ellicott rules the experiential reading out, since Peter speaks of the begetting and not of the being born, of the resurrection itself and not of the preaching of it

How the word should be rendered: Barnes judges that begotten again would be better than born again in every instance where the compound occurs, and Ellicott likewise prefers begat us again to the perfect, fixing the historical moment as the resurrection
Where the word came from: Robertson reports Bigg's view that the mystery religions probably borrowed it from Christianity rather than the reverse, and notes the Stoic use of the cognate noun

How God is both God and Father to Christ: Henry and Wesley answer alike, God according to his human nature and Father according to his divine, while Calvin turns the relation into a test, that those who conceive God in naked majesty apart from Christ have an idol instead
outliers: Ellicott's illustration of regeneration as the change that would pass over an animal suddenly receiving the powers of a human being
Ellicott's claim that the new birth is an act of creation parallel only to those of matter, of life and of humanity
Calvin's charge that those who seek God apart from Christ hold an idol, as he says is the case with the Jews and the Turks
Clarke's textual note that one copy of the Itala, with Augustine, Gildas, Vigilius of Tapsum and Cassiodorus, read the hope of life eternal
Henry's distinction that believers rise by virtue of Christ's resurrection as a head rather than by virtue of his power as a Judge
Robertson's remark that the disciples, Peter included, were slow at first to believe the hope that rose with Christ from the dead

4.pericope_label: An inheritance incorruptible, undefiled and unfading, reserved in heaven for those kept by the power of God

schools.summary: John Gill says the inheritance is a further explanation of the lively hope, or hope laid up in heaven, which regenerate ones are begotten to: it is an inheritance, a large estate and rich possession which they are born heirs apparent to, not to be got by industry or obtained by the works of the law, for they that are of the law are not heirs, but what is the pure bequest and free gift of God as a Father to his children; for an inheritance is proper and peculiar to children, nor does it belong to any but them, and it comes to them through the death of the testator, Christ, and of it the Holy Spirit is the pledge and earnest. Gill's block breaks off at this point in mid-sentence. On the following verse he says this is a description of the persons for whom the inheritance is reserved in heaven: they are not only chosen to salvation and begotten again to an inheritance but they are preserved unto it, their happiness is very great, their inheritance is safe in heaven for them, and they are kept below amidst a thousand snares and difficulties till they safely arrive at the possession of it. They are kept, Gill says, not in and by themselves, for the way of man is not in himself, nor in the hands of angels, for no such trust does God put in them, but in the hands of Jesus Christ where they are safe and out of which none can pluck them, on him as a foundation and in him as a strong hold; they are kept in the love of God and on his heart, from whence they can never be separated, and in the covenant of grace out of which they will never be put, and in a state of justification, and shall never enter into condemnation, and in the family of God, for being sons they are no more servants. John Calvin says the three words which follow are intended to amplify God's grace, for Peter had this object in view, to impress our minds thoroughly as to its excellency; and he deems the clause about the inheritance and the clause about salvation ready to be revealed as being in apposition, the latter explanatory of the former, since he expresses the same thing in two ways. Every word which follows is weighty, Calvin says: the inheritance is said to be preserved that we may know it is beyond the reach of danger, for were it not in God's hand it might be exposed to endless dangers, and if it were in this world how could we regard it as safe amidst so many changes; that he might then free us from every fear, he testifies that our salvation is placed in safety beyond the harms which Satan can do. But as the certainty of salvation can bring us little comfort except each one knows that it belongs to himself, Calvin says, Peter adds the words that follow, for consciences will calmly rest here, that is, when the Lord cries to them from heaven, Behold, your salvation is in my hand and is kept for you; and as salvation is not indiscriminately for all, he calls our attention to faith, that all who are endued with faith might be distinguished from the rest and might not doubt but that they are the true and legitimate heirs of God, for as faith penetrates into the heavens so also it appropriates to us the blessings which are in heaven. We are to notice the connection, Calvin says, when he says that we are kept while in the world and at the same time our inheritance is reserved in heaven, otherwise this thought would immediately creep in: what does it avail us that our salvation is laid up in heaven when we are tossed here and there in this world as in a turbulent sea, what can it avail us that our salvation is secured in a quiet harbour when we are driven to and fro amidst a thousand shipwrecks. The apostle therefore anticipates objections of this kind when he shows that though we are in the world exposed to dangers we are yet kept by faith, and that though we are thus nigh to death we are yet safe under the guardianship of faith; but as faith itself, through the infirmity of the flesh, often quails, we might be always anxious about the morrow were not the Lord to aid us. Under the Papacy a diabolical opinion prevails, Calvin says, that we ought to doubt our final perseverance because we are uncertain whether we shall be tomorrow in the same state of grace; but Peter did not thus leave us in suspense, for he testifies that we stand by the power of God, lest any doubt arising from a consciousness of our own infirmity should disquiet us. How weak soever we may then be, our salvation is not uncertain because it is sustained by God's power, Calvin says: as we are begotten by faith, so faith itself receives its stability from God's power, and hence is its security, not only for the present but also for the future. As we are by nature impatient of delay and soon succumb under weariness, he reminds us that salvation is not deferred because it is not yet prepared but because the time of its revelation is not yet come, a doctrine intended to nourish and sustain our hope; and salvation here means that of the body as well as of the soul at the resurrection. He calls it the day of judgment because the restitution of all things is not to be previously expected, the intervening time being still in progress, Calvin says: what is elsewhere called the last time is the whole period from the coming of Christ, so called from a comparison with the preceding ages, but Peter had regard to the end of the world.

Albert Barnes says that through the resurrection of the Lord Jesus we now cherish the hope of that future inheritance in heaven, Christians being regarded as the adopted children of God and heaven spoken of as their inheritance, what their Father will bestow on them as the proof of his love. Incorruptible means it will not fade away and vanish as that which we inherit in this world does, Barnes says: the inheritance will be imperishable or will endure for ever, for here, to whatever we may be heirs, we must soon part with the inheritance, while there it will be eternal. The word rendered undefiled does not elsewhere occur in the New Testament, Barnes notes, and as applied to an inheritance means that it will be pure: it will not have been obtained by dishonesty nor held by fraud, it will not be such as will corrupt the soul or tempt to extravagance, sensuality and lust as a rich inheritance often does here, but such that its eternal enjoyment will never tend in any manner to defile the heart. Here he quotes Benson, asking how many estates have been got by fraudulent and unjust methods, by poisoning or in some other way murdering the right heir, by cheating of helpless orphans, by ruining the fatherless and widows, by oppressing their neighbours or grinding the faces of the poor and taking their garments or vineyards from them; but this future inheritance of the saints is stained by none of these vices, it is neither got nor detained by any of these methods, nor shall persons polluted with vice have any share in it. Here no one can be heir to an inheritance of gold or houses without danger of soon sinking into indolence, effeminacy or vice, Barnes adds, whereas there the inheritance may be enjoyed for ever and the soul continually advance in knowledge, holiness and the active service of God. The third word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, Barnes says, though a cognate is applied later in the epistle to a crown or garland, and it is properly applied to that which does not fade or wither in contradistinction from a flower that fades; the idea is therefore not precisely the same as that expressed by incorruptible, for both words denote perpetuity, but that refers to perpetuity in contrast with decay while this denotes perpetuity in the sense that everything there will be kept in its original brightness and beauty, so that the crown of glory, though worn for millions of ages, will not be dimmed, the golden streets will lose none of their lustre, and the flowers that bloom on the banks of the river of life will always be as rich in colour and as fragrant as when we first beheld them. On the following verse Barnes says the word rendered kept means to keep as in a garrison or fortress, or as with a military watch, the idea being that a faithful guardianship was exercised over them to save them from danger as a castle is watched against the approach of an enemy; they were weak in themselves and surrounded by temptations, and the only reason why they were preserved was that God exerted his power to keep them, which is the only reason any Christians have to suppose they will ever reach heaven. He does not keep us by the mere exertion of power, Barnes says, but excites faith in our hearts and makes that the means of keeping us, so that as long as we have faith in God and in his promises we are safe. Barnes takes the verse to teach that Peter as well as Paul believed in the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints, asking how he could otherwise have addressed them in this manner, and argues the point in three steps: that it is very desirable the doctrine should be true, since man is so weak and feeble, so liable to fall and so exposed to temptation that it is every way a thing to be wished that his salvation should be in some safer hands than his own; that if it is desirable it is fair to infer that it is true, for God has made all the arrangements for the salvation of his people which are really desirable and proper; and that the only security for the salvation of any one is founded on that doctrine, since if it were left entirely to the hands of men, even the best of men, there could be no assurance, for did not Adam fall, did not holy angels fall, and have not some of the best of men fallen into sin. Any man must know little of himself and of the human heart, Barnes says, who supposes he has such a strength of virtue that he would never fall away if left to himself. Charles Ellicott says the inheritance is structurally parallel to and explanatory of the living hope, since we are, as the saying is, born to an estate, and this notion of an inheritance or property that we have come in for is particularly Hebrew, occurring very frequently in the Old Testament; the Pontine dispersion had lost their inheritance in Palestine, but there is a better in store for them. The three epithets he calls an exuberant description of the excellencies of the new Canaan, Ellicott says: the first contrasts its imperishable nature with the fleeting tenure of the earthly Canaan; the second speaks of its freedom from pollutions such as desecrated the first Holy Land, and perhaps may specially mean that the new Holy Land will never be profaned by Gentile incursions and tyrannies; the third, and most poetical of all, which is only found besides in the book of Wisdom, conveys the notion of the unchanging beauty of that land, no winter in the inheritance to which the resurrection brings us. Reserved is the perfect tense, Ellicott says, which has been reserved unto you, either in the temporal sense of kept all this while until you came, or with a view to you; and he now adds explicitly that it is no earthly but a heavenly possession. The clause about being kept explains the word you, Ellicott says, meaning those who are under the guardianship of God's power, and he quotes Bengel that as the inheritance has been preserved so are the heirs guarded, neither shall it fail them nor they it. The Apostle is fearful lest the last words should give a false assurance, Ellicott says, for God can guard none of us, in spite of his power, unless there be a corresponding exertion upon our part, which is here called faith, combining the notions of staunch fidelity and of trustfulness in spite of appearances, and it is through such trustful fidelity that we are guarded. The words unto arise like point beyond point in the endless vista, Ellicott observes: begotten unto an inheritance, which has been reserved unto you, who are kept safe unto a deliverance. This salvation must not be taken in the bald sense of salvation from damnation, Ellicott insists, for the thought of the perdition of the lost does not enter at all into the passage; the salvation or deliverance is primarily a deliverance from all the trials and persecutions, struggles and temptations of this life, an emergence into the state of peace and rest, as we can see from the verses that follow. How such an assurance helps to form the very faith through which the treasure is secured, Ellicott says: that perfect state of peace, that heavenly inheritance, is not something to be prepared hereafter, but there it is, and if only our eyes were opened we should already see it, all ready and only waiting for the great moment. The tense of the word revealed implies the suddenness of the unveiling, Ellicott says, for it will be but the work of an instant to put aside the curtain and show the inheritance which has been kept hidden so long behind it; this will not take place till the exact period, and that period will be the last of the world's history, for which teaching the Hebrews would be well prepared by the Old Testament, it being the earliest kind of teaching culled for converts out of the oracles of God. A.T. Robertson says the word for inheritance is an old one from the word for heir, for the property received by the heir, here a picture of the blessedness in store for us pilgrims. Incorruptible is an old compound adjective meaning imperishable, Robertson says, and so many inheritances vanish away before they are obtained; undefiled is an old verbal adjective, and he notes the alliteration, meaning without defect or flaw in the title, found in the New Testament only here and in James and Hebrews; that fadeth not away is alliterative and verbal again, from a verb meaning to dry up or wither, a late and rare word occurring in several inscriptions on tombs, found here only in the New Testament, and Robertson remarks that these inscriptions will fade away but not this inheritance in Christ, which will not be like a faded rose. Reserved is a perfect passive participle of an old verb meaning to take care of or to guard, Robertson says, and no burglars or bandits can break through where this inheritance is kept; the phrase for you is more graphic than the mere dative. On the following verse he says there is no other power like this, and that the word rendered guarded is a present passive participle of a verb meaning to garrison, an old military term from the word for a sentinel, used elsewhere of God's love as here, quoting Bengel that the inheritance is kept and the heirs are guarded. Faith is the intermediate agency, Robertson says, the immediate being God's power; deliverance is the goal of the process and final salvation here, a consummation; ready means prepared, awaiting God's will; to be revealed is a first aorist passive infinitive of the verb to unveil. The precise phrase rendered in the last time occurs nowhere else, Robertson notes, though similar ones appear widely in the New Testament, and Hort translates it here in a season of extremity, but it is usually taken to refer to the Day of Judgment, of which day Jesus said that no one knows it.

Adam Clarke says it is called an inheritance because it belongs to the children of God, and eternal life cannot be a gift to any but these, for even in heaven the lot is dealt out according to law: if children then heirs, if not children then not heirs. Incorruptible means it has no principles of dissolution or decay in it and therefore must be totally different from this earth, Clarke says; undefiled means nothing impure can enter it, so that it not only has no principles or seeds of dissolution in itself but can never admit any, and therefore its deterioration is impossible; fadeth not away means it cannot wither and is always in bloom, a metaphor taken from those flowers that never lose their hue nor their fragrance, and from the Greek word we have our flowers called amaranths because they preserve their hue and odour for a long time. Such a place as that described is not to be expected on earth, Clarke says: it is that which was typified by the earthly Canaan, and in reference to which the patriarchs endured all trials and difficulties in this life, as seeing him who is invisible. On the following verse Clarke says those who are kept are defended as in a fortress or castle, and notes a remarkable correspondence between the two verbs used in the sentence, one signifying to keep, watch or guard, with a cognate noun meaning a place of custody or prison, and the other, from the word for a sentinel, signifying to keep as under a military guard. The true disciples of Christ are under the continual watchful care of God and the inheritance is guarded for them, Clarke says: in some countries military posts are constantly kept on the confines in order to prevent irruptions from a neighbouring people, and in many cases heirs, while in their minority, are kept in fortified places under military guards. By the power of God means by the mighty and miracle-working power of God, Clarke says, for nothing less is necessary to keep and preserve in this state of continual trial a soul from the contagion that is in the world; but this power of God is interested in the behalf of the soul by faith, to believe being our work and the exertion of the almighty power being of God, so that there is no persevering without the power and no power without faith. Ready to be revealed is rather prepared to be revealed, Clarke says: the inheritance is prepared for you, but its glories will not be revealed till the last time, till you have done with life and passed through your probation, having held fast faith and a good conscience; and some by salvation understand the deliverance of the Christians from the sackage of Jerusalem, the end of the Jewish polity being called the last time, while others suppose it to refer to the day of judgment and the glorification of body and soul in heaven. John Wesley says the inheritance is ours for if we are sons then heirs; incorruptible, not like earthly treasures; undefiled, pure and holy, incapable of being itself defiled or of being enjoyed by any polluted soul; and that fadeth not away, that never decays in its value, sweetness or beauty, like all the enjoyments of this world, like the garlands of leaves or flowers with which the ancient conquerors were wont to be crowned. Reserved in heaven for you, Wesley says, for those who by patient continuance in welldoing seek for glory and honour and immortality. On the following verse he says the inheritance is reserved and the heirs are kept for it, by the power of God which worketh all in all and guards us against all our enemies, through faith through which alone salvation is both received and retained; and that revelation is made in the last day, having been more and more ready to be revealed ever since Christ came.

debates: Whether the keeping secures the end: Barnes finds the perseverance of the saints taught here and argues that the doctrine is desirable, that what is desirable may fairly be inferred true, and that no other security exists; Calvin calls the contrary a diabolical opinion prevailing under the Papacy; Ellicott warns that the words may give a false assurance, since God can guard none of us without a corresponding exertion on our part; Clarke balances the two, no persevering without the power and no power without faith

What the salvation is: Ellicott refuses the bald sense of rescue from damnation and makes it deliverance from the trials and persecutions of this life; Calvin means the body as well as the soul at the resurrection; Clarke reports some who take it of the deliverance of Christians from the sack of Jerusalem and others of the day of judgment; Robertson gives Hort's rendering, a season of extremity, against the usual reference to the Day of Judgment

How the epithets differ: Barnes distinguishes perpetuity against decay from perpetuity in original brightness, so that the two words are not synonyms; Robertson takes them as alliteration and notes the last is a tomb-inscription word; Ellicott and Calvin's editor read all three against the earthly Canaan; Clarke and Wesley read them morally, as excluding any polluted possessor
outliers: Robertson's remark that the tomb inscriptions bearing this word will themselves fade away, but not the inheritance, which will not be like a faded rose
Barnes's quotation of Benson on estates got by poisoning, by murdering the right heir, by cheating helpless orphans and by grinding the faces of the poor
Clarke's derivation of the garden amaranth from the word, a flower that preserves its hue and odour long
Ellicott's suggestion that the undefiled land may specially mean one never again profaned by Gentile incursions and tyrannies
Wesley's image of the garlands of leaves or flowers with which the ancient conquerors were wont to be crowned
Clarke's observation that heirs in their minority are in many places kept in fortified places under military guards

6.pericope_label: Rejoicing though grieved by manifold trials, that the proof of faith, more precious than gold tried by fire, be found unto praise

schools.summary: John Gill says the Vulgate Latin version reads in which ye shall rejoice, and so the Syriac version, adding for ever, and refer the words to the last time or times spoken of in the preceding verse, when the saints will greatly rejoice, being in full possession of eternal salvation, in distinction from the present time in which they are in heaviness; but it is better, Gill says, to read the words in the present tense, as expressive of the saints in this life, who are blessed with that fruit of the Spirit, joy, and have always reason to rejoice, and greatly rejoice. The connection is with the whole that goes before, Gill says, the sense being that regenerated persons rejoice in that they are the elect of God according to his everlasting love towards them and free grace and good will; in their regeneration, which is an evidence of their election of God; in the abundant mercy of God displayed in their regeneration; in that lively hope of eternal life which is the effect of it; and in the resurrection of Christ from the dead, which secures their justification of life and their resurrection from the dead. On the following verse Gill says this is the principal end which God has in afflictive providences, to try the faith of his people, and that so the faith of Abraham, Job, Habakkuk and others has been tried. John Calvin says that though the termination of the Greek verb is doubtful the meaning requires that we read ye exult rather than exult ye, and that the relative refers to the whole that is said of the hope of salvation laid up in heaven; but he rather exhorts than praises them, for his object was to show what fruit was to come from the hope of salvation, even spiritual joy, by which not only the bitterness of all evil might be mitigated but also all sorrow overcome, and to exult is more expressive than to rejoice. Some take the verb in a future sense and some as an imperative, Calvin says, but neither of these comports with the context, for the eighth verse proves that he speaks of present joy and states the case as it was among them; it is better to refer the words to the fact stated in the previous verse, that they were kept by God's power for salvation ready to be revealed. It seems somewhat inconsistent that he says the faithful who exulted with joy were at the same time sorrowful, since these are contrary feelings, Calvin allows, but the faithful know by experience how these things can exist together much better than can be expressed in words. To explain the matter in a few words, Calvin says, the faithful are not logs of wood, nor have they so divested themselves of human feelings but that they are affected with sorrow, fear danger, and feel poverty as an evil and persecutions as hard and difficult to be borne; hence they experience sorrow from evils, but it is so mitigated by faith that they cease not at the same time to rejoice, so that sorrow does not prevent their joy but on the contrary gives place to it; and again, though joy overcomes sorrow it does not put an end to it, for it does not divest us of humanity. Hence it appears what true patience is, Calvin says: its beginning and as it were its root is the knowledge of God's blessings, especially of that gratuitous adoption with which he has favoured us, for all who raise their minds thither find it an easy thing calmly to bear all evils; for whence is it that our minds are pressed down with grief except that we have no participation of spiritual things, whereas all they who regard their troubles as necessary trials for their salvation not only rise above them but turn them to an occasion of joy. Is not sorrow also the common lot of the reprobate, Calvin asks, since they are not free from evils; but Peter meant that the faithful endure sorrow willingly while the ungodly murmur and perversely contend with God, so that the godly bear sorrow as the tamed ox the yoke, or as a horse broken in the bridle though held by a child, while God by sorrow afflicts the reprobate as when a bridle is by force put in the mouth of a ferocious and refractory horse, which kicks and offers every resistance but all in vain. Then Peter commends the faithful because they willingly undergo sorrow and not as though forced by necessity, Calvin says, and by speaking of a little while he supplied consolation, for the shortness of time, however hard evils may be, does not a little lessen them, the duration of the present life being but a moment of time. The condition is to be taken for a cause, Calvin says, for he purposed to show that God does not without reason thus try his people, since if God afflicted us without a cause to bear it would be grievous; hence Peter took an argument for consolation from the design of God, not that the reason always appears to us but that we ought to be fully persuaded that it ought to be so because it is God's will; and we must notice that he does not mention one temptation but many, and not temptations of one kind. On the following verse Calvin says the argument is from the less to the greater, for if gold, a corruptible metal, is deemed of so much value that we prove it by fire that it may become really valuable, what wonder is it that God should require a similar trial as to faith, since faith is deemed by him so excellent; and though the words seem to have a different meaning he yet compares faith to gold and makes it more precious than gold, that hence he might draw the conclusion that it ought to be fully proved. The seeming difference arises from this, Calvin says, that the Apostle uses two nouns, a common thing in Scripture, instead of a noun and an adjective or participle, the trial of your faith standing for your tried faith or your faith when tried. It is moreover uncertain how far he extends the meaning of the words tried and trial, Calvin says: gold is indeed tried twice by fire, first when it is separated from its dross and then when a judgment is to be formed of its purity, and both modes of trial may very suitably be applied to faith, for when there is much of the dregs of unbelief remaining in us and when by various afflictions we are refined as it were in God's furnace, the dross of our faith is removed so that it becomes pure and clean before God, and at the same time a trial of it is made as to whether it be true or fictitious; he is disposed to take these two views, and what immediately follows seems to favour this explanation, for as silver is without honour or value before it be refined, so he intimates that our faith is not to be honoured and crowned by God until it be duly proved. This is added that the faithful might learn to hold on courageously to the last day, Calvin says, for our life is now hidden in Christ and will remain hidden and as it were buried until Christ shall appear from heaven, and the whole course of our life leads to the destruction of the external man, all the things we suffer being as it were the preludes of death. It is hence necessary that we should cast our own eyes on Christ if we wish in our afflictions to behold glory and praise, Calvin says, for trials as to us are full of reproach and shame and they become glorious in Christ, but that glory in Christ is not yet plainly seen, for the day of consolation is not yet come; and the praise, honour and glory refer to tried faith, which will be praised or approved by the Judge, honoured before men and angels, and followed by eternal glory.

Matthew Henry says the first word refers to the apostle's foregoing discourse about the excellency of their present state and their grand expectations for the future, and that the apostle grants they were in great affliction and propounds several things in mitigation of their sorrows. Every sound Christian has always something wherein he may greatly rejoice, Henry says, and great rejoicing contains more than an inward placid serenity of mind or sensation of comfort, since it will show itself in the countenance and conduct but especially in praise and gratitude; the chief joy of a good Christian arises from things spiritual and heavenly, from his relation to God and to heaven, his joy arising from his treasure, which consists of matters of great value to which the title is sure. The best Christians, those who have reason greatly to rejoice, may yet be in great heaviness through manifold temptations, Henry says, since all sorts of adversities are temptations or trials of faith, patience and constancy, and these seldom go singly but are manifold and come from different quarters; as men we are subject to sorrows personal and domestic, and as Christians our duty to God obliges us to frequent sorrow, while our compassion towards the miserable, the dishonour done to God, the calamities of his church and the destruction of mankind raise in a generous and pious mind almost continual sorrow. The afflictions and sorrows of good people are but for a little while, Henry says: though they may be smart they are but short, life itself is but for a little while and the sorrows of it cannot survive it, and the shortness of any affliction does much abate the heaviness of it. Great heaviness is often necessary to a Christian's good, Henry says, for God does not afflict his people willingly but acts with judgment in proportion to our needs; there is a conveniency and fitness, nay an absolute necessity in the case, for so the expression signifies, and these troubles that lie heavy never come upon us but when we have need and never stay any longer than needs must. He then expresses the end of their afflictions and the ground of their joy under them, Henry says: the end of good people's afflictions is the trial of their faith, and God's design in afflicting his people is their probation and not their destruction, their advantage and not their ruin, a trial being an experiment or search made upon a man by some affliction to prove the value and strength of his faith. This trial is made upon faith principally rather than any other grace, Henry says, because the trial of this is in effect the trial of all that is good in us, since our Christianity depends upon our faith and if this be wanting there is nothing else that is spiritually good in us; Christ prayed for this apostle that his faith might not fail, and if that be supported all the rest will stand firm, the faith of good people being tried that they themselves may have the comfort of it, God the glory of it, and others the benefit of it.
