A tried faith is much more precious than tried gold, Henry says, and here is a double comparison of faith and gold and of the trial of the one with the trial of the other: gold is the most valuable, pure, useful and durable of all the metals, and so is faith among the Christian virtues, lasting till it brings the soul to heaven and then issuing in the glorious fruition of God for ever. The trial of faith is much more precious than the trial of gold, Henry says: in both there is a purification, a separation of the dross and a discovery of the soundness and goodness of the things, but gold does not increase and multiply by trial in the fire, it rather grows less, whereas faith is established, improved and multiplied by the oppositions and afflictions that it meets with; and gold must perish at last, but faith never will. The trial of faith will be found to praise and honour and glory, Henry says: honour is properly that esteem and value which one has with another, and so God and man will honour the saints; praise is the expression or declaration of that esteem, so that Christ will commend his people in the great day; and glory is that lustre wherewith a person so honoured and praised shines in heaven. If a tried faith be found to praise, honour and glory, let this recommend faith as much more precious than gold though it be assaulted and tried by afflictions, Henry says, for if you make your estimate either from present use or the final event of both, this will be found true however the world may take it for an incredible paradox. Jesus Christ will appear again in glory, Henry says, and when he does so the saints will appear with him and their graces will appear illustrious, and the more they have been tried the more bright they will then appear; the trial will soon be over, but the glory, honour and praise will last to eternity, and this should reconcile them to their present afflictions, since they work for them a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.

Albert Barnes says the idea is that the prospect which they had of the future inheritance was to them a source of the highest joy even in the midst of their many sufferings and trials, and that the hope enabled them to rejoice even in the midst of persecutions, not only sustaining them but making them happy; that must be a valuable religion, Barnes says, which will make men happy in the midst of persecutions and heavy calamities. The season would be in fact only a brief period even if it should continue through the whole of life, Barnes says, though it is possible that Peter supposed the trials they then experienced would soon pass over, having perhaps been sufferings he hoped would not long continue. The phrase about need seems to have been thrown in to intimate that there was a necessity for their afflictions, Barnes says, some good being accomplished by them which made it desirable and proper that they should be thus afflicted; the sense is since there is need, though the apostle expresses it more delicately by suggesting the possibility that there might be need instead of saying absolutely that there was need. It is the kind of language which we would use in respect to one who was greatly afflicted, Barnes says, suggesting to him in the most tender manner that there might be things in his character which God designed to correct by trials, instead of saying roughly and bluntly that such was undoubtedly the fact: we would not say to such a person that he certainly needed this affliction to lead him to amend his life, but rather that it may be there is something in his character which makes it desirable. They were sorrowing through many kinds of trials, Barnes says, which might have consisted of poverty, persecution, sickness, or the efforts of others to lead them to renounce their religion and go back to their former state of unbelief, any one or all of which would try them and show whether their religion was genuine. On the following verse Barnes says the trial means the putting of their religion to the test and showing what is its real nature, and that the text does not mean that their faith was much more precious than gold but that the testing of it, the process of showing whether it was or was not genuine, was a much more important and valuable process than that of testing gold in the fire, more important results being arrived at by it. The clause about perishing does not mean that gold perishes by the process of being tried in the fire, Barnes says, for this is not the fact and the connexion does not demand this interpretation; the idea is that gold, however valuable it is, is a perishable thing, not an enduring, imperishable, indestructible thing like religion, and though it may not perish in the fire it will in some way, for it will not endure for ever. Barnes draws from the two verses that it is desirable that the faith of Christians should be tried: it is desirable to know whether that which appears to be religion is genuine, as it is desirable to know whether that which appears to be gold is genuine, and as religion is of more value than gold it is more desirable that it should be subjected to the proper tests; it is desirable in order to show its true value, since religion claims to impart consolation in the various trials of life which nothing else can impart and to give a support which nothing else can on the bed of death, so that it is very desirable that its friends should be in these various conditions in order that they may illustrate the true value of religion; and it is desirable that true religion should be separated from all alloy, for gold is often better for some purposes for having some alloy mixed with it, but religion is never better for having a little pride, or vanity, or selfishness, or meanness, or worldliness, or sensuality mingled with it. God takes various methods of trying his people, Barnes says: he tries them by prosperity, often as decisive a test of piety as can be applied, since there is much pretended piety which will bear adversity but which will not bear prosperity, the piety of a man being decisively tested by popularity, by the flatteries of the world and by a sudden increase of property; he tries them by adversity, laying his hand on them heavily to show whether they will bear up and persevere in his service, whether their religion will keep them from murmuring, and whether it is adapted to comfort and sustain the soul; and he tries them by sudden transition from the one to the other, since we get accustomed to a uniform course of life and the religion which is adapted to a uniform course may be little fitted to transitions, for the piety which shone so much on a bed of sickness might be little fitted to shine in circumstances of sudden prosperity. The human frame may become accustomed either to the intense cold of the polar regions or to the burning heats of the equator, Barnes says, but in neither case might it bear a transition from one to the other, and it is such a transition that is a more decisive test of its powers of endurance than either intense heat or cold if steadily prolonged. Charles Ellicott quotes Leighton that the apostle's scope is to stir up and strengthen spiritual joy in his afflicted brethren, and therefore having set the matter of it before them in the preceding verses he now applies it and expressly opposes it to their distresses. There is a little doubt as to the antecedent of the word wherein, Ellicott says: at first sight it would seem to be the last time, and the thought would then be that this last time with all its predicted afflictions was already begun and that the Pontine Hebrews were fulfilling the injunction of our Lord to rejoice, the word being one of enthusiastic and demonstrative joy, in the near approach of their redemption; this makes good sense, but it is better to see the antecedent in the whole complex sense of the preceding verses concerning the hope of glory, and he quotes Leighton again that they rejoice in this thing, that they are begotten again, that there is such an inheritance and that they are made heirs of it, that it is kept for them and they for it, and that nothing can come betwixt them and it, though there be many deserts and mountains and seas in the way. The literal rendering is after having been grieved in the present, if it must be so, for a little while in the midst of manifold temptations, Ellicott says, the Apostle taking his stand at the moment of the revelation and looking back upon the fast-passing present and its griefs. What the temptations were we cannot tell, Ellicott says, but the word manifold shows that it was not only one type of temptation under which all lay alike, the chief being probably the unkind attitude of Gentile neighbours, which was the most searching test of faith; identical words occur in James so as almost to suggest a common origin, possibly to be found in Romans. To encourage them to bear up, Peter throws in the phrase about need so as not to take it for granted that they will have to suffer, Ellicott says, for he hopes it may not be so. On the following verse Ellicott says the word trial here does not mean exactly the same as in the passage of James, where it signifies the active testing of faith, but has rather the meaning of the cognate word translated assurance and proof elsewhere, that is the attested worth, the genuine character; this seems necessitated by the comparison of the trial with the gold itself, for you cannot compare an act or process with gold but you can compare the genuine character brought out by the process, and besides, that which you wish to praise at Christ's coming is not the process by which the faith was proved but the worth of the faith itself. There is no reason, or indeed any grammatical right, to insert the words of gold in that form, Ellicott says: it should be more exceedingly valuable than gold, for he does not say your faith is more valuable than gold but your faith's genuineness is more valuable than gold, since it is worth anything to establish the true character of your faith and it would be a most serious loss to leave a chance of an imputation upon your Christianity. The argument is this, Ellicott says: gold is a perishable thing and comes to an end with the rest of the world, or is worn away with handling and is lost, and yet men take great pains to test it and show that it contains no dross, and do so by means of fire; how much more may we expect a fiery trial to test the character of our belief in the unseen Christ, when that belief is never to come to an end and on its freedom from alloy everything depends. Might be found means might clearly prove to be, Ellicott says: the time will come when the gold will be inspected, and the Judge and all the spectators will find that the testing was sufficient and the character satisfactory; found unto praise is a Hebraism meaning found to be a matter of praise, and Peter is fond of heaping up words of like signification. Praise is the language that will be used about these men's faith, Ellicott says, honour the rank in which they will be placed, and glory the fervent admiration accorded to them, the three words corresponding to the regions of word, act and feeling. Revelation would have been a better rendering than appearing, Ellicott says, as the word in the Greek is the same as earlier, and this gives the date at which the trial will have done its work, the same as the last time when the deliverance will be revealed; and he adds that there are several words and thoughts in the whole passage which would suggest that the twelfth chapter of Daniel was before the mind of the Apostle more or less consciously. A.T. Robertson says the translation wherein refers the relative to the word for season, but that it is possible to see a reference to Christ or to God or even to the entire content of the preceding verses, either making sense though possibly the season is correct. Ye greatly rejoice is a present middle indicative rather than an imperative of a late verb found only in the Greek Old Testament, the New Testament and ecclesiastical literature, Robertson says; now for a little while is an accusative of time, and if need be is a present active neuter singular participle in a condition of the first class, some manuscripts having a periphrastic construction. Though ye have been put to grief is a first aorist passive participle in the concessive circumstantial use of an old and common verb, Robertson says, and the phrase for manifold temptations is just the phrase in James, trials being clearly right here as there, while seven New Testament writers use the adjective rendered manifold. On the following verse Robertson says the phrase for the proof of faith is identical with that in James and probably derived from there by Peter; there is no word for being in the Greek, and the secondary uncials have a different comparative, the text being the comparative of a late adjective from Plutarch meaning of great price. That perisheth is a present middle articular participle, Robertson says, since even gold perishes or wears away; though it is proved by fire is a present passive articular participle of the common verb for testing metals, with a particle which gives a concessive sense to the participle, so that faith stands the test of fire better than gold, but even gold is refined by fire. That might be found is a purpose clause with the first aorist passive subjunctive of the common verb to find, Robertson says, and this is the result of the probation by God as the Refiner of hearts; the three nouns are probably to be referred both to God and man in the result; and the phrase at the revelation of Jesus Christ is used here and elsewhere, following Bigg, of the second coming of Christ as the Judge and Rewarder.

Adam Clarke says some refer the word wherein to the salvation mentioned above, others to the last time, others think that it applies to the being kept by the power of God through faith, and others that it refers to all the preceding advantages and privileges; it was in the present salvation of God that they rejoiced or gloried, Clarke says, though not without having an eye to the great recompense of reward. For a season means a little while yet, during their pilgrimage here below, which is but a point when compared with eternity, Clarke says; and if need be means if it be necessary, if their situation and circumstances be such that they are exposed to trials and persecutions which they cannot avoid unless God were to work a miracle for their deliverance, which would not be for their ultimate good, as he purposes to turn all their trials and difficulties to their advantage. Sometimes there is a kind of necessity that the followers of God should be afflicted, Clarke says, for when they have no trials they are apt to get careless, and when they have secular prosperity they are likely to become worldly-minded; God, said a good man, can neither trust me with health nor money, therefore I am both poor and afflicted. But the disciples of Christ may be very happy in their souls though grievously afflicted in their bodies and in their estates, Clarke says: those to whom Peter wrote rejoiced greatly, danced for joy, while they were grieved with various trials, the verb signifying to grieve or to make sorrowful; perhaps heaviness is not the best rendering of the original word, as this can scarcely ever consist with rejoicing, but to be sorrowful on account of something external to ourselves and yet exulting in God from a sense of his goodness to us is quite compatible, so that we may say with Paul, always sorrowing yet still rejoicing. On the following verse Clarke says that as by the action of fire gold is separated from all alloy and heterogeneous mixtures and is proved to be gold by its enduring the action of the fire without losing anything of its nature, weight, colour or any other property, so genuine faith is proved by adversities, especially such as the primitive Christians were obliged to pass through; for the word was then, Renounce Jesus and live, Cleave to him and die, since every Christian was in continual danger of losing his life. He then who preferred Christianity to his life gave full proof not only of his own sincerity but also of the excellency of the principle by which he was influenced, Clarke says, as his religion put him in possession of greater blessings and more solid comforts than anything the earth could afford. Though gold will bear the action of the fire for any given time, even millions of years were they possible, without losing the smallest particle of weight or value, Clarke says, yet even gold in process of time will wear away by continual use, and the earth and all its works will be burnt up by that supernatural fire whose action nothing can resist; but on that day the faith of Christ's followers will be found brighter and more glorious, for the earth and universal nature shall be dissolved but he who doeth the will of God shall abide for ever, and his faith shall then be found to the praise of God's grace, the honour of Christ and the glory or glorification of his own soul throughout eternity: God himself will praise such faith, angels and men will hold it in honour, and Christ will crown it with glory. John Wesley says wherein means in being so kept, and that they even now greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, such being our whole life compared to eternity; if need be, for it is not always needful, if God sees it to be the best means for their spiritual profit. They are in heaviness or sorrow, Wesley says, but not in darkness, for they still retained faith, hope and love, and at this very time were rejoicing with joy unspeakable. On the following verse he says the trial of your faith means your faith which is tried, and that it is much more precious than gold because gold, though it bear the fire, yet will perish with the world; may be found, though it doth not yet appear; unto praise, from God himself; and honour, from men and angels; and glory, assigned by the great Judge.

debates: What the relative pronoun refers to: Robertson allows the season, Christ, God or the whole preceding content and prefers the season; Clarke sets out four candidates and settles on the present salvation; Ellicott prefers the whole complex sense of the preceding verses on Leighton's authority; Calvin refers it to their being kept by God's power and rejects both a future and an imperative reading; Gill reports that the Vulgate and Syriac do read it as future and refer it to the last time

Whether the trial means the process or the result: Ellicott denies that the word here means what it means in James and takes it as the attested worth, since a process cannot be compared with gold; Barnes takes it as the testing itself, which he says is a more valuable process than the trying of gold; Calvin says the noun stands for the adjective, tried faith, and applies both refinings of gold to it
Whether the phrase came from James: Robertson says the wording is identical and probably derived from there by Peter; Ellicott notes the same identity and suggests instead a common origin in Paul

How the closing triad is distributed: Ellicott assigns the three to word, act and feeling; Henry makes honour the esteem, praise its declaration and glory the lustre in heaven; Wesley assigns praise to God, honour to men and angels and glory to the Judge; Clarke agrees but gives the crowning to Christ
outliers: Calvin's insistence that the faithful are not logs of wood, and his contrast of the tamed ox and the ferocious horse into whose mouth the bit is forced
Clarke's quotation of a good man who said that God could trust him with neither health nor money, and that he was therefore both poor and afflicted
Barnes's argument that prosperity is often as decisive a test of piety as adversity, and that sudden transition between them is more decisive than either prolonged
Barnes's analogy of the human frame accustomed to polar cold or equatorial heat but unable to bear the passage from one to the other
Clarke's report that the word to the primitive Christians was, Renounce Jesus and live, Cleave to him and die
Ellicott's suggestion that the twelfth chapter of Daniel was before the mind of the Apostle more or less consciously

8.pericope_label: Loving and believing on the unseen Christ, rejoicing with joy unspeakable, receiving the end of faith, the salvation of souls

schools.summary: John Gill says the persons meant are Jesus Christ, whom they had never seen with their bodily eyes, being Jews who dwelt not in Judea when Christ was upon earth but were scattered about in several parts of the Gentile world; yet Christ being made known to them through the preaching of the Gospel, they received and embraced him and their affections were strongly set upon him. They loved him because of his excellencies and perfections, Gill says, because of the loveliness of his person, and because he first loved them; they loved him because of the fulness of grace that was in him, because of what he had done for them and was unto them, and because of the offices he sustained on their account and the relations he stood in to them; they loved him above all creatures and things, and all of him and that belong unto him, his people, truths, ordinances, ways and worship; they loved him with all their hearts and in the sincerity of their souls, though they had never seen his face in the flesh, whereas sight often begets and increases love, so that their love was not carnal but spiritual. On the following verse Gill says the salvation received is a just and sufficient ground of joy and rejoicing, and that salvation intends spiritual and eternal salvation, that which God appointed his people to from all eternity, which is obtained by Christ, applied by the Spirit, and will be fully enjoyed in heaven. This is the salvation of souls, Gill says, which are of more worth than a world, and the redemption of which is precious and requires a great price, and for which a great price is paid. The word your is rightly supplied in our version, Gill notes, as in the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions, though the Vulgate Latin version reads only the salvation of souls; and this is to be understood not to the exclusion of bodies, for God has designed the salvation of them and Christ has procured the redemption of them, and these will be preserved unto the coming of Christ, being united to him, and will be raised by him and with their souls enjoy everlasting happiness with him, though in the present state of things salvation rather takes place in the soul than in the body, which is exposed to various evils. John Calvin says he lays down two things, that they loved Christ whom they had not seen and that they believed on him whom they did not then behold, but that the first arises from the second, for the cause of love is faith, not only because the knowledge of those blessings which Christ bestows on us moves us to love him, but because he offers us perfect felicity and thus draws us up to himself. He then commends the Jews because they believed in Christ whom they did not see, Calvin says, that they might know that the nature of faith is to acquiesce in those blessings which are hid from our eyes; they had indeed given some proof of this very thing, though he rather directs what was to be done by praising them. The first clause in order is that faith is not to be measured by sight, Calvin says, for when the life of Christians is apparently miserable they would instantly fail were not their happiness dependent on hope; faith indeed has also its eyes, but they are such as penetrate into the invisible kingdom of God and are contented with the mirror of the Word, for it is the demonstration of invisible things as it is said in the letter to the Hebrews, whence true is that saying of Paul that we are absent from the Lord while we are in the flesh, for we walk by faith and not by sight. The second clause is that faith is not a cold notion but that it kindles in our hearts love to Christ, Calvin says, for faith does not, as the sophists prattle, lay hold on God in a confused and implicit manner, for this would be to wander through devious paths, but it has Christ as its object; moreover it does not lay hold on the bare name of Christ or his naked essence but regards what he is to us and what blessings he brings, for it cannot be but that the affections of man should be led there where his happiness is, according to the saying that where your treasure is there is also your heart. He again refers to the fruit of faith which he had mentioned, and not without reason, Calvin says, for it is an incomparable benefit that consciences are not only at peace before God but confidently exult in the hope of eternal life; and he calls it unutterable because the peace of God exceeds all comprehension. What is added, glorified, admits of two explanations, Calvin says: it means either what is magnificent and glorious, or what is contrary to that which is empty and fading, of which men will soon be ashamed, so that it is the same with what is solid and permanent, beyond the danger of being brought to nothing; after unspeakable, glorified must mean something greater, or it may be viewed as more specific, a joy unspeakable, being a glorified joy in a measure, or the joy of the glorified in heaven, so that the words may be rendered with joy unspeakable and heavenly. The editorial matter in Calvin's block gives the paraphrase, with unutterable and even glorified joy, with such a joy as seems to anticipate that of the saints in glory. Those who are not elevated by this joy above the heavens, Calvin says, so that being content with Christ alone they despise the world, in vain boast that they have faith. On the following verse Calvin says he reminds the faithful where they ought to direct all their thoughts, even to eternal salvation, for this world holds all our affections ensnared by its allurements, and this life and all things belonging to the body are great impediments which prevent us from applying our minds to the contemplation of the future and spiritual life; hence the Apostle sets before us this future life as a subject of deep meditation, and he indirectly intimates that the loss of all other things is to be deemed as nothing provided our souls be saved. By speaking of receiving he takes away all doubt, Calvin says, in order that they might more cheerfully go on, being certain of obtaining salvation; and the editorial matter adds that it is necessary either to give a future meaning to the participle, being about to receive, or to view the Apostle as speaking of the salvation of the soul now as distinct from the salvation of the soul and body hereafter, the latter view seeming most appropriate to the passage, since the soul is now saved by faith and the end of faith, its object and accomplishment, is reconciliation with God, and reconciliation is salvation. In the meantime he shows what the end of faith is, Calvin says, lest they should be over-anxious because it is as yet deferred, for our adoption ought now to satisfy us, nor ought we to ask to be introduced before the time into the possession of our inheritance; we may also take the word for reward, but the meaning would be the same, for we learn from the Apostle's words that salvation is not otherwise obtained than by faith, and we know that faith leans on the sole promise of gratuitous adoption, so that doubtless salvation is not owing to the merits of works nor can it be hoped for on their account. But why does he mention only souls, Calvin asks, when the glory of a resurrection is promised to our bodies; and he answers that as the soul is immortal salvation is properly ascribed to it, as Paul sometimes is wont to speak, but that it is the same as though he had said eternal salvation, for there is an implied comparison between it and the mortal and fading life which belongs to the body, while at the same time the body is not excluded from a participation of glory when annexed to the soul.

Albert Barnes says the epistle was addressed to strangers scattered abroad and it is evident they had not personally seen the Lord Jesus, yet they had heard of his character, his preaching, his sacrifice for sin, and his resurrection and ascension, and they had learned to love him. It is possible to love one whom we have not seen, Barnes says, for thus we may love God whom no eye has seen, and thus we may love a benefactor from whom we have received important benefits whom we have never beheld; we may love the character of one whom we have never seen and from whom we may never have received any particular favours, loving his uprightness, his patriotism, his benignity as represented to us. That may be a very pure love which we have for one whom we have never seen, Barnes says, since it may be based on simple excellence of character, and in such a case there is the least chance for any intermingling of selfishness or any improper emotion of any kind; and we may love a friend as really and as strongly when he is absent as when he is with us, for the wide ocean that rolls between us and a child does not diminish the ardour of our affection for him, and the Christian friend who has gone to heaven we may love no less than when he sat with us at the fireside. Millions have been led to love the Saviour who have never seen him, Barnes says, having seen, not with the bodily eye but with the eye of faith, the inimitable beauty of his character; and there is every reason why we should love him, since his character is infinitely lovely and he has done more for us than any other one who ever lived among men, having died for us to redeem our souls, risen and brought life and immortality to light, and living ever to intercede for us in heaven. The strongest attachments which have ever existed on earth have been for this unseen Saviour, Barnes says, a love stronger than that for father or mother or wife or sister or home or country, so strong that thousands have been willing on account of it to bear the torture of the rack or the stake, so strong that thousands of youth of the finest minds and the most flattering prospects have been willing to leave the comforts of a civilised land and go among the benighted heathen to tell them the story of a Saviour's life and death. He is now in heaven and to mortal eyes invisible like his Father, Barnes says, and faith in him is the source and fountain of our joy, making invisible things real and enabling us to feel and act in view of them with the same degree of certainty as if we saw them; indeed the conviction in the mind of a true believer that there is a Saviour is as certain and as strong as if he saw him, and the same may be said of his conviction of the existence of heaven. If it should be said that faith may deceive us, Barnes replies by asking whether the bodily senses may not also deceive us: does the eye never deceive, are there no optical illusions, does the ear never deceive, are there no sounds that are mistaken, do the taste and the smell never deceive, and does the sense of feeling never deceive about the size, the hardness, the figure of objects which we handle; yet for all the practical purposes of life the senses are correct guides and do not in general lead us astray. So there are objects of faith about which we are never deceived, Barnes says, and where we do act and must act with the same confidence as if we had personally seen them: are we deceived about the existence of London or Paris or Canton though we may never have seen either, may not a merchant embark with perfect propriety in a commercial enterprise on the supposition that there is such a place as London or Canton though he has never seen them, and would he not be reputed mad if he should refuse to do it on this ground; and so may not a man in believing that there is a heaven, and in forming his plans for it though he has not yet seen it, act as rationally and as wisely. The text says ye do rejoice and not merely ye ought to rejoice, Barnes observes: it may be said of Christians that they do in fact rejoice and are happy, though the people of the world often suppose that religion makes its professors sad and melancholy. That there are those who have not great comfort in their religion no one can doubt, Barnes says, but this arises from causes entirely independent of their religion, some having melancholy temperaments and not being happy in anything, and some having little evidence that they are Christians, so that their sadness arises not from religion but from the want of it; that true religion does make its possessors happy any one may easily satisfy himself by asking any number of sincere Christians of any denomination, who with one accord will say that they have a happiness they never found before and never knew solid and substantial peace till they found it in religion. Joy unspeakable is a very strong expression, Barnes says, yet verified in thousands of cases among young converts and among those in the maturer days of piety, thousands being able to say that their happiness when they first had evidence that their sins were forgiven was unspeakable, since they had no words to express it, it was so full and so new; and he asks why all Christians are not enabled to say constantly that they rejoice with joy unspeakable, whether it is not a privilege they might possess, and whether there is anything in the nature of religion which forbids it. Full of glory means both of anticipated glory, the prospect of enjoying the glory of heaven, and of present glory, a joy even now which is of the same nature as that in heaven, a happiness the same in kind though not in degree as that which will be ours in a brighter world. On the following verse Barnes says the end means the result or object of their faith, what their faith is designed and adapted to secure, and that the word rendered receiving is used here as indicating that they would surely obtain it: they even now had such peace and joy in believing that it furnished undoubted evidence that they would be saved, and such that it might be said that even now they were saved, the condition of one who is a true Christian here being so secure that it may even now be called salvation. Charles Ellicott says the words are said in contrast to the word revelation in the last verse, meaning whom you love already though he is not yet revealed so that you have not as yet seen him, and that there seems to be a kind of tender pity in the words as spoken by one who himself had seen so abundantly. In this and the following verse we return again from the sorrow to the joy, Ellicott says, and to the true cause of that joy, which is only to be found in the love of Jesus Christ; and there is another reading, though not so good either in sense or in authority, whom without knowing him ye love, on which Bengel remarks that this is intended for a paradox, sight and knowledge being the usual parents of love. The word for love is that of calm and divinely given attachment, in fact the usual word in the New Testament, Ellicott says, that which Christ used in questioning the writer, and not the word of warm human friendship with which Peter then answered him. The phrase in whom is to be construed not with ye rejoice but with believing, Ellicott says, the participles giving the grounds of the rejoicing; and he notes again the stress laid on faith, which has already been mentioned three times. Peter, whose own faith gained him his name and prerogative, is at least as much the Apostle of faith as Paul is, Ellicott says, though his conception of it perhaps slightly differs, and the definition given by the writer of the letter to the Hebrews might have been, perhaps was, drawn from a study of Peter's writings; the present verse gives the leading thought of faith as it appears in both of these works addressed to Hebrews, namely its being the opposite of sight, the evidence of things not seen, rather than the opposite of works, and the main object of both epistles is to keep the Hebrews from slipping back from internal to external religion. The Apostle is full of admiration for a faith which, unlike his own, was not based on sight, Ellicott says, referring to the incident with Thomas which may have been in the writer's mind. The beautiful Greek word for unspeakable, which means unable to find expression in words, seems to have been coined by Peter, Ellicott says; and full of glory is literally that hath been glorified, that is a joy that has reached its ideal pitch and feels no further sense of imperfection. On the following verse Ellicott says the end of our faith means the object to which our faith is directed, the thing we believed for, and that faith catches up the believing of the last verse so that in reading the accent falls on end and not on faith, the whole clause being added to justify the statement that we rejoice with a joy which has already attained its full perfection; the reason is that we receive already, in the present life, the object of all this trusting without sight, and need not wait till the next world to attain our glorification. It might be simply salvation of souls, including other men's besides our own, Ellicott says, but the context is against it, and the absence of articles is characteristic of Peter. It seems at first sight not a very exalted object for our faith to work to, the deliverance or safety of our own souls, Ellicott says, and yet our Lord fully recognises the instinct of the higher self-preservation as that to which the ultimate appeal must be made; he could give his own soul a ransom for many, he could save others and not himself, Paul could wish himself accursed from Christ for his brethren's sake, and Moses could ask to be blotted out of the book, and yet the fact remains that in seeking our own welfare in the highest sense we are fulfilling a primal law of our being imposed upon us by the Creator, which we are bound to make our first object if it were only to gratify him who has no pleasure in the death of him that dieth. Here Ellicott quotes the hymn beginning that a charge to keep I have, a God to glorify, a never-dying soul to save and fit it for the sky, and adds that the Buddhist longing for extinction is as far as possible removed from the healthy spirit of Christianity. Salvation here seems to have widened its meaning since the earlier verse, Ellicott says: while there the main thought was final deliverance from the afflictions of life, here the salvation is said to be received in the very midst of all these afflictions, the addition of the word souls appearing to make the difference, for the soul there is present salvation because persecutions do not touch it and it is capable of the most complete emancipation from the evils of sin; salvation then is the restoration of man to the ideal excellence from which he was fallen, and contains here at any rate no allusion to damnation as an opposite. A.T. Robertson says the relative refers to Christ just before and is in the accusative, the object of both participles, and that not having seen is a second aorist active participle with a negative that negatives an actual experience rather than a hypothetical case. It is possible that Peter here has in mind the words of Jesus to Thomas as recorded in John, Robertson says, that happy are those not seeing and yet believing, for Peter was present and heard the words of Jesus to Thomas and so could use them before John wrote his Gospel. Ye rejoice greatly is the same form as in the earlier verse, only active here instead of middle, Robertson says, and with joy is an instrumental of manner; unspeakable is a late and rare double compound verbal, here only in the New Testament, occurring in Dioscorides and Heliodorus and meaning unutterable, like Paul's indescribable gift; full of glory is a perfect passive participle meaning glorified joy, like the glorified face of Moses. On the following verse he says receiving is a present middle participle of an old verb meaning to receive back or to get what is promised, that the end of your faith means the conclusion or culmination of faith, and that there is no word for even in the text, the phrase being an accusative in apposition, namely final salvation.

Adam Clarke says those to whom the apostle wrote had never seen Christ in the flesh, and yet such is the realizing nature of faith that they loved him as strongly as any of his disciples could to whom he was personally known; for faith in the Lord Jesus brings him into the heart, and by his indwelling all his virtues are proved and an excellence discovered beyond even that which his disciples beheld when conversant with him upon earth. In short, Clarke says, there is an equality between believers in the present time and those who lived in the time of the incarnation, for Christ to a believing soul is the same to-day that he was yesterday and will be for ever. They rejoice with joy unspeakable, Clarke says, having unutterable happiness through believing and the fullest, clearest, strongest evidence of eternal glory; though they did not see him on earth and men could not see him in glory, yet by that faith which is the evidence of things not seen and the subsistence of things hoped for they had the very highest persuasion of their acceptance with God, their relation to him as their Father, and their sonship with Christ Jesus. On the following verse Clarke says they are put in possession of the salvation of their souls, which was the thing presented to their faith when they were called by the Gospel of Christ, so that their faith has had a proper issue and has been crowned with a proper recompense, the word rendered end being often used so as to imply the issue or reward of any labour or action. The object of the Jewish expectations in their Messiah was the salvation or deliverance of their bodies from a foreign yoke, Clarke says, but the true Messiah came to save the soul from the yoke of the devil and sin, and this glorious salvation these believers had already received. John Wesley says receiving means now already, and that the salvation meant is from all sin into all holiness, which is the qualification for, the forerunner and pledge of, eternal salvation.

debates: Whether the receiving is present or future: Calvin's editor says one must either render the participle as being about to receive or take it of the soul's present salvation as distinct from that of soul and body hereafter, and prefers the latter; Barnes says their present peace was such that it might be said they were already saved; Clarke says the salvation was already received; Wesley makes it present outright, from all sin into all holiness, and only then the pledge of the eternal

Why only souls are named: Gill says the word your is supplied, standing in the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic where the Vulgate reads only the salvation of souls, and denies that bodies are excluded; Ellicott rejects the wider reading that would take in other men's souls, on the context and on Peter's habit of dropping articles; Calvin asks the same question and answers that salvation is properly ascribed to what is immortal, the body not being excluded from the glory

What faith is set against: Ellicott holds that in this epistle and in Hebrews faith is the opposite of sight rather than of works, and suggests the definition in Hebrews may have been drawn from Peter's writings; Calvin sets it against sight as well, saying faith has eyes that penetrate the invisible kingdom and are content with the mirror of the Word, and denies the sophists' confused and implicit grasp of God

What salvation excludes: Ellicott states that here at any rate the word contains no allusion to damnation as an opposite, and defines it as the restoration of man to the ideal excellence from which he fell
outliers: Ellicott's observation that the verb for love is the one Christ used in questioning Peter, not the warmer word with which Peter answered
Robertson's argument that Peter heard the saying to Thomas in person and could use it before John wrote his Gospel
Barnes's reply to the charge that faith deceives, that the senses deceive too, and that a merchant refusing to trade with London or Canton for never having seen them would be reputed mad
Ellicott's report of the variant reading, whom without knowing him ye love, and Bengel's note that the clause is meant for a paradox
Ellicott's quotation of the hymn beginning a charge to keep I have, and his contrast of Christian self-concern with the Buddhist longing for extinction
Calvin's warning that those not raised by this joy above the heavens boast their faith in vain

10.pericope_label: The prophets who searched what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them pointed to, testifying the sufferings and the glories to follow

schools.summary: John Gill says the prophets greatly desired the coming of the Saviour and to see him, longed after the salvation to be accomplished by him and expressed their wishes for it, and inquired into the nature of it and gave an account thereof according to the measure of light and knowledge communicated to them, pointing out Christ as a Redeemer of his people and his salvation as spiritual and eternal. On the following verse Gill says the prophets made a very diligent inquiry into the exact time when Christ should come to work out the salvation of his people, to whom it was made known that his coming should be before the sceptre, or tribe of Judah, and all civil government in it ceased, and before the second temple was destroyed, into which the Messiah, the messenger of the covenant, was to come as the Lord and proprietor of it, and that it should be seventy weeks, or four hundred and ninety years, from a date given in as it was revealed to the Prophet Daniel, who particularly inquired and diligently searched into this matter and was eminently a man of desires this way, as he is styled. They not only searched into the exact time, Gill says, but into the manner and quality of the time when the Saviour should come, and foretold that it would be, with respect to the nations of the world, a time of profound peace, and with respect to the Jews, that it would be a time of great blindness, ignorance, unbelief and hardness of heart, and that such would be that generation or age for wickedness and barbarity. John Calvin says he hence commends the value of salvation because the prophets had their minds intensely fixed on it, for it must have been a great matter, and possessing peculiar excellency, which could have thus kindled in the prophets a spirit of inquiry respecting it; but still more clearly does God's goodness toward us shine forth in this case, because much more is now made known to us than what all the prophets attained by their long and anxious inquiries. At the same time he confirms the certainty of salvation by this very antiquity, Calvin says, for from the beginning of the world it had received a plain testimony from the Holy Spirit; and two things ought to be distinctly noticed, that he declares more has been given to us than to the ancient fathers, in order to amplify by this comparison the grace of the gospel, and then that what is preached to us respecting salvation cannot be suspected of any novelty, for the Spirit had formerly testified of it by the prophets. When he says that the prophets searched and sedulously inquired, Calvin says, this does not belong to their writings or doctrine but to the private desire with which every one boiled over, while what is said afterwards is to be referred to their public office. He arranges the passage under certain propositions: first, that the prophets who foretold of the grace which Christ exhibited at his coming diligently inquired as to the time when full revelation was to be made; second, that the Spirit of Christ predicted by them of the future condition of Christ's kingdom, such as it is now and such as it is expected yet to be, even that it is destined that Christ and his whole body should through various sufferings enter into glory; third, that the prophets ministered to us more abundantly than to their own age, and that this was revealed to them from above, for in Christ only is the full exhibition of those things of which God then presented but an obscure image; fourth, that in the Gospel is contained a clear confirmation of prophetic doctrine but also a much fuller and plainer explanation, for the salvation which he formerly proclaimed as it were at a distance by the prophets he now reveals openly to us and as it were before our eyes; and last, that it hence appears evident how wonderful is the glory of that salvation promised to us in the Gospel, because even angels, though they enjoy God's presence in heaven, yet burn with the desire of seeing it. All these things tend to show this one thing, Calvin says, that Christians, elevated to the height of their felicity, ought to surmount all the obstacles of the world, for what is there which this incomparable benefit does not reduce to nothing. Had not the fathers the same salvation as we have, Calvin asks, and why then does he speak as though they possessed not what is now offered to us; the answer is plain, that salvation is to be taken here for that clear manifestation of it which we have through the coming of Christ, and the words of Peter mean no other thing than those of Christ when he said that many kings and prophets have desired to see the things which ye see and have not seen them. As the prophets had but a limited knowledge of the grace brought by Christ, as to its revelation they justly desired something more, Calvin says; and when Simeon, after seeing Christ, prepared himself calmly and with a satisfied mind for death, he showed that he was before unsatisfied and anxious, such being the feeling of all the godly. There was a difference between the law and the gospel, Calvin says, a veil as it were being interposed, that they might not see those things nearer which are now set before our eyes, nor was it indeed proper, while Christ the Sun of righteousness was yet absent, that the full light should shine as at midday; and though it was their duty to confine themselves within their prescribed limits, yet it was no superstition to sigh with a desire of having a nearer sight, for when they wished that redemption should be hastened and desired daily to see it, there was nothing in such a wish to prevent them patiently to wait as long as it pleased the Lord to defer the time. To seek as to prophecies the particular time seems to him unprofitable, Calvin says, for what is spoken of here is not what the prophets taught but what they wished. It is worthy of observation that he does not say the prophets searched according to their own understanding as to the time when Christ's kingdom would come, but that they applied their minds to the revelation of the Spirit, Calvin says: thus they have taught us by their example a sobriety in learning, for they did not go beyond what the Spirit taught them, and doubtless there will be no limits to man's curiosity except the Spirit of God preside over their minds, so that they may not desire anything else than to speak from him; and further, the spiritual kingdom is a higher subject than what the human mind can succeed in investigating, except the Spirit be the guide. By the expressions that the Spirit was in them and was testifying, Calvin says, he intimates that the prophets were endued with the Spirit of knowledge, and indeed in no common manner, as those who have been teachers and witnesses to us, and that yet they were not partakers of that light which is exhibited to us; at the same time a high praise is given to their doctrine, for it was the testimony of the Holy Spirit, the preachers and ministers being men but he the teacher. Nor does he declare without reason that the Spirit of Christ then ruled, Calvin says, and he makes the Spirit sent from heaven to preside over the teachers of the Gospel, for he shows that the Gospel comes from God and that the ancient prophecies were dictated by Christ. That they might bear submissively their afflictions he reminds them that these had been long ago foretold by the Spirit, Calvin says, but he includes much more than this, for he teaches us that the Church of Christ has been from the beginning so constituted that the cross has been the way to victory and death a passage to life, and that this had been clearly testified; there is therefore no reason why afflictions should above measure depress us, as though we were miserable under them, since the Spirit of God pronounces us blessed. The order is to be noticed, Calvin says: he mentions sufferings first and then adds the glories which are to follow, intimating that this order cannot be changed or subverted, since afflictions must precede glory; so there is to be understood a twofold truth in these words, that Christians must suffer many troubles before they enjoy glory, and that afflictions are not evils because they have glory annexed to them, and since God has ordained this connection it does not behove us to separate the one from the other. It is no common consolation that our condition, such as we find it to be, has been foretold so many ages ago, Calvin says: hence we learn that it is not in vain that a happy end is promised to us, we know that we are not afflicted by chance but through the infallible providence of God, and prophecies are like mirrors to set forth to us in tribulations the image of celestial glory. Peter says that the Spirit had testified of the coming afflictions of Christ, Calvin observes, but he does not separate Christ from his body, so that this is not to be confined to the person of Christ but a beginning is to be made with the head, that the members may in due order follow, as Paul also teaches that we must be conformed to him who is the first-born among his brethren; in short, Peter does not speak of what is peculiar to Christ but of the universal state of the Church. It is much fitted to confirm our faith when he sets forth our afflictions as viewed in Christ, Calvin says, for we thereby see better the connection of death and life between us and him, and doubtless this is the privilege and manner of the holy union, that he suffers daily in his members, that after his sufferings shall be completed in us glory also may have its completion.

Matthew Henry says the apostle, having described the persons to whom he wrote and declared to them the excellent advantages they were under, goes on to show them what warrant he had for what he had delivered; and because they were Jews and had a profound veneration for the Old Testament, he produces the authority of the prophets to convince them that the doctrine of salvation by faith in Jesus Christ was no new doctrine but the same which the old prophets did inquire and search diligently into. Those who made this diligent search were the prophets, Henry says, persons inspired by God either to do or to say things extraordinary, above the reach of their own studies and abilities, as foretelling things to come and revealing the will of God by the direction of the Holy Spirit. The object of their search was salvation and the grace of God which should come, Henry says, the general salvation of men of all nations by Jesus Christ and more especially the salvation afforded to the Jews, the grace that should come to them from him who was not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; they foresaw glorious times of light, grace and comfort coming upon the church, which made the prophets and righteous men desire to see and hear the things which came to pass in the days of the gospel. The manner of their inquiry was that they inquired and searched diligently, Henry says: the words are strong and emphatic, alluding to miners who dig to the bottom and break through not only the earth but the rock to come to the ore, so that these holy prophets had an earnest desire to know and were proportionably diligent in their inquiries after the grace of God which was to be revealed in the days of the Messiah. Their being inspired did not make their industrious search needless, Henry says, for notwithstanding their extraordinary assistance from God they were obliged to make use of all the ordinary methods of improvement in wisdom and knowledge: Daniel was a man greatly beloved and inspired, yet he understood by books and study the computations of time; and even their own revelation required their study, meditation and prayer, for many prophecies had a double meaning, in their first intention aiming at some person or event near at hand while their ultimate design was to describe the person, sufferings or kingdom of Christ. The doctrine of man's salvation by Jesus Christ has been the study and admiration of the greatest and wisest of men, Henry says, the nobleness of the subject and their own concern in it having engaged them with most accurate attention and seriousness to search into it; a good man is much affected and pleased with the grace and mercy of God to others as well as to himself, and the prophets were highly delighted with the prospects of mercy to be shown both to Jews and Gentiles at the coming of Christ; those who would be acquainted with this great salvation and the grace that shines therein must inquire and search diligently into it, for if it was necessary for an inspired prophet to do so, much more for persons so weak and injudicious as we are; and the grace that came by the gospel excels all that was before it, the gospel dispensation being more glorious, evident, intelligible, extensive and effectual than any dispensation that ever did precede it. The particular matters which the ancient prophets chiefly searched into are expressed in the next verse, Henry says: Jesus Christ was the main subject of their studies, and in relation to him they were most inquisitive into his humiliation and death and the glorious consequences of it, the sufferings of Christ and the glories that should follow, an inquiry which would lead them into a view of the whole gospel, the sum whereof is that Christ Jesus was delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification; and into the time and the manner of the times wherein the Messiah was to appear, since undoubtedly these holy prophets earnestly desired to see the days of the Son of man, and therefore, next to the thing itself, their minds were set upon the time of its accomplishment, so far as the Spirit of Christ which was in them had signified anything towards that purpose.

Albert Barnes says the object of this reference to the prophets seems to be to lead them to value the religion which they professed more highly and to encourage them to bear their trials with patience, since they were in many respects in a condition far superior to that of the prophets: they had the full light of the gospel, while the prophets saw it only at a distance and but dimly and were obliged to search anxiously that they might understand the nature of that system of which they were appointed to furnish the comparatively obscure intimations. The word rendered inquired is intensive, Barnes says, meaning that they sought out or scrutinised with care the revelations made to them that they might understand exactly what was implied in that which they were appointed to record; and the word rendered searched diligently means to search out, to trace out, to explore, and is not elsewhere used in the New Testament, though one of the words from which it is compounded occurs. The idea is that they perceived that in their communications there were some great and glorious truths which they did not fully comprehend, and that they diligently employed their natural faculties to understand that which they were appointed to impart to succeeding generations, Barnes says: they thus became students and interpreters for themselves of their own predictions, for they were not only prophets but men, having souls to be saved in the same way as others and hearts to be sanctified by the truth; the mere fact that they were the channels or organs for imparting truth to others would not save them, any more than the fact that a man now preaches truth to others will save himself, or than the fact that a sutler delivers bread to an army will nourish his own body. The apostle does not mean to say that they prophesied particularly of those persons to whom he was then writing, Barnes says, but that their prophecies were in fact for their benefit, for the things which they predicted had actually terminated on them, and the benefit was as real as though the predictions had been solely on their account. On the following verse Barnes says they were examining their own predictions with care to ascertain what they meant, studying them as we do the predictions which others have made, so that though the prophets were the medium through which the truth was made known, yet their own predictions became a subject of careful investigation to themselves. The expression rendered what may mean, so far as the Greek is concerned, either what time or what people or what person, Barnes says, and the latter seems to him the correct interpretation, meaning that they inquired in regard to him, who he would be, what would be his character, and what would be the nature of the work which he would perform; there can be no doubt that they understood that their predictions related to the Messiah, but it is not improper to suppose that it was with them an interesting inquiry what sort of a person he would be. This interpretation is not that which is commonly given of the passage, Barnes admits: Bloomfield, Rosenmuller, Doddridge, Whitby, Benson and Grotius suppose it to refer to time, meaning that they inquired when these things would occur, and Macknight thinks it refers to people, meaning that they diligently inquired what people would put him to death; but the most obvious interpretation is that they made particular inquiry to whom their prophecies related, what was his rank and character, and what was to be the nature of his work, than which what could be a more natural inquiry for them, or more important. How interesting is the thought, Barnes says, that when Isaiah, for example, had given utterance to the sublime predictions which we now have of the Messiah, he sat himself down with the spirit of a little child to learn by prayer and study what was fully implied in the amazing words which the Spirit had taught him to record. The phrase rendered what manner of time would properly relate not to the exact date when these things would occur but to the character or condition of the age when they would take place, Barnes says, perhaps referring to the state of the world at that period, the preparation to receive the gospel, and the probable manner in which the great message would be received; though perhaps the inquiry in their minds pertained to the time as well, and the meaning of the Greek phrase would not exclude this latter sense, since there are not unfrequent indications of time in the prophets, and these were of so clear a character that when the Saviour actually appeared there was a general expectation that the event would then occur. The mention of the Spirit of Christ does not prove that the prophets knew that this was the Spirit of Christ, Barnes says, but is only a declaration of Peter that it was actually so; it is not probable that they distinctly understood that the Spirit of inspiration by which they were led to foretell future events was peculiarly the Spirit of Christ, for they understood that they were inspired, but there is no intimation in their writings that they regarded themselves as inspired by the Messiah. It was not improper, however, for Peter to say that the Spirit by which they were influenced was in fact the Spirit of Christ, Barnes says, so called because that Spirit which suggested these future events to them was given as the great Medium of all revealed truth to the world; and it is clear from this passage that Christ must have had an existence before his incarnation, and that he must have understood then what would occur to him when he should become incarnate, that is, it must have been arranged or determined beforehand. They saw clearly that the Messiah was to suffer, Barnes says, and doubtless this was the common doctrine of the prophets and the common expectation of the pious part of the Jewish nation, yet it is not necessary to suppose that they had clear apprehensions of his sufferings or were able to reconcile all that was said on that subject with what was said of his glory and his triumphs; we have no reason to suppose that there were any views of the sufferings of the Messiah communicated to the prophets except what we now have in the Old Testament, and to see the force of what Peter says we ought to imagine what would be our views of him if all that we have known of Christ as history were obliterated and we had only the knowledge which we could derive from the Old Testament. They saw that there would be glory which would be the result of his sufferings, Barnes says, but they did not clearly see what it would be: they had some knowledge that he would be raised from the dead, they knew that he would see of the travail of his soul and would be satisfied, and they had some large views of the effects of the gospel on the nations of the earth, but there were many things respecting his glorification which it cannot be supposed they understood. Charles Ellicott says the preposition stands for concerning or with regard to, and that the salvation which formed the subject of investigation to the prophets was the present deliverance of the believing soul from sin and gloom as well as the salvation yet future; it is difficult not to believe that the song of Zacharias was in Peter's mind when he thus wrote, Ellicott says, since the theme of that song is precisely the glory of present salvation through Christ and the fulfilment of prophecy thereby. The rendering should be did inquire, Ellicott says, for our present version tends to convey the notion that the prophetic writings which we now possess are the result of the inquiry, which would be wrong; and here he quotes Calvin as rightly saying that when Peter states that the prophets inquired and examined, this refers not to their writings or teaching but to the private longing with which each was fired. In fact Peter goes on to say that the writings which the Holy Spirit impelled them to make were actually the text on which their longings were the comment, Ellicott says, since they endeavoured to understand what they themselves had written; the two Greek words give a much more lively picture than the English of the intense eagerness of the search and of the depth to which it penetrated, and if these great prophets took such pains to understand our present salvation we ought to take heed not to let it slip, precisely the same argument being used for precisely the same purpose by our Lord in Matthew. The whole subject of the Old Testament is the bounty of God under the New, Ellicott says, and this was what the prophets tried to realise; the italicised words might with advantage be changed into the grace in reserve for you, and grace here seems to mean little more than favour or bounty and not the ordinary theological sense, the favour consisting in our salvation. On the following verse Ellicott says the present passage is perhaps the most striking in the whole New Testament in regard to the doctrine of prophetic inspiration: assuming that the prophets did not speak simply of their own human calculation but somehow under the influence of the Divine Spirit, we are brought to face the question how far their utterances were their own and how far suggested to them from on high. The doctrine of Montanism, which has not altogether died out of the Church yet, asserts that from first to last prophecy is superhuman, Ellicott says, that every word and letter is forced upon the man by a power not his own which leaves him no choice, God and God alone being responsible for every syllable, so that the human will and intelligence need not even concur in the message they deliver nor even be conscious that they are delivering it; thus Montanus makes God say through him that man is as a lyre and God as that which strikes the chords, the man being unconscious and God alone awake. On the other hand some of the early opponents of Montanism went so far as to say that the inspired writers had a clear and immediate perception, a complete insight into the mysteries which they foretold, that Isaiah for instance saw as plainly as we do Mary and Jesus in his prophecy of Immanuel, Ellicott says; but the present verses show a doctrine between the two, since the prophets find themselves impelled to say words which they are conscious of choosing and using but which they feel to have a deeper meaning than they themselves were conscious of intending, and it is clear to them that what they meant primarily as applying to present circumstances was in reality being overruled by the Spirit to apply more fully to the future, though what that future was they struggled, and half in vain, to know. We may apply to them what Keble says of the Greek poets, Ellicott adds, that as little children lisp and tell of heaven, so thoughts beyond their thoughts to those high bards were given. The simplest translation would be, to whom or what period the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing, Ellicott says, which would give new significance to the sentence: they were aware that they were speaking of a Messiah, but who the man should be who would hold that office, or at what period of their history he would arise, this was what they longed to know, so that they foresaw a Christ but could not foresee Jesus and could give to their Christ no definite position in future history. They are conscious of a power within them which is not themselves, moving them, and this power is described as the Spirit of Christ, Ellicott says; but observe that a change has come over Peter's way of speaking, for hitherto he has always said Jesus Christ, his object being to keep constantly before the eyes of these Hebrews the truth which he was the first man to enunciate, that Jesus was the person who fulfilled all that was expected of the Messiah; the title is not once used by Peter, as it is often by Paul, as a proper name, for it always marks the office and not the person. Therefore we may not prove by this expression two doctrines, however true they may be in themselves, which are commonly sought to be supported by it, Ellicott says, namely the pre-existence of our Lord and the procession of the Holy Ghost from him as well as from the Father; in spite of a well-quoted passage in Barnabas, that the prophets had the gift from him and prophesied of him, it cannot here mean the Holy Ghost given them by our Lord himself, and besides, it is theologically incorrect to say that Christ as the Anointed had any pre-existence except as an indefinite hope in the minds of the Hebrews, since the Son, the unincarnate Word, pre-existed, but it is Apollinarianism to say that Jesus had any existence before the Incarnation, still more the Christ, it being doubtful whether the Incarnate Word became Christ until his baptism. The Spirit of Messiah, then, at any rate when applied to the ages before Christ came, must have a different meaning, Ellicott says, probably not exactly the Spirit that was to anoint and be in the Messiah but rather the Messianic spirit, the prophets wondering who the man was and where he would live to whom this inspiration which they felt within was pointing. The word rendered testified beforehand is much more solemn in the original than it looks in the English and is used by no other writer than Peter, Ellicott says: it does not mean simply that it bore witness beforehand, but testifying means an appeal to Heaven to mark and record the words so spoken, and he asks whether the writer was not thinking of the awful appeal in Daniel. The English unduly contracts the fulness of the Greek, Ellicott says, which reads the sufferings for Christ, that is, these sufferings in reserve for Messiah, and the Old Testament passages chiefly indicated may be supposed to be the fifty-third of Isaiah and still more the ninth of Daniel; if it be asked how Peter knew that the prophets had these longings and doubts, the answer is that it was not only a probable guess but the result of a study of Daniel, who records again and again the prophetic agony of his search into the future. Beware of treating the title as a proper name, Ellicott warns: eight out of the ten times that Peter uses the word by itself, that is without Jesus or the Lord, it is in direct connection with suffering, and conversely he never speaks of the sufferings of Jesus Christ, loving to dwell upon the Passion of our Lord not in its personal but its official aspect, since the striking point is that the Messiah should have suffered thus, which it was especially necessary to show in any effort to retain the faith of the Hebrews. We can see a reason for the insistence in Peter's history, Ellicott says: the very same day, apparently, when he had announced his belief that Jesus was the Messiah, he took him to task for speaking of sufferings and shame, and he never could forget the reprimand, like a sword-cut, which he received, so that the whole Epistle may be said to be an expansion of what Jesus said in answer. Some commentators include in the phrase the thought of the sufferings of the Church as well, Ellicott says, but it seems far-fetched, especially when we see the true meaning of the word Christ; and some would join very closely together the words for signify and testifying beforehand, which is possible and keeps the same sense but unnecessarily complicates the sentence. The literal rendering of the last clause is and the glories after them, Ellicott says, the plural corresponding to the plural sufferings, the one as multiform as the other, namely resurrection, ascension, reassumption of the divine glory, triumphs of Church history and restitution of all things, the sufferings and subsequent glories of the Christ forming together the whole of the gospel. A.T. Robertson says this is another relative clause taking up the word salvation from the previous verse and incorporating it in this long sentence, all connected by relatives, and quotes Bigg that Peter lingers over the word salvation with something new to say each time, the sense here being the general one of the gospel of grace. Sought is a first aorist active indicative of a late and rare compound found only in the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament save once in Aristides, Robertson says, and searched diligently is a first aorist active indicative of an old and common compound found here only in the New Testament, both of these words occurring together in the first book of Maccabees. On the following verse Robertson says searching is a present active participle of a late form of the uncompounded verb, the compound occurring in the preceding verse, and that the qualitative interrogative keeps its proper sense here though elsewhere it is losing its distinctive force; the prophets knew what they prophesied but not at what time the Messianic prophecies would be fulfilled. Peter definitely asserts here that the Spirit of Jesus Christ the Messiah was in the Old Testament prophets, Robertson says, the Holy Spirit being called the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God, who spoke to the prophets as he would speak to the apostles. Did point unto is an imperfect active meaning did keep on pointing to, though they did not clearly perceive the time, Robertson says; and the word for testifying beforehand is a present middle participle of a late compound unknown elsewhere save in a writer of the fourteenth century and now in a papyrus of the eighth, which is neuter here because the word for Spirit is neuter, but this grammatical gender should not be retained as it in English and should be rendered he. Here we have predictive prophecy concerning the Messiah, Robertson says, though some modern critics fail to find predictions of the Messiah in the Old Testament; the phrase means the sufferings destined for Christ, like the similar use of the preposition in the preceding verse, and the last clause means the glories after these sufferings, the plural of the word for glory being rare but occurring in Exodus and Hosea, since the glories of Christ followed the sufferings.

Adam Clarke says the incarnation and suffering of Jesus Christ, and the redemption procured by him for mankind, were made known in a general way by the prophets, but they themselves did not know the time when these things were to take place nor the people among and by whom he was to suffer; they therefore inquired accurately or earnestly and searched diligently, inquiring of others who were then under the same inspiration and carefully searching the writings of those who had before their time spoken of these things. The prophets plainly saw that the grace which was to come under the Messiah's kingdom was vastly superior to anything that had ever been exhibited under the law, Clarke says, and in consequence they made all possible inquiry and searched as after grains of gold hidden among sand or compacted with ore, for such is the meaning of the original word, in order to ascertain the time and the signs of that time in which this wondrous display of God's love and mercy to man was to take place; but all that God thought fit to instruct them in is what is mentioned in the verse that follows. On the glory that should follow, Clarke says it means not only the glory of his resurrection, ascension, exaltation and the effusion of his Spirit, but that grand manifestation of God's infinite love to the world in causing the Gospel of his Son to be everywhere preached, and the glorious moral changes which should take place in the world under that preaching, and the final glorification of all them who had here received the report and continued faithful unto death; and we may add to this the ineffable glorification of the human nature of Jesus Christ, which throughout eternity will be the glorious Head of his glorified body, the Church. John Wesley says the salvation spoken of is so far beyond all that was experienced under the Jewish dispensation, and that the very prophets who prophesied long ago of the grace of God toward them spoke of his abundant, overflowing grace to be bestowed on believers under the Christian dispensation. Inquired means they were earnestly inquisitive, Wesley says, and searched diligently means like miners searching after precious ore, after the meaning of the prophecies which they delivered. On the following verse Wesley says searching what time means what particular period, and what manner of time means by what marks to be distinguished; and the glories that were to follow his sufferings are the glory of his resurrection, ascension, exaltation and the effusion of his Spirit, the glory of the last judgment and of his eternal kingdom, and also the glories of his grace in the hearts and lives of Christians.
