debates: What the prophets were searching for: Barnes takes the phrase of a person and lists Bloomfield, Rosenmuller, Doddridge, Whitby, Benson and Grotius against him for time and Macknight for people; Ellicott reads it as person or period together and says they foresaw a Christ but could not foresee Jesus; Robertson keeps to time; Gill holds that they were shown the answer, before the sceptre departed from Judah and four hundred and ninety years from Daniel's date

Whether the verse proves the pre-existence of Christ: Barnes says it is clear from the passage that Christ existed before his incarnation and knew beforehand what would befall him; Ellicott denies that it may be used so, since the title marks the office and not the person, and refuses on the same ground the argument for the procession of the Spirit from the Son; Robertson and Calvin both take the Spirit of Christ as asserted of the prophets outright

How far prophecy is the prophet's own: Ellicott sets the passage between the Montanist doctrine that every syllable is forced upon an unconscious man and the opposite view that Isaiah saw Mary and Jesus plainly, and takes the middle, that they chose their words yet meant less than the Spirit meant; Calvin says they applied their minds to the revelation of the Spirit and did not go beyond what it taught, which he calls a sobriety in learning

Whose sufferings are meant: Calvin refuses to confine them to the person of Christ, since Peter does not separate him from his body and the cross is the way to victory for the whole Church; Ellicott calls that extension far-fetched and holds the phrase strictly of the Messiah's own passion
outliers: Ellicott's quotation of Calvin by name and with approval, on a point Calvin's own block in this catena makes
Ellicott's quotation of Montanus, that man is as a lyre and God as that which strikes the chords, the man unconscious and God alone awake
Ellicott's count that eight of the ten times Peter uses the bare title it stands with suffering, and that he never speaks of the sufferings of Jesus Christ
Ellicott's reading of the epistle as an expansion of the reprimand Peter received, like a sword-cut, for rebuking Christ over his sufferings
Barnes's comparison that being a channel of truth no more saves the prophet than delivering bread to an army nourishes the sutler
Robertson's note that the participle is neuter only by grammatical agreement and should be rendered he rather than it

12.pericope_label: To the prophets it was revealed that they ministered not to themselves but to you, in things angels desire to look into

schools.summary: John Gill says what was revealed to the prophets was the salvation they searched and inquired into, and the grace of it, the time of its being wrought out, and what sort of times they would be when Christ should come, both to the church and to the world, among Jews and Gentiles, as also what cruel sufferings the Messiah should undergo and what great glory should be put upon him afterwards. John Calvin says this passage has been strangely perverted by fanatics so as to exclude the fathers who lived under the law from the hope of eternal salvation, for it does not deny that the prophets usefully ministered to their own age and edified the church, but teaches us that their ministry is more useful to us because we are fallen on the ends of the world. We see how highly they extolled the kingdom of Christ, Calvin says, how assiduous they were in adorning it, how diligently they stimulated all to seek it, but they were by death deprived of the privilege of seeing it as it now is; what else then was this but that they spread the table that others might afterwards feed on the provisions laid on it. They indeed tasted by faith of those things which the Lord has by their hands transmitted to be enjoyed by us, Calvin says, and they also partook of Christ as the real food of their souls, but what is spoken of now is the exhibition of this blessing, and we know that the prophetic office was confined as it were within limits in order that they might support themselves and others with the hope of Christ who was to come; they therefore possessed him as one hidden and as it were absent, absent not in power or grace but because he was not yet manifested in the flesh, so that his kingdom also was as yet hid as it were under coverings. At length descending on earth he in a manner opened heaven to us, Calvin says, so that we might have a near view of those spiritual riches which before were under types exhibited at a distance, and this fruition of Christ as manifested forms the difference between us and the prophets; hence we learn how they ministered to us rather than to themselves. But though the prophets were admonished from above that the grace which they proclaimed would be deferred to another age, Calvin says, yet they were not slothful in proclaiming it, so far were they from being broken down with weariness; and if their patience was so great, surely we shall be twice and thrice ungrateful if the fruition of the grace denied to them will not sustain us under all the evils which are to be endured. He again marks the difference between the ancient doctrine and the preaching of the gospel, Calvin says, for as the righteousness of God is revealed in the gospel, having a testimony from the law and the prophets, so also the glory of Christ, of which the Spirit testified formerly, is now openly proclaimed; and at the same time he hence proves the certainty of the gospel, because it contains nothing but what had been long ago testified by the Spirit of God, and he further reminds them that under the banner of the same Spirit, by his dictation and guidance, the gospel was preached, lest they might think of anything human in this case. It is indeed the highest praise to the gospel that it contains treasures of wisdom as yet concealed and hidden from angels, Calvin says; but some one may object and say that it is not reasonable that things should be open and known to us which are hidden from angels, who always see the face of God and are his ministers in ruling the church and in the administration of all his blessings. To this Calvin answers that things are open to us as far as we see them in the mirror of the word, but our knowledge is not said to be higher than that of angels, Peter only meaning that such things are promised to us as angels desire to see fulfilled; Paul says that by the calling of the Gentiles the wonderful wisdom of God was made known to angels, for it was a spectacle to them when Christ gathered into one body the lost world, alienated for so many ages from the hope of life, and thus daily they see with admiration the magnificent works of God in the government of his church. How much greater will their admiration be at witnessing the last display of divine justice, when the kingdom of Christ shall be completed, Calvin says: this is as yet hidden, the revelation of which they still expect and justly wish to see. The passage admits of a twofold meaning, Calvin allows, either that the treasure we have in the gospel fills the angels with a desire to see it, as a sight especially delightful to them, or that they anxiously desire to see the kingdom of Christ, the living image of which is set forth in the gospel; but the last seems to him the most suitable meaning.

Albert Barnes says the prophets were not permitted to know fully the import of the predictions which they were made the instruments of communicating to mankind, but they understood that these were intended for the benefit of future ages. We are not to suppose that they derived no benefit from their own predictions, Barnes says, for as far as they understood the truth it was as much adapted to sanctify and comfort them as it is us now; but the meaning is that their messages had reference mainly to future times, and that the full benefit of them would be experienced only in distant ages. The ministration was not to those addressed by name, Barnes says, but had reference to the times of the Messiah, and those to whom Peter wrote, in common with all Christians, were those who were to enjoy the fruits of the communications made; those who preached the gospel to them were the apostles, who had made known in their true sense the things which the prophets predicted, accompanied by the influences of the Holy Ghost bearing those truths to the heart, it being the same Spirit which inspired the prophets which conveyed those truths to the souls of the early Christians and which discloses them to true believers in every age. The object of Peter in thus referring to the prophets seems to have been to impress on them a deep sense of the value of the gospel and of the great privileges which they enjoyed, Barnes says: they were reaping the benefit of all the labours of the prophets, permitted to see truth clearly which the prophets themselves saw only obscurely, and in many respects more favoured than even those holy men had been, since it was for them that the prophets had spoken the word of the Lord, and while the prophets had not been allowed to understand the full import of their own predictions, the most humble believer was permitted to see what the most distinguished prophet never saw. The object of the reference to the angels is the same, Barnes says, to impress on Christians a sense of the value of that gospel which they had received and to show them the greatness of their privileges, since it had excited the deepest interest among the most holy men on earth and even among the inhabitants of the skies; the things referred to are those which the prophets were so desirous to understand, the great truths respecting the sufferings of Christ, the glory which would follow, and the nature and effects of the gospel. The word rendered to look means to stoop down near by anything, to bend forward near in order to look at anything more closely, Barnes says, and would denote that state where one who was before at so great a distance that he could not clearly see an object should draw nearer, stooping down in order that he might observe it more distinctly; it is possible, as Grotius supposes, that there may be an allusion here to the posture of the cherubim over the mercy-seat, represented as looking down with an intense gaze as if to behold what was in the ark, but it is not necessary to suppose that this is the allusion, nor is it absolutely certain that that was the posture of the cherubim, all that is necessarily implied being that the angels had an intense desire to look into these things. In illustration of this sentiment Barnes makes several suggestions: that the angels doubtless desire to look into all the manifestations of the character of God wherever they are made, since it is not unreasonable to suppose that to a great degree they acquire the knowledge of God as all other creatures do, not being omniscient and not able to comprehend at a glance all his doings; that they doubtless employ their faculties substantially as we do in the investigation of truth, seeking from things known to learn those that are unknown; that there are many things in relation to the divine character and plans which they do not yet understand, since they know undoubtedly much more than we do but there are plans and purposes of God yet made known to none of his creatures; that they feel a great interest in the welfare of other beings, there being in the universe one great brotherhood embracing all the creatures of God; and that they cannot but feel a deep interest in man, a fallen creature, tempted, suffering, dying and exposed to eternal death, which they have shown in every period of the world's history. It is probable that in each one of the worlds which God has made there is some peculiar manifestation of his glory and character, Barnes continues, something not to be found at all in any other world, or if found not in so great perfection, and that the angels would feel a deep interest in all these manifestations and would desire to look into them; this is probable from the nature of the case and from the variety which we see in the form, size, movements and glory of the heavenly orbs, and probable also from what we can now see of the worlds which he has made, since we know as yet comparatively little of the heavenly bodies, and yet, as far as we can see, there must be far more striking exhibitions of the power and wisdom and glory of God in many of those worlds that roll above us than there is on our earth. On the body of the sun, and on the planets Jupiter and Saturn, so vast in comparison with the earth, there must be far more impressive exhibitions of the glory of the Creator than there is on our little planet, Barnes says, and he describes Saturn as eighty-two thousand miles in diameter, eleven hundred times as large as our earth, moving at the rate of twenty-two thousand miles an hour and encircled by two magnificent rings five thousand miles apart, the innermost twenty-one thousand miles from the body of the planet and twenty-two thousand miles in breadth, forming a vast illuminated arch above the brightness of our moon. The universe therefore seems fitted up to give eternal employment to mind in contemplating it, Barnes says, and in the worlds which God has made there is enough to employ the study of his creatures for ever, since on our own world the most diligent and pious student of the works of God might spend many thousand years and then leave much which he did not comprehend, and it may yet be the eternal employment of holy minds to range from world to world and in each new world to find much to study and to admire. Charles Ellicott says that as the previous verse expanded and expounded the words inquired and searched, so the first part of this verse expounds the words prophesied of the grace in reserve for you: the revelation here spoken of is not a special revelation sent in answer to their laborious musings but rather the very thing which occasioned them, the perplexity consisting in feeling that God had a further meaning for their words; and the exact limits of the revelation are mentioned, for they were shown that they spoke for the benefit of futurity and no more, which he calls a trial of faith and a sublime disappointment. Far the better reading is unto you rather than unto us, Ellicott says, it being a distinct characteristic of this epistle that we, us and our are so seldom used in the best text where they might have been expected: where Paul throws in his own sympathy and puts himself on a footing with those whom he addresses, Peter utters his lofty pastoral from above, and there are but four places in the epistle where he associates himself thus with his brethren, one of those being really a quotation and one at best a very doubtful reading, while the same tendency may be observed in his speech at the council, where the right reading is made choice among you. In the original the phrase is simply them, Ellicott says, so that a semicolon might better follow than a comma, and the most natural thing is to suppose that the pronoun represents the preceding sufferings in reserve for Messiah and the glories after. In what sense then could the prophets minister, either to themselves or to us, the sufferings and glories of Messiah, Ellicott asks: the word is one which signifies a servant bringing to his master the things which he needs, commonly used of serving up a meal, and the prophets are said to serve the Messianic sufferings and glories to us, to wait upon us with them, to present them to our use and study and comfort; but when it says that they ministered them not to themselves but to us, we must not suppose that they derived no comfort from their predictions, the not being taken in the same sense as in the saying, I will have mercy and not sacrifice. The rendering should be that these things were, not are, openly declared to you, Ellicott says, in all their details, in contrast with the dim and vague way in which they were seen before, such being the force of this compound Greek verb elsewhere; and more correctly it is through those who preached, the difference being that Peter is referring to the first bearers of the gospel to those parts and not to all who from that time to the date of the letter had preached. This is a point well worth noticing, Ellicott says, for the phrase seems to show that Peter himself was not of the number, perhaps half the churches which received the letter looking to Paul as their founder; here then we find the Rock-Apostle authoritatively setting his seal to the teaching of his junior colleague, just as he does in the second epistle, and it seems to imply that these Jewish Christians were beginning to feel a reaction from Paul's evangelical teaching, so that the Apostle of the Circumcision is called in to enforce what the Apostle of the Uncircumcision had taught. It was perhaps only with Jewish Christians that such an appeal from Paul to Peter would be made, Ellicott says, and need not imply superiority throughout the whole Church; Peter's perfect concurrence with Paul here is a sufficient contradiction to the Tubingen theory of their irreconcilable divergence, only the Tubingen school reject the epistle on the ground that it makes the Apostles too harmonious. The magnificent phrase about the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven seems meant to contrast the full effusion of the Spirit now with his limited working in the prophets, Ellicott says, but it contains more teaching than this, for the tense of the participle is such as might without violence be rendered sent once and for ever, sent in a moment; and remembering that almost undoubtedly some of the recipients of the letter were eye-witnesses of his being sent on the Day of Pentecost, Peter here claims for Paul the very same inspiration with which he himself was furnished, as he claims full inspiration for Paul's preaching here and afterwards for his writing. The which things of the last sentence is grammatically parallel to the previous one and would mean the sufferings of Messiah and the glories after, Ellicott says, but logically we have to go back to the beginning of the earlier verse, as though he said, do I say that prophets who had the mysteries of our redemption on their lips yet pored in vain to catch the detailed meaning which you catch; nay, angels, who were present at every detail and bore an active part in it all, covet now to exchange places with you that they may gaze into the mystery. The word which has here shrunk into our word to look into means really to bend aside to see, Ellicott says: in its literal sense it occurs of people standing at the side of the cave so as not to get in their own light and stooping sideways to peer in, and it seems to mean a strained attention to something which has caught your eye somewhat out of your usual line of sight. Here then the intention is to show that we are in a better position to understand the mysteries of redemption not only than prophets but also than angels, and they covet to stoop from their own point of view to ours, Ellicott says; and why so, not because of the inherent mysteriousness of the union of the two natures in Christ, for of that they are as intelligent as we or more so, but because they are incapable of fully understanding human nature, flesh and blood, with its temptations and pains, its need of a Saviour. In Francia's great picture the two angels kneel by weeping Mary and dead Christ without a trace of grief on their countenances, Ellicott observes, and the Son of God himself only became capable of entering into our infirmities through becoming flesh and experiencing the same; several passages show us that the tragedy of human history is by no means enacted only for the benefit of the actors but as a lesson, possibly, as Archbishop Whately pointed out, only a single illustration out of many in one lesson, for the instruction of unfallen spirits. This passage has impressed itself on Christian lyrics as much perhaps as any in the New Testament, Ellicott says, and he quotes two stanzas of Charles Wesley, one asking the Father's wisdom how, him that did the means ordain, angels round our altars bowing to search it out in vain, and the other of angels in fixed amazement hovering around our altars, with eager gaze adoring the grace of our Eternal Lover; and though very possibly the divine intention of the cherubim over the mercy-seat may have been to symbolise that which is here said, it is not to be thought that Peter was consciously thinking of the symbol. A.T. Robertson says the relative is a dative plural referring to the prophets who were seeking to understand, and quotes Bigg that the connexion between study and inspiration is a great mystery, adding that this is surely so but is no argument for ignorance or obscurantism, since we do the best that we can and only skirt the shore of knowledge, as Newton said. It was revealed is a first aorist passive of the old verb to reveal or to unveil, Robertson says, so that here is revelation about the revelation already received, revelation after research; did they minister is an imperfect active, have been announced is a second aorist passive of the verb to report or bring back tidings, and through them marks the intermediate agent, the gospelizers. By the Holy Ghost is an instrumental case of the personal agent without the article, Robertson says, and sent forth from heaven is a second aorist passive participle agreeing with it, the Spirit of Christ of the previous verse; desire means eagerly desire, and to look into is a first aorist active infinitive of an old compound meaning to peer into, while for the interest of angels in the Incarnation he refers to the nativity in Luke.

Adam Clarke says we may presume that in a great variety of cases the prophets did not understand the meaning of their own predictions: they had a general view of God's designs, but of particular circumstances connected with those great events they seem to have known nothing, God reserving the explanation of all particulars to the time of the issue of such prophecies. When they wished to find out the times, the seasons and the circumstances, Clarke says, God gave them to understand that it was not for themselves but for us that they did minister the things which are now reported to us by the preaching of the Gospel; this was all the satisfaction they received in consequence of their earnest searching, and this was sufficient to repress all needless curiosity and to induce them to rest satisfied that the Judge of all the earth would do right. If all succeeding interpreters of the prophecies had been contented with the same information relative to the predictions still unaccomplished, Clarke says, we should have had fewer books and more wisdom. The word rendered look into means to stoop down to, the posture of those who are earnestly intent on finding out a thing, especially a writing difficult to be read, Clarke says: they bring it to the light, place it so that the rays may fall on it as collectively as possible, and then stoop down in order to examine all the parts, that they may be able to make out the whole. There is evidently an allusion here to the attitude of the cherubim who stood at the ends of the ark of the covenant in the inner tabernacle, with their eyes turned towards the mercy-seat or propitiatory in a bending posture, as if looking attentively, or, as we term it, poring upon it, Clarke says. Even the holy angels are struck with astonishment at the plan of human redemption and justly wonder at the incarnation of that infinite object of their adoration, Clarke says, and if then these things be objects of deep consideration to the angels of God, how much more so should they be to us, since in them angels can have no such interest as human beings have. We learn from the above that it was the Spirit of Christ in the Jewish prophets that prophesied of Christ, Clarke says: it was that Spirit which revealed him, and it is the same Spirit which takes of the things of Christ and shows them unto us; Christ was never known by prophecy but through his own Spirit, and he never was known, nor can be known, to the salvation of any soul but by a revelation of the same Spirit, it being he alone that bears witness with our spirits that we are the children of God. John Wesley says the words to whom mean to those so searching, and that it was revealed that not for themselves but for us they ministered, since they did not so much by those predictions serve themselves or that generation as they did us, who now enjoy what they saw afar off. With the Holy Ghost sent down from heaven means confirmed by the inward, powerful testimony of the Holy Ghost as well as the mighty effusion of his miraculous gifts, Wesley says; and the last clause is a beautiful gradation, for prophets, righteous men and kings desired to see and hear what Christ did and taught, while what the Holy Ghost taught concerning Christ the very angels long to know.

debates: Whether the cherubim over the mercy-seat are alluded to: Clarke says the allusion is evident and describes their bending posture over the propitiatory; Barnes reports it from Grotius but doubts both the allusion and whether that was the cherubim's posture at all; Ellicott allows that the symbol may have been divinely intended to mean this without Peter's being consciously aware of it

Why angels must stoop to look: Ellicott says it is not the union of the two natures that baffles them, of which they are as intelligent as we or more, but their incapacity to understand flesh and blood with its temptations and its need of a Saviour; Calvin says instead that things are open to us only as we see them in the mirror of the word, and denies that our knowledge is called higher than theirs; Barnes supposes they acquire knowledge as other creatures do, from things known to things unknown

What the prophets gained: Calvin says the passage has been perverted by fanatics to shut the fathers out of salvation, and answers that they spread the table for others while tasting by faith themselves; Barnes and Ellicott both deny that they derived no benefit, Ellicott taking the negative in the idiom of mercy and not sacrifice; Clarke holds that the answer they received was enough to repress all needless curiosity

Whose preaching is meant: Ellicott argues that the first bearers of the gospel to those parts are intended, that Peter was not among them, and that he is here setting his seal to Paul's teaching and claiming for him the same inspiration, which he says refutes the Tubingen theory of an irreconcilable divergence
outliers: Clarke's remark that if later interpreters of unfulfilled prophecy had been content with the same information we should have had fewer books and more wisdom
Ellicott's count that Peter joins himself to his readers in only four places in the letter, one a quotation and one a doubtful reading, and utters his pastoral from above
Ellicott's appeal to Francia's painting, where two angels kneel by the weeping mother and the dead Christ without a trace of grief on their faces
Ellicott's quotation of two stanzas of Charles Wesley on angels searching the mystery in vain around our altars
Barnes's excursus on other worlds, with Saturn eleven hundred times the size of the earth and its rings twenty-two thousand miles in breadth, as fields of eternal study for holy minds
Robertson's answer to Bigg, that the mystery joining study and inspiration is no argument for obscurantism, since we only skirt the shore of knowledge

13.pericope_label: Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope perfectly for the grace being brought at the revelation of Jesus Christ

schools.summary: John Gill says the loins of the mind are to be girded with the girdle of truth, and that since angels desire to look into the mysteries of grace, the readers should apply their minds and diligently attend unto them, in opposition to all loose and vagrant thoughts of the mind about other things; they should give themselves up wholly to them, meditate upon them and employ themselves in them and about them, seeing they are the study and inquiry of angels and what the prophets have prophesied of and searched into and ministered, and the apostles of Christ have preached, and besides are things which relate to the person, office, sufferings and glory of Christ and the salvation of immortal souls. Though the phrase is sometimes used to denote preparation and readiness, Gill says, and to be in a fit position to do anything, as the Israelites were at the eating of the first passover to march at the least notice out of Egypt, and so to go a journey, to run a race, to serve another, to wait on him and for him, and also to be prepared for battle, being a metaphor taken from the custom of the eastern nations who used to wear long garments. John Calvin says that from the greatness and excellency of grace he draws an exhortation, that it surely behoved them the more readily to receive the grace of God as the more bountifully he bestowed it upon them, and we must notice the connection: he had said that so elevated was the kingdom of Christ to which the gospel calls us that even angels in heaven desire to see it, and what then ought to be done by us who are in the world. Doubtless, as long as we live on earth, so great is the distance between us and Christ that in vain he invites us to himself, Calvin says, and it is hence necessary for us to put off the image of Adam and to cast aside the whole world and all hindrances, that being thus set at liberty we may rise upwards to Christ; and he exhorted those to whom he wrote to be prepared and sober, and to hope for the graces offered to them, and also to renounce the world and their former life, and to be conformed to the will of God. The editorial matter in Calvin's block cites Pareus as observing that the Apostle in this part of the chapter exhorted the faithful to sobriety, holiness, humility and brotherly love by five reasons: because they were the children of God, because God is holy and requires holiness, because God is no respecter of persons, because of the value of the price for their redemption, and because they had been born again of an immortal seed. The first part of the exhortation is to gird up the loins of their mind and to direct their thoughts to the hope of the grace presented to them, Calvin says, and in the second part he prescribes the manner, that having their minds changed they were to be formed after the image of God. It is a similitude taken from an ancient custom, Calvin says, for when they had long garments they could not make a journey nor conveniently do any work without being girded up, whence the expressions to gird up oneself for a work or an undertaking; he then bids them remove all impediments, that being set at liberty they might go on to God. Those who philosophize more refinedly about the loins, as though he commanded lusts to be restrained and checked, depart from the real meaning of the Apostle, Calvin says, for these words mean the same with those of Christ, let your loins be girded about and burning lamps in your hands, except that Peter doubles the metaphor by ascribing loins to the mind; and he intimates that our minds are held entangled by the passing cares of the world and by vain desires, so that they rise not upward to God, so that whosoever really wishes to have this hope must learn first to disentangle himself from the world and gird up his mind that it may not turn aside to vain affections. For the same purpose he enjoins sobriety, Calvin says, for he commends not temperance only in eating and drinking but rather spiritual sobriety, when all our thoughts and affections are so kept as not to be inebriated with the allurements of this world; since even the least taste of them stealthily draws us away from God, when one plunges himself into these he must necessarily become sleepy and stupid, and he forgets God and the things of God. He intimates that those who let their minds loose on vanity did not really and sincerely hope for the grace of God, Calvin says, for though they had some hope, yet as they vacillated and were tossed to and fro in the world there was no solidity in their hope. God ought to be sought though far off, Calvin says, but he comes of his own will to meet us; how great then must be our ingratitude if we neglect the grace that is thus set before us, this amplification being especially intended to stimulate our hope. What he adds may be explained in two ways, Calvin says: that the doctrine of the Gospel reveals Christ to us, and that, as we see him as yet only through a mirror and enigmatically, a full revelation is deferred to the last day; the first meaning is approved by Erasmus, nor does he reject it, but the second seems more suitable to the passage, for the object of Peter was to call us away beyond the world, and for this purpose the fittest thing was the recollection of Christ's coming, since when we direct our eyes to this event, this world becomes crucified to us and we to the world. Nor is it a new thing for the apostles to employ the one preposition in the sense of the other, Calvin says; thus he explains the passage as saying that you have no need to make a long journey that you may attain the grace of God, for God anticipates you, inasmuch as he brings it to you; but as the fruition of it will not be until Christ appears from heaven, in whom is hid the salvation of the godly, there is need in the meantime of hope, for the grace of Christ is now offered to us in vain except we patiently wait until the coming of Christ.

Matthew Henry says the apostle here begins his exhortations to those whose glorious state he had before described, thereby instructing us that Christianity is a doctrine according to godliness, designed to make us not only wiser but better, and that he exhorts them to sobriety and holiness. As if he had said, Henry writes, wherefore, since you are so honoured and distinguished, gird up the loins of your mind: you have a journey to go, a race to run, a warfare to accomplish and a great work to do, and as the traveller, the racer, the warrior and the labourer gather in and gird up their long and loose garments that they may be more ready, prompt and expeditious in their business, so do you by your minds, your inner man and affections seated there; gird them, gather them in, let them not hang loose and neglected about you, restrain their extravagances, and let the loins or strength and vigour of your minds be exerted in your duty, disengaging yourselves from all that would hinder you and going on resolutely in your obedience. Be sober, be vigilant against all your spiritual dangers and enemies, Henry continues, and be temperate and modest in eating, drinking, apparel, recreation, business and in the whole of your behaviour, and be sober-minded also in opinion as well as in practice, and humble in your judgment of yourselves. Some refer the last clause to the last judgment, Henry says, as if the apostle directed their hope to the final revelation of Jesus Christ, but it seems more natural to take it as it might be rendered, hope perfectly or thoroughly for the grace that is brought to you in or by the revelation of Jesus Christ, that is by the gospel, which brings life and immortality to light: hope perfectly, trust without doubting to that grace which is now offered to you by the gospel. Henry draws the lessons: that the main work of a Christian lies in the right management of his heart and mind, the apostle's first direction being to gird up the loins of the mind; that the best Christians have need to be exhorted to sobriety, since these excellent Christians are put in mind of it, and it is required of a bishop, of aged men, taught to the young women and directed to the young men; that a Christian's work is not over as soon as he has got into a state of grace, for he must still hope and strive for more grace, and when he has entered the strait gate he must still walk in the narrow way and gird up the loins of his mind for that purpose; and that a strong and perfect trust in God's grace is very consistent with our best endeavours in our duty, since we must hope perfectly and yet gird up our loins and address ourselves vigorously to the work we have to do, encouraging ourselves from the grace of Jesus Christ.

Albert Barnes says the allusion is to the manner in which the Orientals were accustomed to dress, wearing loose, flowing robes, so that when they wished to run or to fight or to apply themselves to any business they were obliged to bind their garments close around them; the meaning here is that they were to have their minds in constant preparation to discharge the duties or to endure the trials of life, like those who were prepared for labour, for a race or for a conflict. The translation in the text, hope to the end, is the most correct against the marginal perfectly, Barnes says: it means that they were not to become faint or weary in their trials, not to abandon the hopes of the gospel but to cherish those hopes to the end of life, whatever opposition they might meet with and however much might be done by others to induce them to apostatise. For the grace that is to be brought unto you means for the favour that shall then be bestowed upon them, to wit salvation, Barnes says, the word brought here meaning that this great favour which they hoped for would be borne to them by the Saviour on his return from heaven; and the revelation of Jesus Christ is when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven in his glory, that is when he comes to judge the world. Charles Ellicott says the phrase is a metaphor from persons gathering up the flowing Oriental dress, which had been let down for repose, so as to be ready for energetic action, as in the book of Kings for running and in Job for arguing, and that what exact kind of action Peter meant them here to prepare for we need not inquire. A mind, rather than soul or heart, seems to bespeak practical intelligence, Ellicott says: thus when the Galatians too began to fall from evangelical to Judaic religion Paul calls them senseless. Be sober is not in the literal sense but with the same notion of alertness as in gird up, Ellicott says, sobriety and wakefulness being often combined. Literally it is hope perfectly, or thoroughly, or with completeness, Ellicott says, and he quotes Leighton that indeed this hope is perfect in continuance, it is a hope unto the end, because it is perfect in its nature; the chief thought, however, is that the hope should not be half-hearted, dispirited, Peter bringing us back to what he began with, that ours is a living hope. The exhortation is exactly of the same nature as that which pervades the Epistle to the Hebrews, Ellicott says, and for the same reason, that spiritual sloth combined with fear of man was beginning to turn these Jewish Christians back to dead works, so that hope on in these passages is tantamount to remain Christians. It is not exactly hope for the grace, that is expect confidently that it will come, Ellicott says, but rather hope upon the grace, as in the only other place where the same construction is used and where it is rendered trusteth in God; here therefore it is, confidently hope on the strength of the grace, the grace being the same as spoken of earlier. If we will render it strictly it is that is a-bringing to you, Ellicott says, and he quotes Leighton that this blessedness, this consummation of grace, the saints are hastening forward to, walking on in their way wheresoever it lies indifferently, through honour and dishonour, through evil report and good report, and as they are hastening to it, it is hastening to them in the course of time, every day bringing it nearer to them than before; and notwithstanding all difficulties and dangers in the way, they that have their eye and their hopes upon it shall arrive at it, and it shall be brought safe to their hand, all the malice of men and devils being unable to cut them short of this grace that is a-bringing to them against the revelation of Jesus Christ. Notice also that it is now the personal Name and not the official title, Ellicott says: Peter is enforcing the gospel as we know it, and we no longer search unto whom the title of the Messiah belongs. A.T. Robertson says the opening word means because of which thing, the glorious free grace opened for Gentiles and Jews in Christ in the preceding verses. Girding up is a first aorist middle participle of a late and rare verb found here only in the New Testament, Robertson says, a vivid metaphor for the habit of the Orientals, who quickly gathered up their loose robes with a girdle when in a hurry or starting on a journey; loins is the old word for the part of the body where the girdle was worn, used as a metaphor here as elsewhere, and mind is the old word for the faculty of understanding, of seeing through a thing. Be sober is a present active participle of an old verb which in the New Testament is always metaphorical, Robertson says; and the adverb rendered perfectly is an old word found here alone in the New Testament, connected with the imperative set your hope in the Revised Version, but Bigg, Hort and most modern commentators take it according to Peter's usual custom with the preceding verb, so that it is being perfectly sober and not hoping perfectly. That is to be brought is a present passive articular participle picturing the process, that is being brought, Robertson says.

Adam Clarke says they are to take courage from this display of God's love now made known to them, and though they must expect trials, yet to fortify their minds with the consideration that he who has given them his Son Jesus will withhold from them no manner of thing that is good. The allusion here is to the long robes of the Asiatics, Clarke says, which, when they were about to perform any active service, they tucked in their girdles, and this they did also when they waited on their superiors at meals. Hope to the end for the grace means continue to expect all that God has promised, Clarke says, and particularly that utmost salvation, that glorification of body and soul, which they shall obtain at the revelation of Christ when he shall come to judge the world; but if the apostle alludes here to the approaching revelation of Christ to inflict judgment on the Jews for their final rebellion and obstinacy, then the grace or benefit may intend their preservation from the evils that were coming upon that people, and their wonderful escape from Jerusalem at the time that the Roman armies came against it. John Wesley says the opening word means having such encouragement, and that as persons in the eastern countries were wont in travelling or running to gird up their long garments, so they are to gather up all their thoughts and affections and keep the mind always disencumbered and prepared to run the race which is set before them. Be watchful means as servants that wait for their Lord, Wesley says; and hope to the end means maintain a full expectation of all the grace, the blessings flowing from the free favour of God, which shall be brought to them at the final revelation of Jesus Christ, and which are now brought to them by the revelation of Christ in them.

debates: What the adverb governs: Barnes prefers the text's hope to the end over the margin's perfectly and takes it of not fainting under trial; Ellicott renders it hope perfectly, thoroughly, with completeness, and quotes Leighton that the hope is perfect in continuance because perfect in nature; Robertson reports the Revised Version joining it to the imperative but follows Bigg, Hort and most moderns in attaching it to the participle before, so that it is being perfectly sober

What the revelation of Jesus Christ means here: Henry reports that some refer it to the last judgment but prefers the grace brought by the gospel; Calvin sets out both, crediting Erasmus with the first and preferring the second, the deferred revelation at the last day; Barnes takes it of the coming to judgment; Clarke suggests a judgment on the Jews, in which case the grace may be the believers' escape from Jerusalem before the Roman armies; Wesley holds both the final revelation and the present revelation of Christ within

What girding the loins forbids: Calvin rebukes those who philosophize refinedly about the loins as though lusts were meant, saying they depart from the Apostle's real meaning, and takes it of minds entangled by the passing cares of the world; Gill takes it of loose and vagrant thoughts and turns it into a call to study the mysteries angels look into; Henry and Barnes take it of readiness for a journey, a race or a conflict

How the grace is to be hoped for: Ellicott holds that the construction gives not hope for the grace but hope upon it, confident on the strength of it, citing the one other place where the same construction occurs
outliers: Clarke's detail that the eastern robes were tucked into the girdle also when waiting on superiors at meals
Ellicott's remark that a mind rather than a soul or a heart bespeaks practical intelligence, as Paul calls the Galatians senseless when they slip back to Judaic religion
Ellicott's reading of hope on, in this epistle and in Hebrews alike, as tantamount to remain Christians
Leighton's figure, quoted by Ellicott, that while the saints hasten toward the consummation it is hastening toward them, every day bringing it nearer
Calvin's argument that no long journey is needed to attain the grace of God, since God anticipates us and brings it to us
Pareus's outline, cited in Calvin's block, of five reasons for the exhortation running through the rest of the chapter

14.pericope_label: As children of obedience, not fashioned by the former lusts of your ignorance, but holy in all conduct after the Holy One who called you

schools.summary: John Gill says the phrase means children of obedience, and that this may be connected either with what goes before, that seeing they were children of God by adopting grace, and in regeneration brought to the obedience of faith, to whom the inheritance belonged, therefore they ought to continue hoping for it; or with what follows, that since they were manifestly the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus, being begotten again to a lively hope, they ought to be followers of him and imitate him in holiness and righteousness, and show themselves to be obedient ones to his Gospel and ordinances, as children ought to honour and obey and imitate their parents. On the following verse Gill says the description is a periphrasis of God the Father, who had called them, not merely in an external way by the outward ministry of the word but internally, powerfully and efficaciously by his Spirit and grace, and who had called them to holiness of life and conversation as well as in calling had implanted principles of holiness in them, and therefore is said to call them with an holy calling; and who himself is holy, naturally, perfectly and originally, and in such sense as no creature is, angels or men, and is glorious in holiness and is the source and fountain of holiness in others. John Calvin says he first intimates that we are called by the Lord to the privilege and honour of adoption through the Gospel, and secondly that we are adopted for this end, that he might have us as his obedient children; for though obedience does not make us children, as the gift of adoption is gratuitous, yet it distinguishes children from aliens. How far this obedience extends Peter shows when he forbids God's children to conform to or comply with the desires of this world, and when he exhorts them on the contrary to conform to the will of God, Calvin says: the sum of the whole law, and of all that God requires of us, is this, that his image should shine forth in us, so that we should not be degenerate children, but this cannot be except we be renewed and put off the image of old Adam. Hence we learn what Christians ought to propose to themselves as an object throughout life, Calvin says, that is, to resemble God in holiness and purity; but as all the thoughts and feelings of our flesh are in opposition to God, and the whole bent of our mind is enmity to him, hence Peter begins with the renunciation of the world, and certainly, whenever the Scripture speaks of the renewal of God's image in us, it begins here, that the old man with his lusts is to be destroyed. The time of ignorance he calls that before they were called into the faith of Christ, Calvin says, and we hence learn that unbelief is the fountain of all evils; for he does not use the word ignorance as we commonly do, since that Platonic dogma is false, that ignorance alone is the cause of sin. But yet, how much soever conscience may reprove the unbelieving, nevertheless they go astray as the blind in darkness, Calvin says, because they know not the right way and are without the true light, according to which meaning Paul says that they henceforth walk not as the Gentiles in the vanity of their mind, having the mind darkened and being alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them; where the knowledge of God is not, there darkness, error, vanity, destitution of light and life prevail. These things, however, do not render it impossible that the ungodly should be conscious of doing wrong when they sin, and know that their judge is in heaven and feel an executioner within them, Calvin says; in short, as the kingdom of God is a kingdom of light, all who are alienated from him must necessarily be blind and go astray in a labyrinth, and we are in the meantime reminded that we are for this end illuminated as to the knowledge of God, that we may no longer be carried away by roving lusts, so that as much progress as any one has made in newness of life, so much progress has he made in the knowledge of God. Here a question arises, Calvin says: since he addressed the Jews, who were acquainted with the law and were brought up in the worship of the only true God, why did he charge them with ignorance and blindness as though they were heathens; to this he answers that it hence appears how profitless is all knowledge without Christ, for when Paul exposed the vain boasting of those who wished to be wise apart from Christ he justly said in one short sentence that they did not hold the head. Such were the Jews, Calvin says: being otherwise imbued with numberless corruptions, they had a veil over the eyes so that they did not see Christ in the Law, and the doctrine in which they had been taught was indeed a true light, but they were blind in the midst of light as long as the Sun of Righteousness was hid to them; and if Peter declares that the literal disciples even of the Law were in darkness like the heathens as long as they were ignorant of Christ, the only true wisdom of God, with how much greater care it behoves us to strive for the knowledge of him. On the following verse Calvin says he reasons from the end for which we are called: God sets us apart as a peculiar people for himself, and then we ought to be free from all pollutions; and he quotes a sentence which had been often repeated by Moses, for as the people of Israel were on every side surrounded by heathens, from whom they might easily have adopted the worst examples and innumerable corruptions, the Lord frequently recalled them to himself, as though he had said, Ye have to do with me, ye are mine, then abstain from the pollutions of the Gentiles. We are too ready to look to men so as to follow their common way of living, Calvin says, and thus it happens that some lead others in troops to all kinds of evil until the Lord by his calling separates them. In bidding us to be like himself the proportion is not that of equals, Calvin says, but we ought to advance in this direction as far as our condition will bear, and as even the most perfect are always very far from coming up to the mark we ought daily to strive more and more; and we ought to remember that we are not only told what our duty is, but that God also adds, I am he who sanctify you. There is then no part of our life which is not to be redolent with this good odour of holiness, Calvin says, for we see that in the smallest things and almost insignificant the Lord accustomed his people to the practice of holiness, in order that they might exercise a more diligent care as to themselves.

Albert Barnes says they are to conduct themselves as becomes the children of God, by obeying his commands, by submitting to his will, and by manifesting unwavering confidence in him as their Father at all times. Not fashioning yourselves means not forming or modelling your life, Barnes says: the idea is that they were to have some model or example in accordance with which they were to frame their lives, but that they were not to make their own former principles and conduct the model, for the Christian is to be as different from what he was himself before conversion as he is from his fellow-men, governed by new laws, aiming at new objects, and moulding his life in accordance with new principles. Before conversion, Barnes says, he was supremely selfish; he lived for personal gratification; he gave free indulgence to his appetites and passions, restrained only by a respect for the decencies of life and by a reference to his own health, property or reputation, without regard to the will of God; he conformed himself to the customs and opinions around him rather than to the requirements of his Maker; he lived for worldly aggrandisement, his supreme object being wealth or fame; and in many cases those who are now Christians gave indulgence to every passion which they wished to gratify, regardless of reputation, health, property or salvation. Now they are to be governed by a different rule, Barnes says, and their own former standard of morals and of opinions is no longer their guide, but the will of God; the former lusts in your ignorance means when you were ignorant of the requirements of the gospel and gave yourselves up to the unrestrained indulgence of your passions. On the following verse Barnes says the model or example in accordance with which they were to frame their lives should be the character of that God who had called them into his kingdom, since they were to be like him, and the meaning is that since God is holy, and we profess to be his followers, we ought also to be holy in all our conduct. The quoted command was addressed at first to the Israelites, Barnes says, but it is with equal propriety addressed to Christians as the professed people of God, the foundation of the command being that they professed to be his people, and that as his people they ought to be like their God. It is a great truth that men everywhere will imitate the God whom they worship, Barnes says: they will form their character in accordance with his, they will regard what he does as right, they will attempt to rise no higher in virtue than the God whom they adore, and they will practise freely what he is supposed to do or approve; hence, by knowing what are the characteristics of the gods which are worshipped by any people, we may form a correct estimate of the character of the people themselves, and hence, as the God who is the object of the Christian's worship is perfectly holy, the character of his worshippers should also be holy. Hence also we may see that the tendency of true religion is to make men pure, Barnes says, for as the worship of the impure gods of the heathen moulds the character of the worshippers into their image, so the worship of Jehovah moulds the character of his professed friends into his image, and they become like him. Charles Ellicott says the phrase is literally children of obedience, children in the sense of relationship and not of age, and that it is characteristic of the writer to keep one thought underlying many digressions, so that here the appeal to them as children is based on the begetting again and the inheritance earlier in the chapter and comes up again in the Father, the brethren and the second mention of begetting; the usual characteristic of Jews in the New Testament, he adds, is disobedience, and the word as means in keeping with your character of, just as we say in common English, do so like obedient children. The rare verb is the same as is translated be not conformed in the letter to the Romans, Ellicott says, from which some think it is borrowed, and the expression is a little confused, the lusts themselves being spoken of as a model not to be copied where we should rather have expected not being conformed to your former selves; the former lusts in your ignorance means those which you indulged before you came to know the gospel truth, of course implying also that the ignorance was the mother of the lusts. The same assumption is made here which we find again later in the letter, Ellicott says, that the recipients had lived in ignorance and in vice up to a certain point of their lives, and it is contended with much plausibility that both accusations show the recipients to be of Gentile and not of Jewish origin: it is true that lusts of the flesh are not usually laid to the charge of the Jews as they are of the Gentiles, and true also that the ignorance with which the Jews are charged elsewhere has quite a different tendency from this. But it may be answered that such details are of little weight in comparison with the direct evidence of the first verse and the indirect evidence of the whole tone of the letter, Ellicott says; that ignorance is surely not an unnatural word to represent the contrast between the state of unregenerate Jews and the same persons when they have attained to knowledge higher than that of prophets or of angels; that even Jews were men of flesh and blood and therefore not exempt from the temptations of the flesh, from which mere legalism was quite insufficient to protect them; that in the letter to the Hebrews Jewish people are supposed to have need of a high priest to bear with and atone for their ignorances; and that the same writer contemplates the possibility of many of his Hebrews being defiled through fleshly sin and deems it necessary to urge strongly the sanctions of marriage. More correctly the next clause is, but according to, or after, that is in the likeness of, the Holy One who called you, Ellicott says: the calling is mentioned because of the obligation it imposes upon us, and Bengel notices how fond Peter is of the words call and calling, the call here seeming to mean specially the call to be children of God. Perhaps the imperative would come out stronger thus, Ellicott says, do ye also show yourselves holy in every part of your conduct; and he quotes Leighton that God has severed them from the mass of the profane world and picked them out to be jewels for himself, and has set them apart for this end, that they may be holy to him, as the Hebrew word that signifies holiness imports setting apart or fitting for a peculiar use, so that they are not to be untrue to his design, since it is sacrilege for them to dispose of themselves after the impure manner of the world and to apply themselves to any profane use whom God has consecrated to himself. The better reading in the quoted command is, ye shall be holy, Ellicott says: it is still, however, a command and not a promise, except that all God's commands are promises; and the command comes some five or six times in the book of Leviticus, addressed not only to the Levites but to all the people, so that it would apply twice over to the recipients of this letter by virtue of their twofold consecration, in the old and in the new Israel. A.T. Robertson says the phrase is a common Hebraism, a descriptive genitive frequent in the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament, suggested by the word obedience earlier in the chapter and meaning children marked by obedience. Not fashioning yourselves is the usual negative with the participle of a rare compound found in the New Testament only here and in Romans, Robertson says, the outward pattern being in contrast with the inward change, as elsewhere the pattern is contrasted with the form; according to your former lusts is an associative instrumental case with the bad sense of the noun as elsewhere, and in the time of your ignorance uses an old word found in the New Testament only here and in three other places. The use of the preposition in the next clause is a regular Greek idiom, here in contrast with the fashioning just forbidden, Robertson says: it means according to the holy one who called you, so that God is our standard or pattern and not our lusts; and be ye yourselves also holy is a first aorist ingressive passive imperative, with an allusion to God as our example, do ye also become holy. On the word for manner of life, which Peter uses eight times, Robertson says the original meaning of turning up and down, back and forth suited the Latin word but not our modern conversation, which is talk and not walk. Because it is written uses a stronger conjunction than the one below, Robertson says, and the perfect passive is the regular formula for an Old Testament quotation, the citation being from three places in Leviticus and reinforced by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, while the future here is volitive like an imperative.

Adam Clarke says that as the offices of certain persons are known by the garb or livery they wear, so are transgressors: where we see the world's livery we see the world's servants, since they fashion or habit themselves according to their lusts, and we may guess that they have a worldly mind by their conformity to worldly fashions. On the following verse Clarke says heathenism scarcely produced a god whose example was not the most abominable, their greatest gods especially being paragons of impurity, and none of their philosophers could propose the objects of their adoration as objects of imitation; here Christianity has an infinite advantage over heathenism, for God is holy and he calls upon all who believe in him to imitate his holiness, and the reason why they should be holy is that the God who has called them is holy. John Wesley says the desires spoken of are those which they had while they were ignorant of God, and on the quoted command he refers the reader simply to the eleventh chapter of Leviticus.

debates: Whether the readers were Gentiles: Ellicott states the case plainly, that the letter assumes its recipients lived in ignorance and vice and that this is contended with much plausibility to make them Gentiles, and answers from the opening verse, the tone of the letter, the flesh and blood of Jews whom legalism could not protect, and the letter to the Hebrews with its ignorances and its defiled; Calvin meets the same difficulty by holding that the Jews were blind in the midst of light, having a veil over the eyes so that they did not see Christ in the Law

What ignorance means here: Calvin denies the word its common sense and rejects the Platonic dogma that ignorance alone is the cause of sin, holding that the unbelieving may be reproved by conscience and still walk as the blind; Ellicott says the ignorance was the mother of the lusts; Barnes takes it of the time before they knew the requirements of the gospel

How the clause about the caller should be rendered: Ellicott and Robertson agree that the preposition gives after the Holy One who called you, in his likeness, and Robertson sets it against the conforming just forbidden, God being the standard and not our lusts; Barnes keeps the received sense and reaches the same duty by a general law of imitation

Whether the quoted words are command or promise: Ellicott prefers the future reading, ye shall be holy, and calls it still a command except that all God's commands are promises; Robertson calls the future volitive, that is imperative in force
outliers: Barnes's rule that men everywhere imitate the God they worship, so that a people's character may be estimated from the character of their gods
Clarke's observation that no heathen philosopher could propose the objects of their adoration as objects of imitation
Clarke's figure that where we see the world's livery we see the world's servants
Leighton's saying, quoted by Ellicott, that it is sacrilege to apply to any profane use those whom God has consecrated to himself
Ellicott's point that the command stands several times in Leviticus addressed to all the people, and so binds these readers twice over, in the old Israel and in the new
Robertson's complaint that the old word for manner of life suited the Latin but not our modern conversation, which is talk and not walk

17.pericope_label: Calling on a Father who judges impartially, pass your sojourning in fear, knowing you were ransomed not with silver but with precious blood

schools.summary: John Gill says this is a fresh argument engaging to holiness of life and conversation, and that invocation of God includes the whole worship of him, the performance of every outward duty and the exercise of every inward grace, particularly designing prayer, since whoever is concerned in either, God will be sanctified by all them that draw nigh unto him; or the phrase may intend an asserting God to be their Father under the influence of the spirit of adoption, and all such as claim so near a relation to God ought to honour and obey him and to be followers of him, whoever calls God their Father being careful that they do not blaspheme, or cause to be blasphemed, that worthy name by which they are called. On the following verse Gill says they know this from the Scriptures of truth, by the testimony of the Spirit, by his work upon the soul, and by the application of the benefits of redemption, such as justification, pardon, adoption and sanctification. John Calvin says they are said here to call on God the Father who professed themselves to be his children, as Moses says that the name of Jacob was called on Ephraim and Manasseh that they might be counted his children; but he had a regard to what he had said before, as obedient children, and from the character of the Father himself he shows what sort of obedience ought to be rendered. No outward mask is of any account with God, Calvin says, as the case is with men, but he sees the heart and his eyes look on faithfulness, which is also what Paul means when he says that God's judgment is according to truth, for he there inveighs against hypocrites who think that they deceive God by a vain pretence. The meaning is that we by no means discharge our duty towards God when we obey him only in appearance, Calvin says, for he is not a mortal man whom the outward appearance pleases, but he reads what we are inwardly in our hearts, and he not only prescribes laws for our feet and hands but also requires what is just and right as to the mind and spirit. By the phrase about every man's work he does not refer to merit or to reward, Calvin says, for Peter does not speak here of the merits of works nor of the cause of salvation, but only reminds us that there will be no looking to the person before the tribunal of God, and that what will be regarded will be the real sincerity of the heart, faith being in this place included in the work. It hence appears evident how foolish and puerile is the inference that is drawn, Calvin says, that since God judges every one of us by the integrity of his conscience and not by the outward appearance, therefore we obtain salvation by works. The fear that is mentioned stands opposed to heedless security, such as is wont to creep in when there is a hope of deceiving with impunity, Calvin says, for as God's eyes are such that they penetrate into the hidden recesses of the heart, we ought to walk with him carefully and not negligently; and he calls the present life a sojourning, not in the sense in which he called the Jews to whom he was writing sojourners at the beginning of the Epistle, but because all the godly are in this world pilgrims. On the following verse Calvin says here is another reason, drawn from the price of our redemption, which ought always to be remembered when our salvation is spoken of, for to him who repudiates or despises the grace of the gospel not only his own salvation is worthless but also the blood of Christ, by which God has manifested its value; and we know how dreadfully sacrilegious it is to regard as common the blood of the Son of God, so that there is nothing which ought so much to stimulate us to the practice of holiness as the memory of this price of our redemption. For the sake of amplifying he mentions these things in contrast, Calvin says, so that we may know that the whole world and all things deemed precious by men are nothing to the excellency and value of this price; and he says they had been redeemed from their vain conversation in order that we might know that the whole life of man, until he is converted to Christ, is a ruinous labyrinth of wanderings. He also intimates that it is not through our merits that we are restored to the right way, Calvin says, but because it is God's will that the price offered for our salvation should be effectual in our behalf, so that the blood of Christ is not only the pledge of our salvation but also the cause of our calling; and Peter warns us to beware lest our unbelief should render this price void or of no effect. As Paul boasts that he worshipped God with a pure conscience from his forefathers, Calvin says, and commends to Timothy for his imitation the piety of his grandmother Lois and of his mother Eunice, and as Christ also said of the Jews that they knew whom they worshipped, it may seem strange that Peter should assert that the Jews of his time learnt nothing from their fathers but mere vanity. To this he answers that Christ, when he declared that the way or the knowledge of true religion belonged to the Jews, referred to the law and the commandments of God rather than to the people, for the temple had not to no purpose been built at Jerusalem, nor was God worshipped there according to the fancies of men but according to what was prescribed in the Law, so that he said the Jews were not going astray while observing the Law. As to Paul's forefathers, and as to Lois and Eunice and similar cases, there is no doubt but that God ever had at least a small remnant among that people in whom sincere piety continued, Calvin says, while the body of the people had become wholly corrupt and had plunged themselves into all kinds of errors: innumerable superstitions were followed, hypocrisy prevailed, the hope of salvation was built on the merest trifles, they were not only imbued with false opinions but also fascinated with the grossest dotages, and they who had been scattered to various parts of the world were implicated in still greater corruptions, so that the greater part of that nation had either wholly fallen away from true religion or had much degenerated. When therefore Peter condemned the doctrine of the fathers, Calvin says, he viewed it as unconnected with Christ, who is the soul and the truth of the Law; but we hence learn that as soon as men depart from Christ they go fatally astray, and in vain is pretended in this case the authority of the Fathers or an ancient custom, for the Prophet Ezekiel cried to the Jews, Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers. This ought also to be no less attended to by us in the present day, Calvin says, for in order that the redemption of Christ may be effectual and useful to us we must renounce our former life, though derived from the teaching and practice of our fathers; thrice foolish then are the Papists, who think that the name of Fathers is a sufficient defence for all their superstitions, so that they boldly reject whatever is brought forward from the Word of God.

Matthew Henry says holy confidence in God as a Father and awful fear of him as a Judge agree together, and that to regard God always as a Judge makes him dear to us as a Father; if believers do evil, God will visit them with corrections, and therefore let Christians not doubt God's faithfulness to his promises, nor give way to enslaving dread of his wrath, but let them reverence his holiness. The fearless professor is defenceless, Henry says, and Satan takes him captive at his will, while the desponding professor has no heart to avail himself of his advantages and is easily brought to surrender. The price paid for man's redemption was the precious blood of Christ, Henry says, and not only openly wicked but unprofitable conversation is highly dangerous, though it may plead custom, since it is folly to resolve that one will live and die in such a way because one's forefathers did so. God had purposes of special favour toward his people long before he made manifest such grace unto them, Henry says, but the clearness of light, the supports of faith and the power of ordinances are all much greater since Christ came upon earth than they were before; and the comfort is that, being by faith made one with Christ, his present glory is an assurance that where he is we shall be also. The soul must be purified before it can give up its own desires and indulgences, Henry says, and the word of God planted in the heart by the Holy Ghost is a means of spiritual life.

Albert Barnes says that if they call on the Father they are true Christians, piety being represented in the Scriptures as calling on God or as the worship of God, and that the word Father is used here evidently not to denote the Father in contradistinction to the Son but as referring to God as the Father of the universe, whom Christians worship as one having all the feelings of a kind and tender parent towards them. Without respect of persons means impartiality, Barnes says, God not being influenced in his treatment of men by a regard to rank, wealth, beauty or any external distinction, and judging each one according to his character or to what he has done; the meaning is that they worship a God who will judge every man according to his real character, and they should therefore lead such lives as he can approve. Their sojourning is their temporary residence on earth, Barnes says, this not being their permanent home, and the fear is true reverence or veneration for God and his law, religion being often represented as the reverent fear of God. On the following verse Barnes says this is an argument for a holy life derived from the fact that they were redeemed and from the manner in which their redemption had been effected, there being no more effectual way to induce true Christians to consecrate themselves entirely to God than to refer them to the fact that they are not their own but have been purchased by the blood of Christ. The word here means that they were rescued from sin and death by the blood of Christ as the valuable consideration on account of which it was done, Barnes says, that is, the blood or the life of Christ offered as a sacrifice effected the same purpose in regard to justice and to the maintenance of the principles of moral government which the punishment of the sinner himself would have done; it was that which God was pleased to accept in the place of the punishment of the sinner as answering the same great ends in his administration, so that the principles of his truth and justice could as certainly be maintained in this way, and if so there was no obstacle to their salvation. Silver and gold usually constitute the price or the valuable consideration paid for the redemption of captives, Barnes says, and it is clear that the obligation of one who is redeemed to love his benefactor is in proportion to the price paid for his ransom; the idea here is that a price far more valuable than any amount of silver or gold had been paid for the redemption of the people of God, and that they were under proportionate obligation to devote themselves to his service, since between the value of the life of the Son of God and silver and gold there could be no comparison. The word vain applied to conduct means properly empty, fruitless, Barnes says, and is a word often applied to the worship of idols as being nothing, worthless, unable to help, and is probably used in a similar sense in this place: the apostle refers to their former worship of idols and to all the abominations connected with that service as being vain and unprofitable, the worship of nothing real, and as resulting in a course of life that answered none of the proper ends of living. Received by tradition from your fathers means the mode of worship which had been handed down from father to son, Barnes says, since the worship of idols depends on no better reason than that it is that which has been practised in ancient times, and is kept up now in all lands, in a great degree, only by the fact that it has had the sanction of the venerated men of other generations. Charles Ellicott says the word if casts no doubt but on the contrary serves to bring out the necessary logical connection between invoking the Father, and such a Father, and fear, so that we might paraphrase by, if you use the Lord's Prayer; the word seems not only to mean if you appeal to the Father but if you appeal to the Father by the title of Father. The word judgeth or decideth refers not only to the great judgment of the last day, Ellicott says, but is used in reference to the calling upon the Father, that word having a forensic sense of lodging an appeal, so that every time we lodge our appeal to the Father on the ground of his Fatherhood he decides the case, but decides it without favour, making no allowance to our wrongdoing on the ground of being his regenerate children and certainly none on the ground of being of the Hebrew race, which last notion, Ellicott says, finds place here as we may see from Peter's words at the house of Cornelius. He decides according to every man's work, that is upon the individual merits of the case before him, Ellicott says, the man's work in the singular embracing all his conduct in the lump as a single performance which is either good on the whole or bad on the whole. The word for pass is really the same as the word for conduct earlier, Ellicott says, and is intended to take our thought back to it: as obedient children, be holy in every part of your conduct, and if you wish for favour from the Father see that that conduct is characterised by fear. This fear, says Leighton as Ellicott quotes him, is not cowardice, for it drowns all lower fears and begets true fortitude, the righteous daring do anything but offend God, as Moses was bold and fearless in dealing with a proud and wicked king but when God appeared said that he exceedingly feared and quaked; and this extract well contrasts, Ellicott adds, with the meaning which some would apparently thrust into the word fear, as though it meant that the position of the Christians as aliens in the midst of a hostile world required a timid attitude towards man. The expression about sojourning sets a limit for the discipline of fear and at the same time suggests a reason for it, Ellicott says, since children though they are, they are not yet entered on their inheritance and have to secure it. On the following verse Ellicott says security, which is the opposite of the fear of the Father, is incompatible with knowing by whose and what anguish alone the inheritance could be purchased for us; Peter's contempt for silver and gold is shown early in his history, and gold and silver will come to an end with everything else that is material.
