Observe that by contrast the blood of Christ is implied to be not corruptible, Ellicott says, and that not because of the miraculous incorruption of Jesus Christ's flesh but because the blood of Christ of which the Apostle here speaks is not material, the natural blood of Jesus being only the sign and sacrament of that by which he truly and inwardly redeemed the world. Properly the word redeem means to ransom a person, to get them out of slavery or captivity by paying a ransom, Ellicott says, but the notion of an actual ransom paid was apt to slip away, as in the case of Moses, who certainly gave nothing of the nature of an equivalent to Pharaoh for the loss of his serfs; so that here, as in all passages relating to the Atonement, we must be very careful not to press the metaphor or to consider it as more than a metaphor, the leading notion here being not that of paying an equivalent but to call closer attention to the state in which the readers were before, a servitude like that of Egypt or a captivity like that of Babylon, from which they needed a ransomer like Moses or Zerubbabel. The question is whether a Gentile or Jewish mode of life is intended, Ellicott says: if it meant merely as regards religious worship it would suit either way, for it was of the essence of Roman state religion that it should be the same from generation to generation; but manner of life is far too wide a word to be thus limited, and at the same time the word tradition implies in the New Testament something sedulously taught, purposely handed down from father to son as an heirloom, so that it could not be applied to the careless, sensual life of Gentiles, learned by example only, whereas among the Jews tradition entered into the minutest details of daily life, it being a matter of serious tradition how a cup was to be washed. Vain, that is frivolous, seems not an unnatural epithet to apply to such a mode of life, Ellicott says, especially to one who had heard our Lord's words on the traditions of men; it would seem then that the readers of this letter were certainly Jews by birth. But would the Apostle of the Circumcision, the supposed head of the legal party in the Church, dare to call Judaism a vain conversation, Ellicott asks, to stigmatise it as imposed by tradition of the fathers, the single compound adjective in the Greek having a contemptuous ring, and to imply that it was like an Egyptian bondage; we have only to turn to the council at Jerusalem and we find him uttering precisely the same sentiments and calling Judaism a slavish yoke, which was not only so bad for Gentiles that to impose it upon them was to tempt God, but also was secretly or openly felt intolerable by himself, by all the Jews there present, and even by the fathers who had imposed it. Judaism itself then, in the form it had then assumed, was one of the foes and oppressors from which Christ came to ransom and save his people, Ellicott concludes. A.T. Robertson says the condition is of the first class with a present middle indicative of the verb to call a name on, and that as Father is a predicate accusative in apposition; the word for without respect of persons is found nowhere else except in the later epistles of Clement of Rome and of Barnabas, formed in imitation of the Hebrew, and the phrase means according to the deed of each one, God judging just as Christ judges also. Pass is a second aorist passive imperative used metaphorically, Robertson says, the time being an accusative of extent, and the word for sojourning a late one found in the Greek Old Testament and in the New Testament only here and in the Acts and in ecclesiastical writers, coming from a verb meaning to dwell beside, and so used of pilgrims or strangers, of Jews away from Palestine or of Christians here on earth, and then of a local region, our parish; Peter here recurs to his opening address, and in fear stands in an emphatic position at the beginning of the clause. On the following verse Robertson says knowing is a causal participle, the appeal being to an elementary Christian belief, as Hort says, the holiness and justice of God, with the added thought of the high cost of redemption, as Bigg says. Ye were redeemed is a first aorist passive of an old verb from the noun for a ransom for the life of a slave, meaning to set free by payment of ransom, with abundant examples in the papyri, Robertson says, the ransom being the blood of Christ, and Peter here amplifying the language of Isaiah; slaves were set free by silver and gold. The adjective rendered handed down from your fathers, though predicate in position, is really attributive in idea, like the French idiom, Robertson says, and this double compound verbal adjective, though here alone in the New Testament, occurs in Diodorus and Dionysius of Halicarnassus and in several inscriptions; the Jews made a wrong use of tradition, but the reference here seems mainly to Gentiles.

Adam Clarke says that seeing they invoke the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and their Father through Christ, and profess to be obedient children and sojourners here below for a short time only, they are to see that they maintain a godly reverence for this Father, walking in all his testimonies blameless. God is said to be no respecter of persons for this reason among many others, Clarke says, that being infinitely righteous he must be infinitely impartial: he cannot prefer one to another because he has nothing to hope or fear from any of his creatures, and all partialities among men spring from one or other of these two principles, hope or fear, which God can feel neither of, and therefore God can be no respecter of persons. He approves or disapproves of men according to their moral character, Clarke says: he pities all and provides salvation for all, but he loves those who resemble him in his holiness, and he loves them in proportion to that resemblance, the more of his image he sees in any the more he loves him; and every man's work will be the evidence of his conformity or nonconformity to God, and according to this evidence will God judge him. Here then is no respect of persons, Clarke says: God's judgment will be according to a man's work, and a man's work or conduct will be according to the moral state of his mind, so that no favouritism can prevail in the day of judgment and nothing will pass there but holiness of heart and life. A righteousness imputed, and not possessed and practised, will not avail where God judgeth according to every man's work, Clarke says, and it would be well if those sinners and spurious believers who fancy themselves safe and complete in the righteousness of Christ, while impure and unholy in themselves, would think of this testimony of the apostle. On the following verse Clarke says the word redeem signifies to procure life for a captive or liberty for a slave by paying a price, and the precious blood of Christ is here stated to be the price at which the souls of both Jews and Gentiles were redeemed, a price paid down and a price which God's righteousness required. Corruptible things mean here anything that man usually gives in exchange for another, Clarke says, but the term necessarily includes all created things, as all these are corruptible and perishing; the meaning of the apostle is evidently that created things could not purchase the souls of men, else the sacrifice of Christ had not been offered, for could anything less have done, God would not have given up his only-begotten Son. Even silver and gold, the most valuable medium of commerce among men, bear no proportion in their value to the souls of a lost world, Clarke says, for there should be a congruity between the worth of the thing purchased and the valuable consideration which is given for it, and the laws and customs of nations require this; on this ground, perishable things, or things the value of which must be infinitely less than the worth of the souls of men, cannot purchase those souls, so that nothing but such a ransom price as God provided could be a sufficient ransom, oblation and satisfaction for the sins of the world. Vain conversation means empty, foolish and unprofitable conduct, full of vain hopes, vain fears and vain wishes, Clarke says; and the Jews had innumerable burdens of empty ceremonies and useless ordinances which they received by tradition from their fathers, rabbins or doctors, while the Gentiles were not less encumbered with such than the Jews, all being wedded to their vanities because they received them from their forefathers as they had done from theirs. This antiquity and tradition have been the groundwork of many a vain ceremony and idle pilgrimage, and of numerous doctrines which have nothing to plead in their behalf but this mere antiquity, Clarke says, but such persons seem not to consider that error and sin are nearly coeval with the world itself. John Wesley says that judging according to every man's work means according to the tenor of his life and conversation, that passing the time of your sojourning means your short abode on earth, and that the fear enjoined is humble, loving fear, the proper companion and guard of hope; and he glosses the vain conversation as their foolish, sinful way of life.

debates: Whether the fathers' tradition is Jewish or Gentile: Barnes reads the vain manner of life as idolatry and the tradition as the sanction of venerated men of former generations; Ellicott argues from the word tradition, which implies something sedulously taught and handed down as an heirloom rather than a sensual life learned by example, and concludes the readers were certainly Jews by birth and that Judaism itself was among the oppressors Christ ransomed them from; Calvin agrees the fathers are Jewish but restricts the censure to their doctrine as unconnected with Christ, God having kept a remnant; Clarke holds both nations wedded to inherited vanities, and Robertson leans to Gentiles

Whether judgement by works touches merit: Clarke presses the clause against a righteousness imputed but not possessed and practised, and against those who fancy themselves safe in Christ's righteousness while impure in themselves; Calvin forestalls exactly that inference, calling it foolish and puerile to argue from impartial judgement to salvation by works, and includes faith within the work; Ellicott notes that the singular means all a man's conduct taken as one performance

How far the ransom figure may be pressed: Ellicott warns that in all passages on the Atonement the metaphor must not be pressed beyond a metaphor, since Moses gave Pharaoh no equivalent, the leading notion being the servitude the readers were in; Barnes presses it the other way, that the life of Christ was accepted in place of the punishment of the sinner and answered the same ends in God's administration; Clarke requires a congruity between the worth purchased and the price given

What the blood's incorruptibility rests on: Ellicott denies it is the miraculous incorruption of Christ's flesh, holding that the blood spoken of is not material and that the natural blood was the sign and sacrament of that by which he inwardly redeemed the world
outliers: Clarke's argument that God can be no respecter of persons because all partiality springs from hope or fear, and he has nothing to hope or fear from any creature
Leighton's saying, quoted by Ellicott, that this fear is not cowardice but drowns all lower fears, so that the righteous dare do anything but offend God
Ellicott's paraphrase of the opening clause as, if you use the Lord's Prayer, and his reading of the verb as lodging a formal appeal that God then decides without favour
Calvin's charge that the Papists are thrice foolish for thinking the name of Fathers a sufficient defence of their superstitions
Robertson's note that the word for sojourning gives us our parish
Henry's observation that the fearless professor is defenceless while the desponding professor has no heart to use his advantages

19.pericope_label: The precious blood of a lamb without blemish, foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for you, that your faith and hope might be in God

schools.summary: John Gill says Christ was prophesied of as a Redeemer under the Old Testament, and the Jews frequently ascribe redemption to the word of the Lord God, which the apostle here attributes to the blood of Christ, whose blood is the same with ours, only not tainted with sin, the blood of an innocent person and of one who is God as well as man, freely shed in the room and stead of his people and so a sufficient price for their redemption. It may truly be said to be precious, Gill says, as it is to God, to whom it is a sweet smelling sacrifice and with which he is well pleased, not that he takes delight in the mere effusion of his blood, but as this is the ransom price and the atonement of his chosen ones; and so it is to all them that believe, since by it they are justified, through it they have the forgiveness of their sins, their peace and reconciliation with God is made by it, and by it they are sanctified and have boldness to enter into the holiest of all. On the following verse Gill says foreordained means foreknown, that is by God, and that this intends not barely his prescience of Christ, of what he should be, do and suffer, but such a previous knowledge of him as is joined with love and affection to him, not merely as his own Son and the express image of his person but as Mediator, whom he loved before the world was, with a love of complacency and delight which will last for ever. It includes the choice of him as the head of the election, Gill says, and the pre-ordination of his human nature to the grace of union to his divine Person, and the pre-appointment of him to various things, the Syriac version adding the words to this, that is, to be the lamb for a sacrifice, to be a propitiation for the sins of his people, to be the Saviour and Redeemer of them by his precious blood; the allusion is to the taking of the passover lamb from the sheep or from the goats and keeping it separate from the tenth to the fourteenth day of the month before it was slain, so Christ as man was chosen out from among the people. On the last of these verses Gill says Christ as God is the object of faith, and as Mediator he is the way to the Father by which men come to him, believe in him and lay hold upon him as their covenant God and Father, and is also the author of that faith by which they believe in him, all their encouragement to believe being taken from him; and such as do come to God by Christ and stay themselves upon him, trusting in him, may know and comfortably conclude that Christ, who was foreordained from all eternity to be the Redeemer of his people, was manifest in the flesh for their sakes and to obtain eternal redemption for them. John Calvin says he means by this similitude that we have in Christ whatever had been shadowed forth by the ancient sacrifices, though he especially alludes to the Paschal lamb; and let us hence learn what benefit the reading of the Law brings us in this respect, for though the rite of sacrificing is abolished, yet it assists our faith not a little to compare the reality with the type, so that we may seek in the former what the latter contains. Moses ordered a whole or perfect lamb, without blemish, to be chosen for the Passover, Calvin says, and the same thing is often repeated as to the sacrifices; Peter, by applying this to Christ, teaches us that he was a suitable victim and approved by God, for he was perfect, without any blemish, and had he had any defect in him he could not have been rightly offered to God nor could he pacify his wrath. On the following verse Calvin says he again by a comparison amplifies the grace of God with which he had peculiarly favoured the men of that age, for it was not a common or a small favour that God deferred the manifestation of Christ to that time, when yet he had ordained him in his eternal council for the salvation of the world; at the same time he reminds us that it was not a new or a sudden thing as to God that Christ appeared as a Saviour, and this is what ought especially to be known, for in addition to this, that novelty is always suspicious, what would be the stability of our faith if we believed that a remedy for mankind had suddenly occurred at length to God after some thousands of years. In short, we cannot confidently rest on Christ except we are convinced that eternal salvation is in him and always has been in him, Calvin says; besides, Peter addressed the Jews, who had heard that he had already been long ago promised, and though they understood nothing true or clear or certain respecting his power and office, yet there remained among them a persuasion that a Redeemer had been promised by God to the fathers. It may yet be asked, Calvin says, as Adam did not fall before the creation of the world, how was it that Christ had been appointed the Redeemer, for a remedy is posterior to the disease; and his reply is that this is to be referred to God's foreknowledge, for doubtless God, before he created man, foresaw that he would not stand long in his integrity, and hence he ordained, according to his wonderful wisdom and goodness, that Christ should be the Redeemer to deliver the lost race of man from ruin, for herein shines forth more fully the unspeakable goodness of God, that he anticipated our disease by the remedy of his grace and provided a restoration to life before the first man had fallen into death, on which subject he refers the reader who wishes for more to his Institutes. Included in the words about manifestation, Calvin thinks, is not only the personal appearance of Christ but also the proclamation of the Gospel, for by the coming of Christ God executed what he had decreed, and what he had obscurely indicated to the fathers is now clearly and plainly made known to us by the Gospel; and he says this was done at the last times, meaning the same as when Paul says in the fullness of time, for it was the mature season and the full time which God in his counsel had appointed. He does not exclude the fathers, to whom the promise had not been useless, Calvin says, but as God has favoured us more than them he intimates that the greater the amplitude of grace towards us, the more reverence and ardour and care are required of us. On the last of these verses Calvin says the manifestation of Christ refers not to all indiscriminately but belongs to those only on whom he by the Gospel shines, and that here is shortly expressed what faith is, since God is incomprehensible and faith could never reach to him except it had an immediate regard to Christ. There are two reasons why faith could not be in God except Christ intervened as a Mediator, Calvin says: first, the greatness of the divine glory must be taken into account, and at the same time the littleness of our capacity, our acuteness being very far from capable of ascending so high as to comprehend God, so that all knowledge of God without Christ is a vast abyss which immediately swallows up all our thoughts, a clear proof of which we have not only in the Turks and the Jews, who in the place of God worship their own dreams, but also in the Papists. Common is that axiom of the schools, that God is the object of faith, Calvin says: thus of hidden majesty, Christ being overlooked, they largely and refinedly speculate, but with what success, since they entangle themselves in astounding dotages, so that there is no end to their wanderings, for faith as they think is nothing else but an imaginative speculation; let us therefore remember that Christ is not in vain called the image of God, but that this name is given to him for this reason, because God cannot be known except in him. The second reason is that as faith unites us to God, we shun and dread every access to him except a Mediator comes who can deliver us from fear, Calvin says, for sin, which reigns in us, renders us hateful to God and him to us, so that as soon as mention is made of God we must necessarily be filled with dread, and if we approach him his justice is like fire which will wholly consume us; it is hence evident that we cannot believe in God except through Christ, in whom God in a manner makes himself little that he might accommodate himself to our comprehension, and it is Christ alone who can tranquillise consciences so that we may dare to come in confidence to God. He adds that Christ had been raised up from the dead in order that their faith and hope, by which they were supported, might have a firm foundation, Calvin says, and hereby again is confuted the gloss respecting universal and indiscriminate faith in God, for had there been no resurrection of Christ, still God would remain in heaven, but Peter says that he would not have been believed in except Christ had risen; it is then evident that faith is something else than to behold the naked majesty of God. Rightly does Peter speak in this manner, Calvin says, for it belongs to faith to penetrate into heaven that it may find the Father there, and how could it do so except it had Christ as a leader; as then our salvation depends on the resurrection of Christ and his supreme power, faith and hope find here what can support them, for except he had by rising again triumphed over death and held now the highest sovereignty to protect us by his power, what would become of us, exposed to so great a power as that of our enemies and to such violent attacks.

Albert Barnes says the word precious is one which would be applied to that which is worth much, which is costly, and that the meaning here is that the blood of Christ had a value above silver and gold: it was worth more in itself, being a more valuable thing, and in effecting our redemption, since it accomplished what silver and gold could not do, the universe having nothing more valuable to offer, of which we can conceive, than the blood of the Son of God. As of a lamb means of Christ regarded as a lamb offered for sacrifice, Barnes says, and only such a lamb, without blemish and without spot, was allowed to be offered in sacrifice, which was required both because it was proper that man should offer that which was regarded as perfect in its kind and because only that would be a proper symbol of the great sacrifice which was to be made by the Son of God, the idea being thus kept up from age to age that he of whom all these victims were the emblems would be perfectly pure. On the following verse Barnes says that it was foreordained or predetermined that he should be the great atoning Sacrifice for sin, the sense being that the plan was formed and the arrangements made for the atonement before the world was created; before the foundation of the world means from eternity, before man was formed, before the earth was made, before any of the material universe was brought into being, before the angels were created. It follows from this verse, Barnes says, that the atonement was not an afterthought on the part of God, since it entered into his plan when he made the world and was revolved in his purposes from eternity; that it was not a device to supply a defect in the system, that is, it was not adopted because the system did not work well or because God had been disappointed, being arranged before man was created and when none but God could know whether he would stand or fall; and that the creation of the earth must have had some reference to this plan of redemption, and that plan must have been regarded as in itself so glorious and so desirable that it was deemed best to bring the world into existence that the plan might be developed, though it would involve the certainty that the race would fall and that many would perish. It was, on the whole, more wise and benevolent that the race should be created with a certainty that they would apostatise, Barnes concludes, than it would be that the race should not be created and the plan of salvation be unknown to distant worlds. On the last of these verses Barnes says faith is sometimes represented particularly as exercised in God and sometimes in Christ, and that it is always a characteristic of true religion that a man has faith in God; God gave Christ glory by exalting him at his own right hand in heaven, and by raising up the Lord Jesus and exalting him to heaven he has laid the foundation of confidence in his promises and of the hope of eternal life. Charles Ellicott says precious means not much prized by us but costly, precious in itself, opposed to the perishableness of gold and silver, and notes that it is not Jesus but Christ, that is the Messiah, since no price short of the blood, that is the death, of the Messiah could free the Jews from the thraldom of their vain conversation. How Christ's death freed them from it is not explained here, Ellicott says, but we may give a twofold explanation as we did of his resurrection being our regeneration: historically it did so, because when they came to realise that their Messiah could only reach his glories through suffering it gave them a new insight into the whole meaning of the system under which they had been brought up; and it did also, doubtless, in a more mysterious way such as we cannot imagine, procure in God's sight their emancipation, the following verses showing that Peter is thinking more of the theological than of the phenomenal side of the occurrence. We might roughly paraphrase the next clause by, as of a sacrificial victim to the sufficiency of whose offering no exception can be taken, Ellicott says, and the word as shows that in Peter's mind the notion of a sacrifice in reference to the atonement was only a simile or metaphor, just as it was with the notion of ransom; once more observe that the sacrifice was offered to effect a redemption which for the readers had already taken place. The primary thought in mentioning a lamb is of course that of sacrifice, Ellicott says, but when we come to consider why that particular sacrificial animal was named rather than another it is no doubt for two reasons: first, because of the whiteness, the helplessness, the youth, the innocence and patience which make it a natural symbol of our Lord; and the second reason is to be found in Peter's own life, since the first thing that we know in his history was a putting together of those two words, Messiah and the Lamb, and neither he nor John ever forgot that cry of the Baptist, which they no doubt understood to refer not primarily to the Paschal or any other sacrifice but to the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah, and perhaps to the offering of Isaac. There is a sharp contrast intended between the two clauses of the next verse, Ellicott says, and in the Greek the tenses are different: who had been foreknown, indeed, before the foundation of the world, but for your benefit was only pointed out at the end of the times; Peter is returning once more to the great argument of the earlier verses, as though he said, do not treat your share in the gospel liberation as if it were at best a piece of good luck, and so learn to despise it, neither think of it as if Paul and Silvanus were preaching to you a novel invention at discord with the spirit of the old covenant under which you were bred, for God knew from all eternity who was to be his Messiah and his Lamb, but for your sakes the particular and personal declaration of him was reserved till now. The grammatical antecedent of the relative is not lamb but Christ, Ellicott says, and the word for foreordained is literally foreknown, only with the additional notion of coming to a decision, so that we see Peter's doctrine has not changed since the great day of Pentecost; the foreknowledge includes not only the knowledge and decision that Jesus should be the Christ but that the Christ's history should be what it was, and this seems to involve not only the doctrine that the Incarnation was no mere episode consequent upon the Fall of man, but also the doctrine that before the foundation of the world God had foreknown, and predecided to allow, the Fall itself. Was manifested means unambiguously shown, pointed out, Ellicott says, and the context shows that it does not simply mean the visible life of the Incarnate Word among men, but that the Messiah and Lamb of God was pointed out as being identical with the Man Jesus, and this was the work of John the Baptist, to say of the particular Person whom he saw walking by Jordan, Behold the Lamb; so the Baptist himself described his mission, that the whole purpose of his coming was that he might be manifested, singled out and shown to Israel. In these last times means not merely in modern times or lately but at the end of the times, Ellicott says, showing Peter's belief that the end of the world was not far distant. On the last of these verses Ellicott says the sentence is joined on to the foregoing just as earlier, the relative might be rendered by and you, and the clause adds a kind of proof of the foregoing statement drawn from the result of God's manifestation of Christ to them, as though he said, this Christian doctrine is no innovation, nothing to lead you away from the God of our fathers, since that same God had had the scheme in his thoughts from the beginning and it is in that same God that you have been led thereby to believe. There is a better supported and more forcible reading, who through him are faithful towards God, Ellicott says, which combines the ideas of believing, that is putting the whole trust in God, and of loyal inward observance of him; and if any one asks whether it be possible to say that Hebrew men only came to believe in God through the revelation of Christ, we must answer by pointing to the whole scope of the Epistle to the Hebrews, and especially to the place where it is not faith in Christ but faith in a living God which they are warned not to abandon, and to the place where faith toward God is part of the word of the beginning of Christ. These clauses give the historical facts which had led them, through Christ, to a living faith in God, Ellicott says, and though the thought is common with Paul, Peter was familiar with it years before Paul's conversion, as appears in his Pentecost sermon, which also shows what he means by giving him glory, not to be confined to the Ascension though that is the prominent thought, since the glory was already partly given in the Resurrection. The rendering that your faith might be is inexact and obscures the connection, Ellicott says: literally it is, so that your faith and hope is toward God, that is to say, your faith and hope does not stop short in Jesus; and Hammond seems quite right in paraphrasing, who by believing on him are far from departing from the God of Israel but do indeed the more firmly believe and depend on him as that omnipotent God who hath raised Christ from the dead. The co-equal Son is less than the Father, Ellicott says, and we should terribly mistake the meaning of the gospel were we content to rest in the love of Christ himself without accepting his revelation of the Father; this is the living hope of the earlier verse, brought about by Christ's resurrection. Some of the German commentators translate, so that your faith may be also hope in God, Ellicott notes, which has nothing ungrammatical in it but does not suit the context so well. A.T. Robertson says Peter here applies the old adjective for precious to Christ as he applied a stronger form of it earlier to the testing of faith, and that the blood of anyone is precious or costly far above gold or silver, but that of Jesus immeasurably more so. The word for lamb occurs in the Greek Old Testament of the lamb prescribed for the passover sacrifice, Robertson says, and John the Baptist applies it to Jesus, while it occurs also in the Acts in a quotation from Isaiah, and undoubtedly both the Baptist and Peter have this passage in mind; elsewhere in the New Testament another word is used of Christ, and Jesus is the Paschal Lamb, Peter seeing clearly that it was by the blood of Christ that we are redeemed from sin. Without blemish means without spot as the paschal lamb had to be, Robertson says, and without spot means without stain. Who was foreknown indeed is a perfect passive participle of an old verb agreeing with Christ, Robertson says, and the precise curious phrase before the foundation of the world occurs in the Saviour's mouth in John of his preincarnate state with the Father, as here and in Ephesians, the noun coming from a verb and originally meaning the laying of the foundation of a house; but was manifested is a first aorist ingressive passive participle referring to the Incarnation in contrast with the pre-existence of Christ, and at the end of the times uses a plural doubtless referring to successive periods in human history until the fullness of the time came, while for your sake is proof of God's love and not of their desert or worth. On the last of these verses Robertson says the accusative stands in apposition, giving the through him believers in God, that the participles for raised and gave glory agree with God, and that Peter's speech in the Acts about God glorifying Jesus carries the same idea; the construction that follows is used in the New Testament for either purpose or usually result, and here result is more probable than design.

Adam Clarke says the blood is the valuable blood, how valuable neither is nor could be stated, and that the lamb is such as was required for a sin-offering to God, the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world, without blemish in himself and without spot from the world, being perfectly pure in his soul and righteous in his life. On the following verse Clarke says foreordained means foreknown, appointed in the Divine purpose to be sent into the world because infinitely approved by the Divine justice, and that before the foundation of the world means before the law was given or any sacrifice prescribed by it, since its whole sacrificial system was appointed in reference to this foreappointed Lamb and consequently from him derived all its significance and virtue. The phrase for the foundation of the world occurs often in the New Testament, Clarke says, and is supposed by some learned men and good critics to signify the commencement of the Jewish state, and perhaps it may have this meaning in several places; but if we take it here in its common signification, the creation of universal nature, then it shows that God, foreseeing the fall and ruin of man, appointed the remedy that was to cure the disease. It may here have a reference to the opinion of the Jewish doctors, Clarke adds, who maintain that seven things existed before the creation of the world, one of which was the Messiah; and the last times mean the Gospel dispensation, so called because never to be succeeded by any other. On the last of these verses Clarke says the clause is supposed to refer to the Gentiles, who never knew the true God till they heard the preaching of the Gospel, the Jews having known him long before, while the Gentiles had everything to learn when the first preachers of the Gospel arrived amongst them; God gave him glory by raising him to his right hand, where as a Prince and a Saviour he gives repentance and remission of sins, that their faith in the fulfilment of all his promises, and their hope of eternal glory, might be in God, who is unchangeable in his counsels and infinite in his mercies. John Wesley says that all our faith and hope proceed from the power of his resurrection, that God gave him glory at his ascension, and that without Christ we should only dread God, whereas through him we believe, hope and love.

debates: Which lamb is meant: Calvin says the allusion is especially to the Paschal lamb and makes the comparison of reality with type the profit of reading the Law; Ellicott traces it instead to the Baptist's cry, which he says Peter and John understood of the suffering servant in Isaiah rather than of the passover; Robertson holds that both the Baptist and Peter had that prophecy in mind while granting the word is the paschal one; Barnes and Clarke keep to the requirement of an unblemished victim

What was manifested at the end of the times: Robertson takes the participle of the Incarnation, in contrast with the pre-existence just named; Ellicott denies that it means the visible life of the Incarnate Word at all, holding that the Messiah was pointed out as identical with the man Jesus, which was the Baptist's errand; Calvin includes both the personal appearance of Christ and the proclamation of the Gospel

How foreordination stands to the Fall: Calvin raises the objection that a remedy is posterior to the disease and answers from foreknowledge, that God provided a restoration before the first man had fallen; Ellicott concludes that God had foreknown and predecided to allow the Fall itself, and that the Incarnation was no episode consequent upon it; Barnes concludes that it was more wise and benevolent to create the race with a certainty of apostasy than not to create it and leave the plan of salvation unknown to distant worlds

Who are said to believe through him: Clarke supposes the Gentiles are meant, who never knew the true God till the preaching came; Ellicott meets the objection that Hebrews cannot be said to believe in God only through Christ by appealing to the letter to the Hebrews; Calvin holds generally that faith could never reach an incomprehensible God without the Mediator
outliers: Ellicott's insistence that the word as makes sacrifice, like ransom, no more than a simile in the Apostle's mind
Calvin's charge that the schools, taking God as the object of faith and overlooking Christ, speculate on hidden majesty and entangle themselves in astounding dotages
Calvin's saying that in Christ God in a manner makes himself little, to accommodate himself to our comprehension
Calvin's argument that had Christ not risen God would still remain in heaven, yet Peter says he would not have been believed in
Clarke's report of the rabbinic opinion that seven things existed before the creation of the world, of which the Messiah was one
Ellicott's warning that we should terribly mistake the gospel were we content to rest in the love of Christ without accepting his revelation of the Father

22.pericope_label: Love one another fervently, having been begotten again of incorruptible seed by the living word of God, for all flesh is grass but the word abides

schools.summary: John Gill says the apostle passes to another exhortation, namely to brotherly love, the ground of which he makes to be the purification of their souls, which supposes that they had been impure; and indeed their whole persons, souls and bodies, were so by nature, even all the members of their bodies and all the powers and faculties of their souls. It is internal purity, purity of the heart, that is here particularly respected, Gill says, though not to the exclusion of outward purity, for where there is the former there will be the latter, but there may be an external purity where there is not the inward one; this the apostle ascribes to the saints themselves, but not without the grace of God, the blood of Christ and the operations of his Spirit, since they are said to purify themselves inasmuch as, having the grace of faith bestowed on them, they were enabled under the influences of the Spirit of God to exercise it on the blood of Christ, which cleanses from all sin. Being born again, as they were of God according to his abundant mercy, by the resurrection of Christ, Gill says, and therefore seeing they were brethren in a spiritual relation they ought to love as brethren, being children of the same Father, belonging to the same family and household, having the same spirit and the same nature and disposition, being members one of another and heirs of the same grace and glory; and not only so, but they were taught of God their Father in regeneration to love one another. All men, as born of corruptible seed, are frail, mortal and perishing, Gill says: they spring up like grass and look beautiful for a while but are very weak and tender, and in a little time they are cut down by death and wither away, and while they live are in a good measure nothing but grass in another form, since the flesh they eat is grass turned into it; and this mortality is not only the case of wicked men, as the Jews interpret the word, but of good men, even of the prophets and preachers of the Gospel, and yet the word of God spoken by them continues for ever. Though men die, and ministers of the word too, and everything in the world is uncertain, unstable, fleeting and passing away, and whatever change has been in the ordinances of divine service, Gill says, yet the word of the Lord, the Gospel of Christ, is settled for ever and will never pass away. John Calvin says Erasmus badly renders the words as who have purified, for Peter does not declare what they had done but reminds them of what they ought to do; the participle is indeed in the past tense but may be rendered as a gerund, by purifying, the meaning being that their souls would not be capable of receiving grace until they were purified, by which our uncleanness is proved. The order here is similar to what is often found in Scripture, Calvin says: purification is mentioned before regeneration, as being the most visible and the effect, and then what goes before it as being in a manner the cause; but that he might not seem to ascribe to us the power of purifying our souls, he immediately adds the Spirit, as though he had said, your souls are to be purified, but as ye cannot do this, offer them to God, that he may take away your filth by his Spirit. He only mentions souls, Calvin says, though they needed to be cleansed also from the defilements of the flesh, as Paul bids the Corinthians, but as the principal uncleanness is within and necessarily draws with it that which is outward, Peter was satisfied with mentioning only the former, as though he had said that not outward actions only ought to be corrected but the very hearts ought to be thoroughly reformed. He afterwards points out the manner, Calvin says, for purity of soul consists in obedience to God, the truth being taken for the rule which God prescribes to us in the Gospel; nor does he speak only of works, but rather faith holds here the primacy, as Paul specially teaches that faith is that by which we obey God, and as Peter in the Acts bestows on it this eulogy, that God by it purifies the heart. He briefly reminds us what God especially requires in our life and the mark to which all our endeavours should be directed, Calvin says, as Paul makes the perfection of the faithful to consist in love; and this is what we ought the more carefully to notice, because the world makes its own sanctity to consist of the veriest trifles and almost overlooks this the chief thing, as we see how the Papists weary themselves beyond measure with a thousand invented superstitions while the last thing is that love which God especially commends. He calls it unfeigned, Calvin says, for nothing is more difficult than to love our neighbours in sincerity, since the love of ourselves rules, which is full of hypocrisy, and besides, every one measures the love he shows to others by his own advantage and not by the rule of doing good; and he adds the word for fervently, for the more slothful we are by nature, the more ought every one to stimulate himself to fervour and earnestness, and that not only once but more and more daily. Here is another reason for an exhortation, Calvin says, that since they were new men and born again of God it behoved them to form a life worthy of God and of their spiritual regeneration; the object of Peter was to teach us that we cannot be Christians without regeneration, for the Gospel is not preached that it may be only heard by us but that it may, as a seed of immortal life, altogether reform our hearts. Most commentators represent the seed as the word, Calvin says, but the construction does not admit this, the words being, having been begotten from a seed, not corruptible but incorruptible, through the living word of God: the seed denotes evidently the vital principle of grace, the new nature, the restored image of God, the same with what John means when he says that his seed remaineth in him, and then the word is set forth as the means or instrument by which this seed is implanted. The living here does not mean life-giving, as some interpret it, Calvin says, but stands opposed to what ceases to be valid, and for ever abiding more fully expresses its meaning; the metaphor in the parable of the sower is quite different, for the word there is compared to a seed sown on bad or good ground, but here the turning of a bad into a good ground is the subject, and in this process the word is employed as an instrument. Moreover the corruptible seed is set in opposition to God's word, Calvin says, in order that the faithful might know that they ought to renounce their former nature, and that it might be more evident how great is the difference between the children of Adam who are born only into the world and the children of God who are renewed into a heavenly life; but as the construction of the Greek text is doubtful, we may read the living word of God as well as the word of the living God, and as the latter reading is less forced he prefers it. He aptly quotes the passage from Isaiah to prove both clauses, Calvin says, that is, to make it evident how fading and miserable is the first birth of man and how great is the grace of the new birth; for as the Prophet there speaks of the restoration of the Church, to prepare the way for it he reduces men to nothing lest they should flatter themselves. He knows that the words are wrongly turned by some to another sense, Calvin says: some explain them of the Assyrians, as though the Prophet said that there was no reason for the Jews to fear so much from flesh, which is like a fading flower, and others think that the vain confidence which the Jews reposed in human aids is reproved; but the Prophet himself disproves both these views by adding that the people were as grass, for he expressly condemns the Jews for vanity, to whom he promised restoration in the name of the Lord. This then is what he has already said, Calvin continues, that until their own emptiness has been shown to men they are not prepared to receive the grace of God; and as it was difficult to believe that man, in whom so much excellency appears, is like grass, the Prophet made a kind of concession, as though he had said, be it indeed that flesh has some glory, but lest that should dazzle your eyes, know that the flower soon withers. Many think that this refers only to the outward man, Calvin says, but they are mistaken, for we must consider the comparison between God's word and man: if he meant only the body and what belongs to the present life, he ought to have said in the second place that the soul was far more excellent, but what he sets in opposition to the grass and its flower is the word of God, and it then follows that in man nothing but vanity is found. The Prophet does not show what the word of God is in itself but what we ought to think of it, Calvin says, for since man is vanity in himself it remains that he ought to seek life elsewhere; hence Peter ascribes power and efficacy to God's word so that it can confer on us what is real, solid and eternal, and however fading the nature of man is, yet he is made eternal by the word, for he is remoulded and becomes a new creature. He first reminds us that when the word of God is mentioned we are very foolish if we imagine it to be remote from us in the air or in heaven, Calvin says, for we ought to know that it has been revealed to us by the Lord; and what then is this word of the Lord which gives us life, even the Law, the Prophets, the Gospel, since those who wander beyond these limits of revelation find nothing but the impostures of Satan and his dotages. We ought the more carefully to notice this, Calvin says, because impious and Luciferian men, craftily allowing to God's word its own honour, at the same time attempt to draw us away from the Scriptures, as that unprincipled man Agrippa, who highly extols the eternity of God's word and yet treats with scurrility the Prophets, and thus indirectly laughs to scorn the Word of God; no mention is here made of the word which lies hid in the bosom of God but of that which has proceeded from his mouth and has come to us, and God designed by the Apostles and Prophets to speak to us, their mouths being the mouth of the only true God. There is here besides no common eulogy on preaching, Calvin says, for Peter declares that what is preached is the life-giving word: God alone is indeed he who regenerates us, but for that purpose he employs the ministry of men, and on this account Paul glories that the Corinthians had been spiritually begotten by him; it is certain that those who plant and those who water are nothing, but whenever God is pleased to bless their labour he makes their doctrine efficacious by the power of his Spirit, and the voice which is in itself mortal is made an instrument to communicate eternal life.

Matthew Henry says the apostle, having given an account of the excellency of the renewed spiritual man as born again, not of corruptible but incorruptible seed, now sets before us the vanity of the natural man, taking him with all his ornaments and advantages about him; and nothing can make him a solid substantial being but the being born again of the incorruptible seed, the word of God, which will transform him into a most excellent creature, whose glory will not fade like a flower but shine like an angel, and this word is daily set before us in the preaching of the gospel. Man, in his utmost flourish and glory, is still a withering, fading, dying creature, Henry says: take him singly, all flesh is grass, and in his entrance into the world, in his life and in his fall, he is similar to grass; take him in all his glory, even this is as the flower of grass, for his wit, beauty, strength, vigour, wealth and honour are but as the flower of grass, which soon withers and dies away. The only way to render this perishing creature solid and incorruptible is for him to entertain and receive the word of God, Henry says, for this remains everlasting truth and, if received, will preserve him to everlasting life and abide with him for ever; and the prophets and apostles preached the same doctrine, since this word which Isaiah and others delivered in the Old Testament is the same which the apostles preached in the New.

Albert Barnes says the apostles were never afraid of referring to human agency as having an important part in saving the soul, since no one is made pure without personal intention or effort, any more than one becomes accomplished or learned without personal exertion; one of the leading effects of the agency of the Holy Spirit is to excite us to make efforts for our own salvation, and there is no true piety which is not the fair result of culture, as really as the learning of a scholar or the harvest of the farmer. The amount of effort which we make in purifying our souls is usually also the measure of our attainments in religion, Barnes says, and no one can expect to have any true piety beyond the amount of effort which he makes to be conformed to God, any more than one can expect wealth or fame or learning without exertion. Obeying the truth means that their yielding to the requirements of truth and to its fair influence on their minds has been the means of their becoming pure, Barnes says, the truth referred to being that revealed in the gospel; and through the Spirit means by the agency of the Holy Spirit, whose office it is to apply truth to the mind, for however precious the truth may be and however adapted to secure certain results on the soul, it will never produce those effects without the influences of the Holy Spirit. The phrase with a pure heart fervently means that it should be genuine love proceeding from a heart in which there is no guile or hypocrisy, and that it should be intense affection, not cold and formal but ardent and strong, Barnes says; and if there is any reason why we should love true Christians at all, there is the same reason why our attachment should be intense. Barnes draws out several points: that truth was at the foundation of their piety, there being no religion in the world which is not the fair development of truth; that they became Christians as the result of obeying the truth, so that religion is always of the nature of obedience, consisting in yielding to what is true and right, and would take place in all men if there were no voluntary resistance; that the agency was that of the Holy Ghost, since truth is adapted in itself to a certain end as seed is adapted to produce a harvest, but will no more of itself produce its appropriate effect on the soul than seed will produce a harvest without rains and dews and suns, no man having ever been converted by the mere effect of truth any more than seed germinates when laid on a hard rock; and that the effect is to produce love to all who are Christians, which is as certain evidence that the seed of truth has germinated as the green blade that peeps up through the earth. Hence, Barnes says, truth is of inestimable value, being as valuable as religion itself; error and falsehood are mischievous in the same degree, since no true religion is the fair result of error; if a system or doctrine cannot be defended by truth it should be at once abandoned; and we should avoid the places where error is taught. On the following verse Barnes says that not of corruptible seed means not by virtue of any descent from human parents, as Doddridge renders it, the result of such a begetting being only corruption and decay, since we are begotten only to die; and of incorruptible means by truth, communicating a living principle to the soul which can never decay, it being the uniform doctrine of the Scriptures that divine truth is made the instrument of quickening the soul into spiritual life. The expression which liveth and abideth for ever may refer either to God as living for ever or to the word of God as being for ever true, Barnes says, critics being about equally divided and the Greek bearing either construction; most of the recent critics incline to the latter opinion, among them Rosenmuller, Doddridge, Bloomfield, Wolf, Macknight and Clarke, but it seems to him that the more natural construction refers it to God as ever-living, and this agrees well with the connexion, the idea being that as God is everliving, that which is produced directly by him in the human soul by the instrumentality of truth may be expected also to endure for ever. On the quotation Barnes says the connexion is that the apostle had been contrasting that which is begotten by man with that which is begotten by God in reference to its permanency, so that it was natural to dwell upon the feeble, frail, decaying nature of man in contrast with God; the comparison of a human being with grass or with flowers is very beautiful and quite common in the Scriptures, turning on the fact that the grass or the flower, however green or beautiful, soon loses its freshness and is cut down. Barnes quotes the psalm on man's days as grass and the fuller passage in Isaiah, and adds that the sentiment is beautifully imitated in the speech of Wolsey, that this is the state of man, who today puts forth the tender leaves of hope, tomorrow blossoms and bears his blushing honours thick upon him, and the third day comes a frost, a killing frost, which nips his root and then he falls. All the glory of man means all that man prides himself on, his wealth, rank, talents, beauty, learning, splendour of equipage or apparel, Barnes says, and the word rendered grass properly denotes herbage, that which furnishes food for animals, so that probably Isaiah referred rather to the appearance of a meadow or a field with mingled grass and flowers, constituting a beautiful landscape, than to mere grass. The word of the Lord endureth for ever means it is unmoved, fixed, permanent, Barnes says: amidst all the revolutions on earth, the fading glories of natural objects and the wasting strength of man, his truth remains unaffected, its beauty never fades and its power is never enfeebled, the gospel system being as lovely now as when it was first revealed and having as much power to save as when first applied to a human heart. Let us learn habitually to reflect on our feebleness and frailty, Barnes says: the rose that blossoms on the cheek of youth may wither as soon as any other rose, the brightness of the eye may become dim as readily as the beauty of a field covered with flowers, and the darkness of death may come over the brow of manliness as readily as night settles down on the landscape; but amidst these changes it is cheering to think that the word of the Lord abides, and that the traits drawn on the character by the religion of Christ, more lovely by far than the most delicate colouring of the lily, remain for ever, so that the beauty of religion is the only permanent beauty in the earth. Charles Ellicott says Bengel well points us to the second epistle, where in like manner Peter delights to exhibit gradations of grace, obeying the truth here corresponding to knowledge there with its consequences of self-mastery, endurance and reverence, after which we pass on to love of the brethren and thence, as to a higher grace, to charity. Perhaps the literal phrase in the obedience of the truth does not exactly coincide with obeying the truth, Ellicott says, as implying rather the obedience to God which the knowledge of the truth demands, since truth has a claim not only to be accepted intellectually as truth but to alter moral conduct in accordance, a doctrine which lies at the bottom of the Socratic maxim that virtue is knowledge; that maxim, however, does not sufficiently take into account the inertness of the will to act on principle, and no doubt it was under some such instinct that some copyist first added as a gloss the words, not found in the original text, through the Spirit. The first effect of such knowledge of the truth, under the Spirit's influence, is to purify the soul of selfish aims and to give it that desire for the benefit of the community rather than self which is here described as love of the brethren, Ellicott says. The epithet unfeigned in itself would suggest that Peter was uneasy about the depth of their brotherly kindness, Ellicott says, the brotherly kindness being here as usual attachment to other members of the Church, with special point added because of the notion of regeneration running through the whole passage; and is it not possible that some coolness had arisen between the Jewish and Gentile members of the Church, and that Peter finds it necessary to remind the former that they are truly brethren, sons of one Father, and that they ought not only unaffectedly to have done with all jealousy of the Gentile members but to be far beyond that, loving one another from the heart strenuously, the word pure not being part of the original text and interrupting the run of the sentence. On the following verse Ellicott says the rendering should be, having been begotten again, it being not part of the exhortation as though they had still to be thus begotten but assigning the moral grounds for the exhortation, and might be rendered, seeing that ye have been begotten again. Not of corruptible seed means not of the seed of Abraham but of the seed of God, Ellicott says, the argument being that they must learn not to be selfish or arrogant as being of the chosen race, but to have a true brotherly feeling and earnest love for the Gentile converts and for those who like Paul are specially working for the Gentiles, because their inheritance of the promised salvation is grounded not on Abrahamic descent but on spiritual regeneration, in which matter the Gentile converts are their equals; and that this was the doctrine of Peter is certain from his speech at the Council of Jerusalem, that God put no difference between us and them, having purified their hearts by faith. Seed is more literally the act of sowing or engendering, which sowing is carried on through the living and abiding word of God, this word of God being the actual seed sown, Ellicott says: the seed of all existence is the spoken Word of God, the expressed will and meaning of creative thought, and so here, even when spoken mediately through the lips of men, it is that which begets men afresh, God creating afresh though men speak the creative word for him, just as it is he that hath made us although he does so through natural laws and human powers. The word of God here is no doubt the preaching of the gospel, Ellicott says, but especially as it would seem the preaching of the Resurrection or of the sufferings and glories of Messiah, the truth of the last verse; incorruptible finds a more energetic paraphrase here in living and abiding, the words for ever not being part of the true text. On the quotation Ellicott says the citation varies between the Hebrew and the Greek in the kind of way which shows that the writer was familiar with both, but that the passage is by no means quoted only to support the assertion, in itself ordinary enough, that the Word of the Lord abideth for ever: it is always impossible to grasp the meaning of an Old Testament quotation in the mouth of a Hebrew without taking into account the context of the original, and nothing is commoner than to omit purposely the very words which contain the whole point of the quotation. These sentences in Isaiah stand in the forefront of the herald's proclamation of the return of God to Sion, always interpreted of the establishment of the Messianic kingdom, Ellicott says, and this proclamation comprises words which Peter has purposely omitted which contain the point of the quotation, namely, the Spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it, surely the people, that is Israel, is grass. He quotes Bishop Lowth on the original passage, that the import of the proclamation is that the people, the flesh, is of a vain temporary nature, that all its glory fadeth and is soon gone, but that the Word of God endureth for ever, which is a plain opposition of the flesh to the Spirit, of the carnal Israel to the spiritual, of the temporary Mosaic economy to the eternal Christian dispensation. Here then Peter is quoting one of the greatest of Messianic prophecies, Ellicott says, and his Hebrew readers would at once understand the Hebrew method of the quotation and see that he was calling attention to the absolute equality of Jew and Gentile there proclaimed: generation of the corruptible seed, physical descent from Abraham, was the glory of the flesh, and he observes that according to the best text Peter does not follow the Greek version and insert of man but follows the Hebrew and says all the glory thereof, that is of the flesh; on this the Spirit of the Lord had breathed and the merely fleshly glory had withered like grass. But the word of our God, which, mark well, Peter purposely changes into the Word of the Lord, that is of Jesus Christ, incidentally showing his Hebrew readers that he believed Jesus Christ to be our God, this abideth for ever, Ellicott says: the engendering by this is imperishable, involving a privilege which is not, like that of the Jewish blood, transitory, and no further revelation will ever level up the unregenerate to be the equals of the regenerate, while in this regeneration all flesh share alike, the teaching of the Baptist being here again apparent. The last words are an incorrect rendering of the original tense, Ellicott says, and literally run, and this is the word which was preached unto you; the whole magnificent peroration of this paragraph, as of the last, leads up to this, that in the opinion of Peter the Gospel as delivered by Paul and his followers, the Gospel of equality, or rather of unity, between Jew and Gentile in Jesus Christ, was the living and supreme abiding revelation of the will of God, and well may the Tubingen school wish to disprove the genuineness of this Epistle. A.T. Robertson says the participle for purifying is a perfect active of an old verb from the adjective for pure, used here with souls where James uses hearts, as also of moral cleansing in John's epistle, and he notes the ceremonial sense of the word in the Greek Old Testament and elsewhere. In your obedience repeats the idea used earlier of children of obedience, Robertson says, and to the truth is an objective genitive, with which compare the sayings about sanctification in the truth, since there is cleansing power in the truth of God in Christ; unfeigned is a late and rare double compound found here alone in Peter, and no other kind of brotherly love is worth having, while from the heart fervently uses a late adverb found in inscriptions, in Polybius and in the Greek Old Testament. Having been begotten again is a perfect passive participle of the verb used earlier, Robertson says, and not of corruptible seed is an ablative marking the source, the noun for seed coming from the verb to sow and occurring here only in the New Testament; through the word of God is the gospel message, and the present participles for liveth and abideth can be taken with either God or word, both being used of God in Daniel, so that either construction makes sense here. The quotation is partly like the Greek version and partly like the Hebrew, Robertson says, and the best manuscripts read thereof after glory rather than of man, while the verbs for withereth and falleth are timeless aorists.

Adam Clarke says that having purified their souls in obeying the truth, by believing in Christ Jesus through the influence and teaching of the Spirit, and giving full proof of it by unfeigned love to the brethren, they love one another with a pure heart fervently. These persons first heard the truth, that is the Gospel, so called in a great variety of places in the New Testament because it contains the truth without mixture of error and is the truth and substance of all the preceding dispensations by which it was typified; secondly they obeyed that truth by believing on him who came into the world to save sinners; thirdly, through this believing on the Son of God their hearts were purified by the word of truth applied to them by the Holy Spirit; and fourthly, the love of God being shed abroad in their hearts by the Holy Ghost, they loved the brethren with pure hearts fervently, intensely or continually, the full proof that their brotherly love was unfeigned. Being born again, Clarke says, for being born of Abraham's seed will not avail to the entering of the kingdom of heaven; not of corruptible seed, by no human generation or earthly means, but of incorruptible, a divine and heavenly principle which is not liable to decay nor to be affected by the changes and chances to which all sublunary things are exposed; by the word of God, that is by the doctrine of the living God, which remaineth for ever and shall never change, any more than the source whence it proceeds. Earthly seeds, earthly productions and earthly generations shall fail and perish like the grass and flowers of the field, Clarke says, for the grass withereth and the flower falleth off, though in the ensuing spring and summer they may put forth new verdure and bloom; but the doctrine delivered by God concerning Christ endureth for ever, having at all times and in all seasons the same excellence and the same efficacy. He quotes Macknight that this is a quotation from Isaiah where the preaching of the Gospel is foretold, and recommended from the consideration that everything which is merely human, and among the rest the noblest races of mankind with all their glory and grandeur, their honour, riches, beauty, strength and eloquence, as also the arts which men have invented and the works they have executed, shall decay as the flowers of the field, but the Gospel, called by the prophet the word of the Lord, shall be preached while the world standeth. All human schemes of salvation and plans for the melioration of the moral state of man shall come to naught, Clarke says, and the doctrine of Christ crucified, though a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, shall be alone the power of God for salvation to every soul that believeth. Clarke then appends a long account of the nature and properties of gold, since the apostle mentioned gold tried in the fire earlier in the chapter: gold is defined by chemists to be the most perfect, the most ductile, the most tenacious and the most unchangeable of all metals, with a specific gravity of about nineteen and a third, and when exposed to the action of the fire it becomes red hot before it melts but in melting suffers no alteration, having been kept in a state of fusion for several months in the furnace of a glass house without suffering the smallest change. In the focus of a very powerful burning glass, however, it becomes volatilised and partially vitrified, Clarke says, so that we may say with the apostle that though gold is tried by the fire and abides the action of all culinary fires, yet it perisheth by the celestial fire and the solar influence; this is but a late discovery, and previously to it a philosopher would have ridiculed Peter for saying, gold that perisheth. He goes on to report that one grain of gold may be so extended by its malleability as to be divided into two millions of parts, that a grain and a half beaten into leaves an inch square would produce twenty-five millions of little squares each distinctly visible without glasses, and that one pound of gold would be sufficient to gild a silver wire long enough to encompass the whole terraqueous globe, or to extend twenty-five thousand miles. John Wesley says that having purified their souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit, who bestows upon them freely both obedience and purity of heart and unfeigned love of the brethren, they are to go on to still higher degrees of love: love one another fervently, with the most strong and tender affection, and yet with a pure heart, pure from any spot of unholy desire or inordinate passion. All flesh means every human creature is transient and withering as grass, Wesley says, and all the glory of it is his wisdom, strength, wealth and righteousness, while the flower is the most short-lived part of it, the grass being man and the flower his glory, which is fallen off as it were while we are speaking.

debates: What the incorruptible seed is: Calvin says most commentators make it the word but the construction forbids, the seed being the vital principle of grace and the restored image of God while the word is the instrument by which it is implanted; Barnes and Ellicott both take the word itself to be the seed sown, Ellicott holding that the seed of all existence is the spoken word of God; Clarke calls it a divine and heavenly principle

Whether living and abiding describes God or the word: Barnes reports the critics about equally divided, names Rosenmuller, Doddridge, Bloomfield, Wolf, Macknight and Clarke for the word, and himself prefers God as the more natural Greek; Calvin prefers the word of the living God as less forced; Robertson says either construction makes sense

How much the purifying is our own act: Calvin says Erasmus badly renders the participle as a statement of what they had done, since Peter reminds them what they ought to do, and that they are to offer their souls to God because they cannot cleanse them; Barnes insists the apostles were never afraid of referring to human agency, and that the effort we make is usually the measure of our attainments; Gill ascribes it to the saints themselves but not without the blood of Christ and the operations of the Spirit

What the quotation from Isaiah is for: Ellicott holds that the point lies in the words Peter purposely omitted, that the people is grass, so that the withered flesh is the carnal Israel and the passage proclaims the equality of Jew and Gentile, and notes that Peter changes the word of our God into the word of the Lord, showing he held Jesus Christ to be our God; Calvin rejects those who refer the fading flesh to the Assyrians or to Jewish confidence in human aid; Barnes and Henry take it simply of human frailty
outliers: Ellicott's textual observations that pure is no part of the text and that through the Spirit was added by a copyist as a gloss, though Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all expound it
Ellicott's conjecture that the epithet unfeigned betrays Peter's uneasiness at a coolness between the Jewish and Gentile members of the Church
Ellicott's closing remark that the Tubingen school may well wish to disprove the genuineness of this epistle

Clarke's long appendix on the chemistry of gold, with its ductility, its indifference to furnace heat and its destruction in the focus of a burning glass, offered as a late discovery vindicating the apostle's phrase about gold that perisheth
Barnes's quotation of the speech of Wolsey on the killing frost that nips a man's root when he thinks his greatness ripening
Calvin's attack on those who extol the eternity of God's word while treating the Prophets with scurrility, and so laugh the Word of God to scorn
